title: Easy to calibrate. CalBox is nice to have.
text:
So far, it's worked fine, though I wish the instructions had included how to properly dispose of the pH solutions when that time comes. I assume that means that it can go down the drain, but I have no idea what the pH solutions are made from. By reading the instructions line-by-line, it was easy to calibrate the probe. (Though it was still accurate out-of-the-box, I wanted to see how difficult it was to do). The Callbox did make this process much easier, so I like having it. The probe itself came with a small bottle of pH 7 and of pH 4 calibration solutions (good for 15 uses), plus a lanyard and user instructions. The batteries were already installed. In the larger box, we also got 8oz each of pH calibration solutions (pH 7, 4 & 10), one 4oz 3M KCL storage solution, a probe cleaning brush, and an Apera's Calbox for organizing all the solutions. The bottles were sealed in plastic bags, which was good as one of the bottles leaked a little into that bag. You have to provide distilled water to wash the probe after each use.

I've been using this pH meter on my swimming pool, and it's worked very nicely. I've also used it on my hydroponics. I appreciate that you can do a 1 to 3 point calibration so that the accuracy on the more acid or alkaline liquids is good. The accuracy is ±0.1 pH and for the temperature ±0.5˚C. The range is 0 to 14.0 pH and 0 to 50˚C or 122F (and the temperature is to compensate for how the temperature affects the pH reading). Overall, I'm very pleased with the kit.

title: Update: Still Hanging in there [Orig: Spend more money for a better product]
text:
Three years later, and I'm bumping it up a notch. It still has all the issues it had when I first reviewed it three years ago -- but, hey, three years later and it's hanging in there. The welds have held, and it remains supported by the scrap wood base I used to stabilize it. But I still take point off because to give it maximum strength and stability, you need to fabricate your own base.

Original review:

First off, this is not exactly as pictured -- it does not have four uprights, but rather two vertical loops for stacking (see other customers' reviews for photos.) That's a good thing. However, mine arrived with lousy welds, which I assume will break in fairly short order (another reviewer noted that his/hers arrived with a broken weld!) Mine also had rust spots where the uprights were attached to the fastening plates. Unfortunately I am going to be able to see exactly how long it lasts, as I need it now so I can't return it and buy something else :(

Eventually (if it lasts at all!)I am going to use longer screws to attach it to a wood base, as I think that will provide more stability on the basement laundry room floor.

title: Wish I'd known this.  Great, if it works, but it DOES NOT MEASURE EMPTY WATER.
text:
This thing is advertised to work for general liquid solutions. Unfortunately, be aware it does not read water. Yeah, you read that correctly. You need enough stuff IN the water, or it will not read the water. I use reverse osmosis water for my plants, and it is "empty."

I add nutrients to it, but it takes a LOT of stuff in the water before you get an accurate reading. To make matters worse, it will not tell you when it is doing this. You will have no idea. I suddenly thought there was something wrong with my R/O water causing it to be extremely high pH. No, it was not the water; the water was still the same old 5.5 pH it always was, but the pen COULD NOT read it properly and was telling me 8 pH.

THERE IS NO MENTION OF THIS anywhere before you purchase it. It is not mentioned in the instructions either. Therefore, I trusted the meter (which works phenomenally otherwise) and completely ruined months of work.

Additionally, I often want to water my plants with water that is at the right pH of about 6.5, but does not have ANY nutrients. This is common, called a "flush," because you don't want to keep feeding nutrients to plants that don't need it. Well, you can't measure water with this, so I can't do that.

For the high price, it works great, but it does NOT work in all situations, and they make little effort to warn you of this. Now I have to buy one that costs twice as much??? This is stupid.

So now I am left to bumble around confused using both this and the pH strips I was trying to get away from. Now I need yet another unit that will measure empty water. I had a $5 one that did it, which I threw away once I got this, thinking I would no longer need it.

This seems absurd to me. I guess I am one of the few people using reverse osmosis water or something? I think I deserve a refund or upgrade to a version that will WORK, but I doubt I'll even get a response, and if I do, the responses will just blame me instead. My ignorance isn't my fault if you don't make an effort to alert me before purchase. And don't tell me to do more research. I DID research.

title: Very compact valve, not so much BARBED connections, but does works with flexible hose.
text: This little valve is very compact compared to the typical hardware or big box store offerings with threaded connection ports. The valve is advertised as 1/2-inch, and 1/2-inch flexible hose does work on the valve's connection ends, but note that the ends aren't really all barbed like a typical barbed connection. The first ridge is barbed, the next two are square-edged ridges. So using really good hose clamps is important with this valve if you're attaching flexible hose. The barbs look like they're meant for PEX pipe to me. The valve has an inner nflowndiameter of 3/8-inch, so a minor restriction on flow, but considering the small size of the valve body that's a very minor restriction, probably negligible. The valve is advertised as "brass". There's no certification or other indications of the exact metal content, or that the valve is safe for potable water, so you will want to consider what you use the valve for based on that lack of info. For a non-potable use, it's a nice little valve.

title: Apera made good on warranty by replacing meter!!! I submitted ticket through their website
text:
I love this meter and use it every single day. I test drinking water, tap water, store-bought RO water, and fertilizer solution for my plants. It is so much more accurate and easy to read than the old liquid dropper test kit I was using before to determine pH.
One day, a little less than 6 months, it stopped working and would not turn on. I noticed other reviewers saying they tried to email Apera within their warranty time frame, but never got a response. That concerned me but I decided to give it a shot by going to their website and clicked the tab to submit a ticket (https://support.aperainst.com/support/tickets/new). The site states that for this particular meter, they guarantee the glass probe for 6 months and the electronics for 2 years.
Apera got in touch with me via email within an hour. The agent walked me through some instructions to try to troubleshoot the meter but it didn't work. She apologized sincerely for the trouble and sent a replacement meter later the very same day totally free of charge!
Please note that I don't blame Apera at all for the failure of my first meter. I purchased it in Used condition so it had undergone some sort of rough treatment that prevented Amazon from selling it at full price. That the packaging was damaged indicates perhaps the circuit board already had weak connections before it even got to me.
Fast forward to two months after I received my free replacement: my new meter is working like a charm and I still depend heavily on my pH meter. So for anyone reading this who has experienced issues with this or any other Apera product, I strongly recommend using the link I gave above rather than trying to email them directly as others have tried.
The only reason I don't give this product 5 stars is that the replacement calibration solution is costly. Other brands offer less expensive solutions which I tried. They were not compatible and the result was that the Apera meter would display a wildly fluctuating pH reading ranging from less than 1 to over 10 and back and forth. Perhaps the electrical conductivity (EC) is wrong? Anyway, I would also suggest using only the Apera-brand calibration solutions in the future.

title: Failed to give accurate PH readings for tap water.
text:
I ordered the Apera PH test unit to test water samples from our well, and from other water samples. The unit is supposed to give an accuracy level of .1, but failed in every test to get within .1 of PH in comparison to other testing methods. A laboratory test of the well water gave a PH of 6.1. Three different reagent tests were consistent with a PH in the range of 5.8 to 6.2. The Apera device consistently produced readings in the 6.7 range. After multiple comparison tests, I came to the conclusion that the unit was defective. I did contact customer support and they were responsive, but in the end unhelpful. They never seemed to accept that the unit was defective. There were a handful of e-mails and they seemed to lose track of the discussion. I did give a two-star rating because I could successfully contact customer support. The unit itself does not warrant that rating.
Before I understood that the unit was defective, I had stored the unit for about a 6 to 7 week period, exactly as instructed by the company. The tip needs to be stored in a solution of Kcl and I purchased their recommended product. I used the exact amount of Kcl as recommended, closed the cap securely on the tip and stored the device in the original product case supplied by the manufacturer. The device and case were located in a room with a stable temperature of 68-70 degrees. During that time frame, the Kcl solution leaked out of the sensor tip cover. As such, the user should beware that the cap is anything but leak proof. Never store the sensor in any position other than vertical, and do not trust the storage case to keep the protective fluid cap secure on the unit.
Finally, customer support indicated that one needs to replace the calibration samples after about every 10 to 12 calibrations. Since one needs to calibrate the unit most every time you use it, you will need to buy a supply of calibration fluids. They are not inexpensive. Those are in addition to the Kcl fluid used to store the unit which you will also need to purchase. Also note that the PH20 model does not provide one of the three standard calibration fluids. In summary, if you want to purchase this unit you will need to purchase a supply of calibration and storage fluids for continued use.

Once you figure out the right sequence, and the difference between short press and long press and what the smiley face means, things become better.

In terms of day-to-day taking a reading, this is a no-brainer. You fill the cap to the fill line (which eventually washed off after a week or so but I remember roughly where the line was) swish the water around. Turn it on, and it shows the PH in a few sections. No confusing color charts to match - I can never get those right with the test strips.

One feature which would be nice would be a backlight. Especially with hot-tubs that many tend to use in the night time. I've recalibrated a few times, but it didn't really seem to need it. title: Perfect wire connections every time
text: I do al lot of wire repair and connections and these are such a time saver. I have made over 200 wire connections with these heat shrink builtin solider connectors and so far each connection is made solid. For outdoor low voltage LED lighting these were the perfect fit and they can withstand being outdoors in the weather with out issue. Have your heat gun set to 370 and the solider just melts in the heat shrink. There is a small learning curve as you need to start at one end and then work your way up the connector so the air can escape and then the solider melts around the bare wire and fills in the small gap. It is so much easier and more reliable than twisting the wires together and saves me time in the end. Would recommend this to anyone who wants to connect two wires together.

title: I'm glad to finally have an accurate PH testing device for my winemaking.
text:
After the uncertainty of PH testing strips and the wild fluctuations of an inexpensive pen type testing device, the Apera PH20 is assuring as it quickly stabilized and gave me PH readings that made sense based on the additions that I made to my wine. The Apera PH20 Kit comes with PH7 and PH4 buffering solutions. These are used as a standard when calibrating the PH20 and must be used in the order I have listed them.

The kit did not come with storage solution, although a 3M KCL solution is recommended. The PH4 buffer can be used for storage according to the instructions but I did not feel from the tone of the instruction leaflet that this storage solution was recommended. Not knowing what storage solution to use as I was ordering my kit, I added an 8 OZ. bottle of Biopharm Electrode Storage Solution to the order. Hopefully, it's an acceptable storage solution as I have my device sitting in it now.

I used the PH20 today for the first time on a 6-gallon batch of Chianti wine that I'm making. The acidity of the wine is high and I am preparing to lessen it with the addition of potassium carbonate. Good PH and total acidity tests were needed so that I can calculate the correct amount of base chemicals to rectify the high acidity issue.

My kit also came with a lanyard, the use of which was not apparent to me. Amazon's write up for this product, however, shows a picture someone testing lake water PH with the lanyard on their wrist. Evidently, the lanyard is used as a safeguard to prevent someone dropping and losing the device in a body of water.

I'm very happy with this PH measuring device's ease of use and with the measurement accuracy. Hopefully, it will continue to give me good service for years to come.

title: Accurate and Easy to Use - But do you Really Need to Spend $50?
text:
I bought this tester mainly to verify two cheaper ones I had already. I was just not confident the ones I was using were giving me accurate readings. When I tested them with calibration solution they both read slightly off one being higher and one lower. So I decided to spend the money on a higher end model.

The Apera model seems to work very well and when tested in calibration solution is usually spot on. It has a nice LCD display which is easy to read during normal operation and is much quicker at determining the PH level versus the cheaper ones where you need to wait a while for them to stabilize and typically have much smaller and darker displays. That is the good news, however, the calibration procedure is a bit clunky compared to even the other cheaper ones I have. Partly due to the instructions which are very poorly written, hard to follow and provide contradictory information when it comes to things like storing the device. I understand it was made in China but for gosh sake, hire someone who knows how to speak and write in English to design the manual so it makes sense.

In my application PH is very important so having more than one tester is not a bad thing. But it I had to pick just one and price was not an issue....then yes, I would chose the Apera model, but by a very small margin. Mainly because it appears to be a higher quality, well made device - even though the included instructions and funky calibration procedure hold it back from a five star rating.

But in the end it is only slightly more accurate then the $10-$15 ones I already have. If the accuracy of the PH reading is that important to you and you want the best and do not care about spending $50, then the Apera is a fine choice. But if you are on a budget and are using a tester to check the PH of say swimming pool water, a cheaper model will work just fine. I would recommend getting two cheaper units from different manufacturers so you can check them against one another. You will spend about half of what it cost for the Apera. And as long as you occasionally test and re-calibrate them, you are better off with two cheaper models than the one more expensive one that does the same thing.

title: Very basic casters, only for very lightweight items
text:
These are an interesting product; they're essentially a single roller ball in a formed plastic snap-together housing. They rely on the ball rolling against the plastic housing and your surface, and can be moved "omnidirectionally" any way you like once mounted. In the package, you get eight of these "casters", as well as 8 pieces of double-sided sticky tape. They are definitely small - mini means mini; the caster is smaller than a matchbook and the ball itself is about the size of a chickpea.

Because the housing is so straightforward and basic, these aren't really appropriate for heavy-duty use or even medium-duty use. I saw another reviewer mentioned a mixer, and a standard kitchen stand mixer would definitely be way too heavy for even four of these. This would be best suited for something lighter that _can_ slide on its own, but which could use a little extra assistance. Think a metal rack of coffee pods you want to be able to move out of the way to access something behind it, for example.

I actually think these would be best suited as a mechanical part to be incorporated into a custom design more than as a fixit item for around the house. For example, this could be the third "caster" to go on a robot that has two wheels and two motors; the robot could spin in place with its wheels driving in opposite directions, and this caster would cheerfully go along for the ride.

These have the potential to mark surfaces they travel on, because they're a metal ball being pushed in with whatever weight you put on top of them. Certainly, using them on soft wood surfaces with heavy objects would be a no-go.

If "a very simple roller ball in a cheap plastic housing that's convenient to mount" sounds like what you want, this is exactly what it appears to be and you'll be happy with your new mechanical parts. If you're trying to solve some difficult household problem, though, these are probably not the solution.

[[VIDEOID:f0347e25849c67167d1b5422ed74e155]] Purchased on 10/08/2020 and it no longer accepts any calibration whatsoever as of August 2021. Reads 5.3ph in a 7.0 buffering solution, and displays Err1 when pressing the Calibration button. Note: You will need to purchase Apera Storage solution to not void the warranty, which I did in October 2020. Called customer service who said that the probe must be damaged, which I can assure (as the only one who uses it) was not by the user. Since it's past their 6 month window, they will not even look at the device, regardless of their 2 year warranty. When trying to get a 7.0 reading, the best that it's ever read was 6.1-6.2, and today I found out from customer service that it should have always read at 6.8 at minimum in a 7.0 buffering solution.
Customer service did try to 'make nice' by offering me the opportunity to re-purchase the PH20 device at $35, which they alledge is "half-price" on the device. Shocking, it's *still* listed at $50 on Amazon as an *entire* *kit*, so at $35, its more like a 'bloated full price' anyways.
I firmly declined their 'generous' offer, because if the warranty is only 6 months, I will just go purchase a cheap one and have far lower expectations.
I will never purchase from Apera again. Lesson learned.

title: Let there be cold air ..
text:
AC died? Blower works and you think the compressor catches too, but you are not sure, but the temperature inside the house keeps climbing?

Well, this has worked for a lot of us - check the AC unit and inspect the condenser and its surrounding area. If the condenser shows a bulge, or if you see oily residue around it, you have a bust condenser. For a small fee - rarely above thirty greenbacks - you can DIY and get back to your Netflix session in a comfortable temperature!

Watch out - and exercise extreme caution when handling the replacement - don't be in a hurry and make sure all power to the AC is shut off. If you are not sure, turn off the mains completely. But generally, there is a fuse right next to the outside AC unit. Make sure that is off. Take pictures before taking out the old condenser/capacitor so you do not have to guess. Also, remember the old capacitor, if it is not faulty, may have residual charge and may shock you. I used wooden prongs to loosen it.

Good luck! Watch thouse YouTube videos too - you may find them very useful.

title: Accurate???
text:
Although I feel this meter is accurate "enough" for my freshwater tanks it concerns me that even after the smiley face pops up that the ph continues to show numbers going up and down then eventually slows down to "almost" settling on a number/reading. However, that number is ALWAYS totally different from the number that it was on when the smiley face popped up. So I am unsure if I am to assume the number that was showing when the smiley face popped up is correct or if the number it finally settled down to is the actual reading. Things that make you go hmmm. If I have to rely on "accurate enough" I do not see myself "settling" for this meter when it comes to my saltwater reef tank. Although my freshwater tanks don't concern me as much if it's "close enough", when it comes to my saltwater tanks this could spell disaster financially. There's a light years difference in losing a $4 fish than losing a $150 fish, not to mention the cost of my corals.

I was disappointed to store the meter in the Apera storage solution (purchased separately) then power it up 36 hours later and the readings were wayyyyyy off. I then recalibrated it with the 7 and 4 ph solutions that came in the kit and then the readings were much more "normal" than the original testing. My problem with that is I would have thought it would stay calibrated at least for a few tests before having to be recalibrated again after the initial calibration. Also, in the kit it states the calibration solutions must be replaced after 15 uses. Since I check my tanks at least every other day I can see this being an ongoing saga and inconvenience.

Another thing I realized upon arrival is that I can't get an accurate reading on my saltwater tank unless I purchase the 10 testing solution, which does not come with the kit but I was aware of that. I just assumed once calibrated the meter would test ph all the way up to 14, as the parameters online stated. I could be incorrect but from my reading all about the meter, calibration, etc I have to assume without that 10 calibration liquid I can't test my saltwater, as it is up in the 8 digits so going over the max of 7 (the highest solution in the kit) then I won't get an accurate reading over that 7. However, I am no scientist so I may be wrong in that assumption???

I did go online to see about buying the 10 calibration solution only to find that I have to purchase a whole "kit" that includes the 4 and 7 solutions, at the tune of another $33. Perhaps I would be ok with that if they sent another storage container to use to test the 10 like comes in the initial test kit with the meter for the 4 and 7, and if I felt I was not going to have to recalibrate my tester after every single use. If this turns out to be the case I am leaning more towards returning it.

The main reason I gave it as many stars as I did with all the many negatives I feel come with it is due to the good customer service I received when I made a call to the manufacturer.

I plan to reach out to the manufacturer, Apera, again soon to see if I am doing something wrong. If I am doing things correctly and I find I have to calibrate after EVERY use I will definitely be sending it back.

title: Know The Application and Be Happy
text:
If you understand, before buying, the application of self-soldering connectors, you will not be disappointed. These connectors are well made, shrink accurately and evenly, and the contained solder is effective. Those that claim the solder doesn't flow must be using something other than a heat gun. Those that claim the connectors will burn before the solder flows are *definitely* using something other than a heat gun (or a badly overpowered one). For testing, I used both a cheap Wagner heat gun and a 20v battery powered Dewalt heat gun - both worked flawlessly for shrinking the connector and flowing the solder.

A free tip: keep in mind that "low temperature solder" doesn't cool anywhere near as fast as "regular" solder. So once you get the connector heated up enough to flow the solder - let the joint cool naturally before stressing or pulling on it.

title: Good quality for the value
text:
This is a good probe and a step up from the cheap yellow stick pens that people use.

For the extra money you are getting a several upgrades which add value. The yellow probes last about a year in my experience. This should hopefully last much longer. This also comes in very well organized packaging with great instructions, which makes it much better to store and more ergonomic to use. It includes a certificate of conformance, likely a better sensor, and more robust electronics that are waterproofed. This allows for a better 3 point calibration process which improves accuracy at higher pH ranges. It comes with premixed solution, versus packets the user must mix, which can induce error. Lastly, this is made with a method storage submerged in KCl solution rather than dry, which is absolutely vital to maintain longevity of the probe.

For the casual user, a quick primer in pH probes: the probe has a glass ball filled with a salt solution. When dipped in a fluid with a different pH, there exists an difference in charge which causes an electric current across the glass. This current is measured to give a pH. Because the glass probe acts like a membrane, it is possible for it to dry out, and for the fluid inside to be impacted by the environment it is in contact with. It is therefore ideal to keep the probe submerged in a similar fluid when not in use, and it is necessary to recalibrate the probe periodically to ensure accuracy is maintained.

title: Tricky to use, nice when done
text:
These are a bit of a challenge to use for one person. You've got to get the wires in both ends, then make sure it doesn't move around too much so that the wires stay both within the range of the solder, then apply heat without moving anything. I did about 8 connections and of them had to redo 2 because the wires shifted. You cant easily hold them while you're working either because youll burn your fingers off with the heat gun.

Ideally you'd clamp everything when applying heat so as to not have anything move.

The connections are VERY solid once done. I have no doubt that theyll never come apart. The solder is strong and the heat shrink holds it together like it was built that way. It's just a question of the application process being a bit of a hassle. I did try to "crimp" one before applying heat and that wasn't the best result. It didn't want to melt as easily then to get the solder to flow. I suspect crimping it just put too much solder in one spot or something.

Anyway, if you need waterproof forever joints then this is a solid option. Definitely not the easiest option, but very solid.

Normally I just solder and heat shrink, but when I saw these, I decided to give them a chance.
I'm using a hot air station (using for soldering and is just like a heat gun, but with air speed & temp control) and the image I posted was the best joint out of 5 attempts. As you can see the solder isn't fully melted. The jacketing started melting and burning, letting out the colored plastic, WAY BEFORE the solder ever melted.
I tried with lower temps for longer, high temps, med temps and it either wouldn't melt at all, or would just burn so badly that it was like having no heat shrink at all.
I know for a fact this product idea does work, but apparently this particular product has the solder formula off by a bit causing the solder to melt at too high of a temperature..
I am going to reach out to the company in particular and let them know what I have found with their product however my guess is I either won't receive a reply or it will be a generic bulk reply with a "Thank you for contacting us..." kind of message..

title: Accurate and easy to use, but takes a minute to "settle" to the correct reading.
text: I already own the PHTek Acid Pump for my Saltwater pool which has a similar device builtin to measure the PH and inject acid when it gets too high.  This keeps my PH in check but I still check my PH weekly during the summer to make sure everything is functioning as it should.  I typically check it with the classic red dye chemical testers and it's usually ok.  When I first tried out the PH20, it read my PH as 8.2 and I was shocked and assumed it was defective, but when I went to check the PHTek pump I discovered I was out of acid and that was the reason for the high PH.  Once I added acid manually I was able to confirm the PH20's reading was matching my PHTek pump's PH level as well as the measurements from my chemical testers.  The only catch I would add is that it seems to take about 1 minuted for the PH20 to reach the correct PH reading.  So you have fill the cap to the marked fill line and then stand the PH20 upside down and power it on for 1 minute before trusting the reading. For me it will generally start out about 8.1 and slowly come down to the 7.4 range where I keep my PH.  Do not make the mistake of just quickly dipping the tip of the probe in the water and expecting an immediately accurate reading.  Once you learn this trick, you can expect reliable results which should match your chemical tests without the need to guess at color matching.  The calibration process was extremely easy but was a little confusing since you have to calibrate it with a 7.0 and 4.0 solution and the steps in the manual were a little unclear at one point.

title: Use a hi-low heat gun for perfect connections.
text:
I have a 1967 Chevelle that I am helping a friend restore and it has all kinds of connection issues. I was looking for a better way that the standard crip connectors that would maybe have a better water seal and that would provide a clean looking installation. So, when this product became available, I ordered it. Here is what I found:

1. After reading a few reviews, I had my reservations so i tried going a couple of “test” connections. This involved taking a 12 inch piece of wire, butting it into two pieces and then using a connector to splice it back together. What I found was that if i used a heat gun on low to set the connector on the wires so it would not move around, I could then use the High setting to set the actual wire connection easily. After cooling, I had a good electrical connection (used a meter to test) and it appears to be water tight when placing into and then back out of a shallow pan of water. At least it was not obvious that any water got into the connection. After taking the connector out of water and wiping it off and placing onto a paper towel, I found no water marks on the towel after 60 minutes, 2 hours, or 3 hours.

2. The assortment is perfect for the connections I am making on the car. Nice to be able to do some color coding based on wire function (brake, running light, supply line, etc.).

3. Since I am using a heat gun, I am not worried about using it in the engine compartment. I would NOT use a match or torch due to fuel vapors from carburetor.

This is a nice set, easy to use, and I am pleased with it. I would recommend it if you have a similar need.

title: Some tips for proper use!!  (great little meter, but pH sensors require some technique)
text:
Tips for use:

- IMPORTANT: Get rid of the bubble in the sensor!!! A bubble will throw your readings off and will mess up your calibrations. Simply shake the unit like a mercury/spirit fever thermometer to get rid of the bubble. I wonder how many people have bubbles that are messing up their readings. I did and my goodness that made a big difference!

- IMPORTANT: Stir the probe in the sample to dislodge any bubbles on the OUTSIDE of the sensor, then let it sit for a bit so the temperature measurement stabilized and the pH is compensated.

- DON'T store it submerged, or wet with distilled/di water! That will damage the electrode. Store it either with tap water (with minerals and other "normal stuff") or a 3M KCL solution (this is the better choice).

- Insert the batteries the correct way :-).

- Calibrate FIRST with the 7pH solution, rinse, and THEN calibrate with the 4pH solution. (not sure why, but that seems to be the recommendation for pH probes).

title: Okay, but won't replace a proper crimed connection.
text:
So I can see where these are handy, but to me they have a few downsides. First the temp is really touch so unless you have a heat gun with dial-able temp it's hard to get it hot enough to melt the solder fully without melting the jacket. If you are working in a tight spot with little room, much harder.

I found that the stick wasn't very good unless you prep the wire ends by both cleaning and using flux on them. If I just tried soldering them, or just cleaning the wires, it wasn't hard to pull them apart, it was only until I cleaned them and used flux that I couldn't pull them apart.

The next downside is it provides no support if the wire flexes, so if the wire has to flex in that area you can end up breaking the solder joint apart. This is probably not a big deal because most wires are protected. However, a properly crimped/sealed butt splice will protect in this case.

It's a nice one stop solution for soldering/sealing if you have the room to evenly heat it, and can prep/flux the wires. I'd probably still put a epoxy heat shrink over it. There's also the fact if you do clean/flux the wires it's probably a more reliable connection than the average butt splice. The tools to do a really good consistent butt splice are not cheap, and many cheap butt splices crack or don't hold when crimped.

title: Good Connectors for Quick Connections of light to moderate electrical loads
text:
[[VIDEOID:c5cdb3e5181ccd54a0a76e452e57e348]] I worked in the electrical field for 45 years and I found that is impossible to beat a soldered connection for electrical conductivity, high amperage and strength. Compression connectors are my next preferred connectors. Crimped connectors are good for medium to light amp loads and have good strength.

I've wanted to try the Solder Seal Butt Connectors for sometime. I recently decided to add lights to my golf cart and thought this would be a good project for these connector.

I watched several videos and did some test connections before I started the actual light project. I tried 3 ways of joining the wires inside the connector, side by side, enter twined and twisting together. You need to slide the connector over 1 wire before joining the wires. Twisting proved to be the strongest, I couldn't pull apart. Side by side was the weakest, I could easily pull the connection apart. I could also pull the enter twined apart however it took a lot of strength. Granted most connections will never have a great amount of pull applied to them. However this gives you a good idea of the electrical conductivity, better connection = higher conductivity. This brings me to my next problem with these connectors.

The Manufacturer has listed 128°C / 263°F temperature required for "full solder flow". Using a 1500 watt electric heat gun I had to use 480 degrees to get solder flow. I checked this with a digital thermometer and 480 was accurate. The solder never fully flow out into the connection leaving a band in the center. I tried heating at a higher temp and melted the covering. I also tried for a long time with the same result.

As you can see in the above pic, I cut one of the connection in half. The solder does not infiltrate into the strands of the copper wire like you would see in a soldered connection. The solder band partially melts and appears to shrink down on the wire providing some compression. I tried adding some flux to the wires but that didn't help with solder flow. At this time I don't have an opinion on the waterproof aspect of the connectors.

I believe this type of connection is used in aviation wiring however they are likely a lot higher quality connector.

I believe the Haisstronica 1000PCS Solder Seal Wire Connectors would be adequate for light to moderate load connections. This set provides a good selection of sizes at a reasonable price.

title: Works great right out of the box; don't forget to calibrate it!
text:
Rather than go for one of the $15 dollar pH testers on Amazon with a pile of fake reviews from Fake Review Farms*, I decided to go for the Apera PH20. It is the highest recommended one I could find with legitimate reviews after about two hours of research in a range I found to be affordable.

In the box, there are two vials of buffer solution for calibration (4.0 pH and 7.0 pH), all four requisite batteries, a nice little two-sided laminated graphical instruction quickstart manual explaining what to do with the aforementioned items, a certificate of quality, a lanyard, a full instruction page, and the device itself.

With the images on the printout and a few minutes' time, I was up and running with a fully calibrated pH meter. It did the trick in getting my drinking water right based on some pH strips I had lying around, and it certainly recognized the pH of vinegar.

I'm going to use it for taking care of some plants and possibly for cooking and chemistry applications (and maybe making some beer ;D ).

I will update this review in a month or two if I remember to do so (okay, let's be honest, only about 5% of people ever actually update their reviews, so let's put my chance of doing this at around the same.)

* Seriously, give ReviewMeta a try on those cheap ones with review scores of over 4--even if it only bumps a review of 4.6 down to a 4.5, you can look at the product title history and see a clear example of review jacking: that what was actually being reviewed before was a ceiling lamp shade or a pair of socks or something silly. It's really lame and makes finding quality products at affordable prices difficult.

title: Awkward to load, doesn't dry TPU
text: Loading filament into this "dryer" is awkward and tedious. The top filament exit hole is placed in a position that puts a substantial bend in the filament when the spool is full, which can cause tension on the filament, which can cause print issues. The door is a bit tricky to place correctly when closing it. The biggest issue I have with this "filament dryer" is that it's pretty bad at drying filament. I put a brand new roll of Priline TPU in this thing (which has always shipped to me rather wet), and even after drying at the highest heat setting for over twelve hours the filament is still printing poorly, because it's still wet. The heated air is expelled out of the center of the spool where it then travels over the sides of the spool and then out the back of the dryer. It doesn't ever travel directly over the filament. The other big problem I have with this "filament dryer" is that the spool of filament has no bearing surface to allow it to feed out without a lot of drag. Overall, this is poorly designed and does not work as intended. I'm sure it will remove some small amount of moisture from filament, but if it can't dry TPU, there is zero chance it will dry Nylon. Since I bought this specifically for TPU and nylon, I'll be returning it. Maybe it can keep filament that's already dry from absorbing moisture, maybe. I like that it's compact. That's it.

title: They work, but you gotta be careful how you solder
text: I have bought these in the past and used similar version from different manufacturers.  I notice a lot of people complaining of the heat shrink melting before the solder does.  It doesn't matter what brand you get, this will happen if you don't hone your technique.  Trying to do it with a lighter or a butane torch will definitely melt the heat shrink if you aren't careful.  My preferred method is with either a heat gun with a reduction adapter on it so it focuses the heat in about a 1/2" area like Steinel offers, or a butane torch with a long extension and heat shrink adapter on the end, like Power Probe offers.  Try shrinking the ends first to lock it in place so it doesn't move on you, then focus on the solder ring, but you HAVE to keep the heat moving.  If it is focused in one spot too long, it will burn or melt the heat shrink for sure.  That's the key, keep the heat moving, keep circling around the solder ring until it collapses, then keep going a few seconds more so you are sure it soaked into the wires, then finish up any uncollapsed parts of the heat shrink and it is good to go.  You have to slow down with these connectors and do not apply too much heat and do not apply in a concentrated area for too long, and they work as good as anything.  I would say that about any brand that has the solder in the middle, it will always take more heat to melt the solder than the heat shrink, so you have to bring the temp up slower so you don't go past the melting point of the heat shrink.  There may be other techniques but this is what works for me.  Hope this helps somebody.

title: Can create strong connections
text:
I like these. They are strong and clean. I suggest practicing with some if you've never used this style of butt connection before. In tight spots, or areas where the wire can't be held easily, it's difficult. As the shrink tube shrinks, you would expect the solder to melt. It doesn't... until after the shrink tube starts stretching. I used a heat gun, and it did fine on the tubing, but didn't get solder melted fast enough to not stretch. If I use my lighter, it melts the solder a lot faster without stretching the tube, but then to shrinking the tube right you need to twist/rotate the wires, which can't always be done.

I found that using my heat gun to shrink the tube first. Let it cool a few seconds, pull out my lighter and melt the solder works ok. I went through about 10 of these experimenting to find the right way that works for me. Watch heating it too long, the solder will flow out. Once they're figured out, they create a strong, clean connection that looks professional done. No messy looking cheap crimps with electrical tape hanging off anymore

title: Saved me a Few Hundred in repairs
text:
Well not a whole lot to say, basically if you made it to this page, You know enough of what you are doing to know what you are and aren't looking for. My house is Dual Zoned, Upstairs/Downstairs Main floor and Basement.

My upstairs unit stopped working, Fan wasn't turning, So after Googling and then Youtubing some Video links, I determined I have a Bad Capacitor, My original one was a GE 30/5 UF MFD 440 Volt - I found one on Amazon and ordered it, came in and installed it and it's working just fine. Well at the time I thought I should order two, But convinced myself the Chances of my other unit going up were on par with me winning the Lottery, since the original one was pricy at $45, I'd gamble and take my chances. Well fate stepped in and my other unit stopped running about 2 weeks later, Back to Amazon to buy another Capacitor, well guess what? OUT of STOCK , It's 90 degrees out and I have No AC in the Main part of my house, A little Research told me that I could "Step-Up" in Capacitors, thus bringing us to the GE 40/5 uf MFD 440 Volt - IMPORTANT: I'm not an HVAC Guy so what worked for me, may not for you, Do some research first, I was told not to go too high, Notice I went from a 30/5 uf to a 40/5 uf - as a Bonus the larger units were(Yes, I ordered Two this time.) cheaper by almost half of the original unit I bought.(Wish I would have known about upsizing the first time around.) Only ONE Downside to upsizing, The New units are longer and Skinnier than my original shorter fatter units, So my Bracket that holds the capacitor didn't wrap around and secure the unit until I relocated and Drilled a New Screw hole, Now it works just fine.

A word of advice, unless You know what you are doing and know AC's - I Highly recommend disconnecting (1) Wire at a time and reconnecting it to the New Capacitor, There's about 5-6 wires and getting them mixed up will create problems you could never imagine, Marking the Wires would also be a Good idea. In all it literally takes 5-10 minutes to change out, Very simple, You'll need a few tools to unscrew the cover plate to the AC, in my case a 10mm socket worked, 3 screws latter I was back in the Cold Air business.

Now onto the Company - This was a Third party seller on Amazon, Shipping was ultra fast (I had the package in 4 days) Units arrived in a large shipping envelope wrapped in bubble wrap, Hopefully My HVAC repair days are now behind me for a few years to come.

If you are inexperienced and decide to try replacing this, Remember to shut the unit OFF at the Thermostat and to pull the Fuse out of the Disconnect Box at the AC unit itself. (Some units have a Breaker switch instead of a Fuse..DISCONNECT IT) Wait about 5-10 minutes for the Capacitor to "Discharge" and then change it out. We don't need anybody Electrocuting themselves.

TJB

title: Learn how to do it the right way
text:
I'm sorry, but these things are pretty terrible. The solder simply doesn't melt before the outer jacket wants to pry itself open because it's too hot. If you use flux on the wires it helps, but not much. All these do is teach you how to be super lazy.

I can solder two wires together in WAY less time than with these. Slide heat shrink tube on the wire. Twist the wires together, and make sure they are tight. Add some flux. Put some solder on the tip of your iron. Touch the solder on the iron to the wires and they will suck the solder right in within about a second. Slide heat shrink over it and use a heat gun to shrink. Done. With these things I'm still holding the heat gun on the solder portion waiting for it to melt.

title: 15 different sized copper washers.
text:
I like that there is a large assortment of sizes of these washers, and that they come in an organizing box.

It is good to have a variety of sizes so you can pick the correctly sized copper washer for projects such as electrical work, where you want to use copper washers, such as on batteries or for electrical connections attached with a brass bolt. I used multiple-sized copper washers on a recent rv solar system install.

They are also handy to have around for automobile projects, such as when changing the oil on your automobile where many oil drain plugs require a copper washer, so when the old copper drain plug gets worn and begins to leak, you can find the correctly sized copper washer and replace the old one.

The assortment will save you time, so you don't have to run to the store and purchase a copper washer.

The plastic storage box that I received, did have two cracked separation pieces, so I will have to try and glue them back into place, so that the different sized copper washers don't get mixed together.

title: Connect and Heat Seal
text: The wire connectors work great to make a good connection without the need for extra tools. Just be sure to fit the right sized connector along the wires before making the initial connection. (Otherwise you have to take the wires apart again to put the connector in place!) once a good initial connection is made, simply slip the solder part of the connector into position where the wires meet. Use your heat gun to melt the embedded solder. DO NOT OVERHEAT or you run the risk of melting the heat seal part of the connection or the wire insulation. Repeat if necessary if that has happened! I liked that a full set of many wire size connectors are in the kit.

title: So much better than the alternative.
text:
In doing wire repairs, I used to slide a heat shrink tube on the wire, then solder the connection and hope the heat from the joint wouldn’t shrink the tube prematurely. (An issue when repairing 3-wire cords where you want to minimize the amount of cord sheath that’s removed).

These wire connectors are fantastic. Use your wire strippers, insert the two wire ends through the opposite ends of the connector and hit it with a heat gun. I got the Wagner small heat gun that was recommended on Amazon and it takes a little while to melt the solder, but it eventually gets the job done.

If you like making simple tasks harder than they need to be, these are not for you. Otherwise, they are worth every penny.

title: Practice your technique first... takes subtle skill...
text:
This assortment is lacking the GREEN... 16-18 gauge... The red is too tight... the blue is too big for my current project. BUY a KIT WITH GREEN included. I ended up adding a bucket of green connectors to this set.

First few I "tested with" didn't stick as well as they should have. I discovered it was MY FAULT. I practiced a few more times and nailed the correct process. Make sure your wires mesh in the middle... DO NOT twist the wires first. It will NOT work. Pick the SMALLEST diameter that will fit over your wire insulation.

I had a situation where the wire would not fit in the RED... So I wet with the BLUE... this was a 100% failure. Too big a connector... ordered the GREEN and it's perfect. I use these connectors for direct connection to my car battery for a maintenance charger.

99.9% happy with this product out of the gate. Needs practice... don't give up.

title: late delivery, stuck handle
text: I couldn't find any 1.5" brass shut off valves in the local hardware stores.  They were online order only. I had to replace a leaking shutoff valve for a Koi pond, with some very large expensive koi,  so I needed these quick! All the online shops couldn't get them delivered for 5-7 days. I found this one. At the time of order it said if I ordered within the hour I could get it the next day. So, I ordered. After ordering, the delivery was changed to the following day.  It's still faster than others, so I let it go. Then the day of delivery came and no delivery. It now said it would be delivered two days later. Two days later turned into 3 more days. So, now it's being delivered later than other online shops. I reach out to find out what is going on and  was told it should have been delivered that day and to wait 3 more days.  Then, unexpectedly,  the item arrives late the next day. I pull out one of the two and couldn't get the handle to turn. I pulled out the other and couldn't get that one to turn. I put some WD4 on the handle nut. It still isn't moving. I use all my strength and sudden it move ever so slightly. I unscrew the handle a little, but that does nothing.  I keep at it for 5 minutes and it finally moves. Water comes spraying out of of the ball as it turns within the chamber, and lets out a whoosh of air. The handle is still hard to turn.. I work the handle a bit and it loosens up. So, for those who can't turn the handle and think it's broken, it's suctioned shut really tight. The manufacturer should probably have the handle turned a little to avoid this issue. It's possible the heat and humidity during delivery caused expansion and contraction; allowing moisture to get in and creating significant suction. That could explain why so much water came flying out once I got the ball to turn? Made it look like I peed my pants. lol. I installed the shut off valve. It fit perfectly and no leaks at connection or the ball seal. I still haven't been able to get the seal in the second valve to crack open. I tried placing it in cool and warm environments to see if that would help, and it didn't. I can't return just one, so I'm stuck trying to get this handle to turn or chucking it. I stored it away for now. It's a good deal for two so I hate to give up and waste it. Quality seems good/solid. The decrease in rating is due to late delivery and difficult handle.

title: Great Price, But Undetermined Quality
text:
The Smalloo 2" x 160' White Reflective Tape High Visibility Industrial Warning Safety Adhesive Tape is very inexpensive at only $0.15 per foot. I think I now have enough reflective tape to last me for the rest of my life! I just wish it were a little better quality...

Smalloo’s White Reflective Tape has a glass bead layer, and it definitely reflects light at night. It can be used on a variety of Non-DOT uses, such as marking guardrails, fences, gates, bicycles, fishing poles, mailboxes, walls, etc. However, for “official” Federal Government DOT (Department of Transportation) uses, like marking large tractor trailer rigs, I have read that it is safer to use reflective DOT tape from a top tier company like Oralite. Oralite is apparently the “gold standard” for reflective tape. For your information, I just checked, and Oralite sells a variety of products on Amazon.com. However, it should be noted that Oralite DOT Tapes are much more expensive than Smalloo’s reflective tape.

I placed the Smalloo reflective tape on a few items, and it definitely sticks onto smooth surfaces. However, the adhesive on the back of Smalloo’s reflective tape could be much stronger in my opinion. I would rate the adhesive strength as average, at best.

Summary: I feel that the Smalloo White Reflective Tape should be rated 3 Stars – Average. As described above, I am not thrilled with the adhesive Smalloo decided to use on their tape. Also, Smalloo’s unusually low price point worries me. How will this reflective tape perform when subjected to rain and/or large temperature variations? I honestly do not know. Nor do I know how the Smalloo reflective tape will stand the test of time.

title: Excellent Instrument for testing PH and Temperature levels.  Well made, and highly functional.
text:
I received the instrument, well packaged, but the plastic clips that secure the case were broken off, so the case will not securely close for transport.

That being said, the instrument works PERFECTLY, and while the instructions for calibration are a little confusing and could be better written, there is a video on their website that shows exactly how to properly calibrate the instrument with the included regents.

The PH/Temp device is seated very nicely in its box, and the addition of a neck strap is a smart and appreciated addition. There is a "cheater" card on the inside of the box that shows the proper, normal use with illustrations. Pretty easy to use.

We tested our tap water after calibrating the instrument, and found it to have a PH value of 6.2, which is a really good level for potable water. We had previously had our water tested professionally, and they had come back with PH value of 6.3, so this instrument is right on the money!

It will be more effectively used by us in our upcoming aquaponics system to regularly test water temperature and PH...which is CRITICAL for plant and fish development in that kind of growing system.

I removed one star for the case clips being broken, and for the less than clear instruction manual included with the unit. Nonetheless, the instrument itself is near perfect, and works exceedingly well. The only recommendation for improvement would be to have a way to select temperature in Fahrenheit vs Celsius, which is the only option now. Other than that, this is a unit that I feel extremely comfortable recommending for anyone who either REALLY needs it, or for those who just want to keep track of their water or other liquid source's PH and/or Temperature levels.

title: Product failed when tested with cheaper brand
text:
I was running low on solder-type, shrinkable butt end connectors. I really like using them so I decided to buy more. The only complaint I've had with the brand I have need using it that sometimes the shrink tubing disintegrates before the solder melts, there seemed to be an inordinate amount of waste and re-stripping of conductors. I did my research and opted for what I thought was the best brand out there, especially having good quality shrink tube insulators.
They arrived today just in time for me to make a repair on a exterior light on my RV. I used the new Haisstronica brand connectors, but the shrink tube failed on one of those too. The insulator burned through similar to the inferior brand but only in one spot, directly adjacent to the color band.
So, I came to the conclusion that the problem was likely my technique and not a quality issue with either brand of the connectors.
So, I decided to get some practice and try to improve my technique using solder butt end connectors. I got together 4 wire specimens of different gauges, and initially practiced with 18 or 20 connectors, about half each brand. I used one or two connector for each different wire gauge.
To my surprise, the cheaper ones faired much better than these Haisstronica brand connectors.
The Haisstronica brand physically look better, they have about the same insulator thickness, but the Haisstronica brand just look better; they have a more pronounced color band and the AWG rating is printer on each connector, very nice. They also shrink much clearer than the cheaper brand. I practiced on a few more connectors, about 36 in total. The inferior connectors were no worse than the Haisstronica brand connectors with those too.
I thought that it was possible that because I knew that the older connectors were inferior, that I may have been applying heat differently to the two brands. So, to assure that I evenly applied heat to each brand of connector, I made a wire loop, and connected the loop on two places. At one connection I used the inferior brand connector and at the other I used the Haisstronica brand connector. I placed the hot air stream from the heat gun exactly between the two connectors and after 10 or 15 seconds, just about when the solder melted, the shrink tube on the Haisstronica brand connector failed at the color band, as can be seen in my pictures, the older, inferior connector is on the left and the Haisstronica brand connector is on the right.
I bought the Haisstronica brand connectors, and paid more for them, specifically to eliminate, or at least, reduce waste and resoldering. I'm not sure that will be the case. This could still be due to my poor technique applying the heat, but seems less likely now after doing the test loop.
I definitely still like the looks of the Haisstronica brand connectors but will probably try another brand in 2-3 months when I start running low on solder connectors.
I should clarify something, none of the 26AWG connectors (white) failed when I applied heat, most failures were with the 14-16AWG connectors (blue), next was the 10-12AWG connectors (yellow), and only one of the 18-22AWG connectors (red) failed with heat. I'm not really sure why I selected the 18-22AWG red connector for the test loop, except that only the Haisstronica brand connector failed during my practice tests, not really sure, but the Haisstronica brand connector definitely failed in the side by side wire loop test,

title: Great for dry foods but Not for moist foods.
text:
I purchased the Southern Champion trays for when my teens have friends over and for feeding the animals raw or messy foods. It’s great for serving snacks, popcorn and even hotdogs and other fairly simple foods. It’s ok for dry foods only, just stay away from the wet foods.

I frequently mix up freeze dried foods for my dog, mixing in warm water and letting it sit. I like the trays because I can just get rid of them afterwards and not worry about cleaning up after raw food. I have purchased the Boardwalk clay coated in the past and never had an issue with leaking. When I fixed my dogs dish, after sitting for a bit, I found the counter pooled with murky water. It had leaked all over. I decided to do a side by side test, placing a small amount of water in both Southern Champion and the Boardwalk food trays, within seconds the SC started soaking up the water, within 30 seconds it was leaking and flimsy. The Boardwalk held the water for 3 minutes before I noticed a small spot in the corner starting to leak but still held its shape and didn't fall apart.

I think the bottom line is that Southern Champion trays are great if you want them for simple dry based foods, nothing with any liquid. Kids snacks, dry animal foods, even holding arts and crafts supplies, they are great. If it’s wet food you need it for stick to the Boardwalk clay coated.

title: Works great -- but STORE UPRIGHT b/c cap doesn't seal properly!
text:
Ph meter works great (was calibrated out of the box and aligned perfectly with several Ph strips I'd purchased). Only negative is that the seal on the cap that is supposed to retain distilled water during storage does not seal properly, so make sure to store the meter so it is oriented vertically so that the water does not leak out and dry out the sensor.

As directed by the manufacturer, I put distilled water in the cap up to the fill line, then put it back in the carrying case. When I went to use it again a few days later, I noticed that all of the water in the cap had leaked out of the cap onto the foam in the carrying case, so the carrying case is basically useless. I now hang the Ph meter by the cord so that the Ph meter hangs down and is oriented vertically when not in use so that the distilled water cannot leak out of the cap. This is a minor inconvenience, and since the Ph meter works well, I didn't deduct a star for this.

title: Good reflectance, but weak adhesive
text:
This tape has excellent reflective qualities. It looks the same as other brands of reflective tape I have that are rated DOT-C2, as this one is. And it has a low price.

However, its one weakness is its adhesive, which is poor. If you use this on exterior applications, it may not adhere well, especially if the surface is cold. (Indoors, it should be fine.) I put a piece on an alcohol-cleaned smooth painted vertical surface on a wooden handrail when it was about 45 deg. F. It rained overnight, and temperatures got down to about 35 deg. The next day, the piece of tape was laying on the ground. I have some other brand of reflective tape on this handrail which I put on last summer, and it's still there. This may not have been a fair test because it's winter where I am now. But you may not be able to wait until summer to use this tape outdoors, so I'd recommend another brand.

I then tried repairing some small wires using a heat gun. This worked better as I can control the heat from the electric gun and have attachments that wrap around the splice for even more control of the heat.

title: Not your ordinary edge trim, this stuff is top shelf
text:
First off, this stuff is not your ordinary edge trim. This is truly top shelf trim.

I had previously use some edge trim I had purchased at an auto parts store, you know the stuff that comes with glue that is pre-applied to the inside. I went for the most durable looking stuff they had but it was worthless. It almost immediately started coming off as soon as I has applied it. So i went in search of some better trim on amazon. That is when I saw the Trim-Lok and decided to give it a try.

I am using the trim protect the sharp lip of the tailgate on my drive-on trailer for my ATV. It was getting really messed up rubbing on the concrete or gravel each time I loaded my atv. Let me tell you, there is a world of difference between what I had purchased before and this product. This trim does not use glue, but rather it has build in fingers on the inside that lock the trim down and hold it in place. Another big difference is this Trim-Lok trim has a integral metal core wrapped in what appears to be some type of highly durable vinyl. This is some really heavy duty stuff and it stays in place even when abused. It was perfect for my application and I highly recommend it.

title: Better than I expected!
text:
My meter worked fine for months. Now it reads the included Ph7 calibration solution as 8.5, shows me an error, and refuses to calibrate. Now I have to figure something out by tomorrow. Thanks.

UPDATE 3/12/21
A few things: I had previously been using tap water to store my meter. Don't do that. Also, apparently the meter wasn't ruined. It was just off it's internal calibration. Letting it sit in storage solution for about a week fixed everything and I was able to recalibrate the meter and continue using it. I keep a glass beaker of tapwater on my work table that I fill every day for rinsing meters and probes. Yesterday, I was not paying attention and I smashed the glass probe on the meter directly on the edge of my beaker as I went to rinse it off. I see now that Apera has a safety piece to prevent this now. Good idea!
Don't store this meter in tapwater. It will slowly degrade the glass probe, which is porous. Also, chances are unless you changed the water every day, bacteria will grow inside the cap and contaminate the probe. Just buy the storage solution, it's 10 bucks. It'll add years to the life of the meter. I owned this meter almost 3 years to the day and it probably would have lasted longer if I payed better attention. I have a Hanna as backup, and I'm thinking about Milwaukee, but honestly it's a tough choice against the Apera. Get it.

title: Lots of trouble installing, but after it's in, it's good
text:
I'm not going to repeat all the positives most other people are stating; Yes, once you install it, it is bar-none the best upgrade you can make to your Ender.

I will however state that I had a lot of trouble installing it. I consider myself at least an intermediate with most handy type things, such as this. But here are the troubles I ran into:

1. The instructions are not very intuitive. They are organized better than some chinese instructions I've received in other items, but when you get to the flash/upgrade portion, unless you are already very experienced with the concept of flashing firmware with super-technical programs (i.e. not "turn key" push a single button), then your best bet is to find a youtube video and follow along there.

2. Apparently my Ender came with the plugs GLUED onto my 1.1.4 motherboard. This absolutely baffled me. When you reach the steps that you need to swap the cables to attach the BLtouch to the motherboard, I had to grab my exacto knife and very careful cut the hardened glue away from the plugs. This added an extra full hour to the process. Note: This is not the fault of the seller of this item, it's the fault of Creality who makes Ender 3 Pro.

3. This bundle did not come with any instructions on how to install the extras, such as the springs or the replacement tube, etc. Fortunately, there is Youtube. Just be forewarned that you're going to need the internet and videos to do this, unless you already know how it works.

All-in-all, it took me nearly 4 hours to install everything, and I was not being casual about it. Unscrewing things, installing, cable managing (!!), flashing, bed leveling, all of this is quite technical, and will absolutely require more than "20 minutes" as some other reviewer posted.

But yes, once you get it going, it is amazing, and you will wonder how you ever lived without it prior. Good luck!

title: IF YOU RECENTLY PURCHASED THE ENDER 3 PRO (since June 2020)
text:
THE SHORT VERSION: installing this kit on a newer Ender 3 Pro is possible but difficult and time consuming. The filament tube is functional but installation of one of the bed springs is difficult since it goes beneath a cord retaining clip. The end result will be adequate if not highly accurate bed leveling.

THE DETAILS:
Although up at the top they tell you this will work with the Ender 3 Pro, down at the bottom they share this:

NOTICE: If you purchased the Ender 3 Pro AFTER JUNE 2020, the 4.2.2 control board included is not yet officially supported by this version of the BL Touch. Creality is developing the firmware for the 4.2.2 board which is expected to be released in the coming months.

I purchased my Ender 3 Pro in August 2020 and it has the newer V4.2.2 board. Since I missed the warning at the bottom I bought this and, once I had it, decided to forge ahead with the installation. In regard to the firmware, I had to try five (5) different versions -- the versions provided by Creality did not work -- before finding one that would make the BLTouch function, and that process took many, many hours. See below for some cautionary information. Also, the V4.2.2 board includes a bootloader so you will not need the bootloader included in this kit to flash the firmware.

With the firmware upgraded, the installation required dropping the extruder to the appropriate distance from the print bed by
1) lowering the extruder along the z-axis to the proper print height (piece of paper)
2) recording the amount you lowered the extruder
3) resetting the z-stop (the height of the unit) manually after adding the existing z-offset to the amount you recorded in step 2)

SO, you will need to manually adjust the height AND do math to make this work. My question is: isn't setting the height the actual job of this thing?

However, I did all that, several times, and at this time it is functioning in what appears to be more or less the correct manner. I have not manually leveled the bed in my last six prints. However, it does not truly level the bed. There is a visible difference in the first layer from one side of the bed to the other in the skirt when I print. Across the 32mm length of a part I am printing there is a 0.3mm difference in height, translating to a 1% grade. If your part was 100mm -- about 4 inches -- then that would translate to a 1mm or 3/64 inch difference (all figures very rough here). Whether that is chiefly the result of the BLTouch or the Ender 3 Pro I do not know, I only know that the combination is not highly accurate in my circumstance.

SO, if you buy this for the Ender 3 Pro:
1) be prepared to spend some time getting it set up and working; I spent many hours getting to this point
2) be prepared for some limitations in the accuracy of the bed leveling

I also installed the new PTFE tube without incident but found the springs problematic as one of the goes beneath a retainer for the cord and so must be compressed a great deal to get it on. A shorter spring is in order.

Although the unit is functional and I have decided to keep and use it, I will not recommend it to others due to the difficulty in installation.

title: GOOD METER BUT ONLY FOR 6-8 MONTHS
text:
I have purchased a few of these and the probe goes bad on all of them. Apparently the meter is only good for about 8 months and then you will have to buy another one.

I registered my meter and sent Apera a warranty request. I cannot be mad at Apera for the response given since they were very honest, but had I known I was going to have to replace the whole meter every year I would've bought a PH60 or Bluelab and cried once.

This is the response from Apera (sensitive info removed "XXX"):

Hi XXX,

I'm sorry you are encountering accuracy issues when trying to calibrate. From what I have heard, it appears your p20s' probes have expired from regular use.
​
The probes, themselves, have a warranty of 6 months and will last roughly 8 months to a year and a half with proper care and usage which it appears yours have. They have gone through normal lifetime service. This is not a short lifespan, this is the normal lifespan of glass sensor ph probes. It is the same across the entire industry.
​
On a side note, the meter body holds a 2-year warranty for issues like the screen malfunction, failure of the circuit board, battery fixture, or general device death.
​
We offer an inexpensive replacement option for worn down ph20s still inside their 2-year warranty. When a ph20's probe goes bad from use, we can offer the customer a discounted replacement for half off ($33.00 with free shipping). This is effectively less cost than the cost of a replacement probe on the higher models, and easier than the previous repair option we used to offer.

​If you are interested in our meter replacement offer, please let us know and we can fill you in on what we would need to do.

​Please let us know if you have any other questions from here and we will help as best as we can.

Be safe and have a wonderful day.

Sincerely,

Michael XXX

Apera Instruments Customer Support

title: Accurate if you ignore smiley icon. Water with low ppm (few ions) adds time to get final results
text:
TL;DR. Accurate results require avoiding pitfalls. The PH20 has 0.1 display and smiley icon appears too early, so upgrading to a meter with 0.01 display might mean less time spent wondering if the test is finished.

The PH20 arrived with moisture in the cap (that's good) and a note saying they added some water.

It seems well-built and provides accurate results (if we ignore the smiley icon and wait longer for the final result).

My PH20 arrived calibrated to measure the pH4.0 and pH7.0 solutions perfectly in about 4-5 seconds.

It's fast if the water has plenty of ions. If it's plain tap water with 70-140 ppm then it can take an extra 10-30+ seconds to reach the final result (with each 0.1 bump taking longer). You're left wondering if the result is correct or if it'll add another 0.1 if you wait.

For reliable results, you need to shake the meter in the air to get rid of the air bubble INSIDE the bulb, and then stir it inside your water to get rid of any air bubbles OUTSIDE the bulb.

Before first-time use, soak the probe in the included pH4.0 solution for 15 minutes. Even better if you soak it in 3M KCl storage solution (not included).

Directions say to use a few drops of tap water (never distilled or deionized) in the cap to maintain moisture.

The probe could last longer and require fewer calibrations if it's stored in 3M KCl storage solution. Fill the cap at least 1/2 way to the "FILL" line because it should rise to that line when you insert the probe. Store the case on its correct side to make sure the bulb is fully submerged in the 3M KCl solution.

An 8 oz bottle of 3M KCl can last a year because you don't need to empty out the cap daily. I'd keep enough of it in the cap to submerge bulb and replace weekly with 4 ml of fresh 3M KCl.

title: Well-thought out, accurate, and a great value
text:
May 29, 2021 Update: After about 10 months of near-daily use, this pen no longer holds calibration. I'm not upset about it as it was precise now and it saw a fair bit of use.

I've been through multiple $10-20 pH pens, none of which would last more than a few dozen uses before they wouldn't hold calibration, couldn't be calibrated, or otherwise failed. As a result, I have been using the drip method of estimating the pH of my nutrient mix. This pH pen comes in a hard case with cut foam for safe storage. Potential point of improvement here is to reorient the pen in the case so it can be stored upright with an OPR solution protecting the probe in the case of longer-term storage.

Calibration was quick and easy even when calibrating to three points. The included "quick start" type insert was laminated which was a great, subtle touch. These units typically get used around water so drops/drips are inevitable but the guide is protected. Also included was a certificate of calibration. My certificate showed that it was calibrated to within +/-0.2, not the advertised +/-0.1. I'm not sure what to trust but at least for my applications, my pH window isn't that tight so 0.1 vs. 0.2 isn't a big deal. Clarification on this point though by the manufacturer or the seller would be appreciated and the confusion is the only reason why I've removed a star at this time.

I'm pretty happy with it so far but I've only used it a handful of times. I hope this one stands the test of time and use.

title: It works it's easy to calibrate and good support.
text: This pen has been a godsend to me it is simplified my testing I compare its test to pH strips every few days and then once a week I will test it against standard liquid pH test. It has remained accurate over the last 30 days and I've only had one issue and that is if the pen randomly stops working it is possible you have humidity or some liquids in the battery compartment of the tool. This can actually happen to this pen even if you never fully submerge the pen but if you keep it and it's protective case because every time you replace the water in the end cap to make sure that the sensor stays wet while stored there's always a little bit of water that gets by at the top after you put the lid on this gets into the case and over time depending on how much you get inside your case will humidify the case if it's in a warm environment and when people are dealing with lots of plants and greenhouses this is a typical thing to encounter the humidity inside the device will stop it from turning on. Simply use a q-tip wipe out any of the interior walls in the battery compartment that you see if there is moisture place in front of a fan for a 15 or 20 minutes let fresh air blow over the components and you should be back up and running in no time. If you do have problems with your device call apparel they will answer their phone they do speak English and they're very helpful. Both of the included emails in the box with a device don't seem to be working so I urge you take the time to call them I'm glad I did.

Tried with an open flame so as to imitate the commercial in thinking the rate of rise in heat to melt the solder before melting the plastic gives way to the same result. The plastic covering is compromised and heat-shrink SEAL is void!
Again.... A hoax, JUNK is the rating. .... Simply solder the wire then slide heat-shrink tubing over the splice, this product does not work as advertised.

title: Buy this pH meter for pool testing; not the cheap one!
text:
I wanted a pH meter for my pool for a variety of reasons, so I initially bought the cheap yellow one. Turns out cheap isn’t cheap after all. First, that one came with dead batteries and the replacements were more expensive than the meter itself. Second, the calibration solution required deionized water (not distilled) which was hard to find, so I ended up buying the premixed kind. Finally, after using it twice, somehow it got some moisture inside that fried it.
Don’t make the same mistake I made! For the same amount of money, you can have this quality instrument instead of junk.
The Apera PH20 comes with excellent instructions, calibration solution, batteries, and a lanyard all nestled safe and secure in foam inside a hard-shell carrying case. The meter is completely encased, so there is no threat of water getting in it. And I love that it also adjusts for and displays the temperature in addition to the pH.
As far as accuracy, it’s been fine for me, but I can only speak to my own situation. I use it primarily to check my pool water, and I trust its readings better than my ability to judge color on either the reagent test or the strips. I’m monitoring a fairly wide range, so my accuracy requirements are quite liberal.
The only criticism I have is that it doesn’t come with the 10.01 calibration solution. Since I’m testing between 7-9 , I like to calibrate on the high end as well, but there isn’t any place in the case to put the other bottle without cutting out some foam.
