title: Take your time
text: These work. They take some patience and trail/error to get it right. I don't usually say things like this but I believe the bad reviews are mostly from impatient people that didn't take the time to learn how to use these. I messed up two of them before getting it right then did 6 in a row perfectly. No fancy tool, basic harbor freight heat gun set to Low. Start the gun several inches away and move closer to find the sweet spot distance. It helps if you can move the gun to hit both sides of the solder ring (I don't mean end to end) so it gets evenly heated. It does melt and tin the wire. You can see that it's shrunken and flowed. It will not flow out like you're used to seeing solder flow but you can see it. Make sure you buy more than you need so you can do some practice runs and if you're doing more than a couple budget enough time as it's a slow process. Good luck.

title: I often fall for products like this
text:
I see the video, where someone logically lays out and shows how easy and superior this product is to all previous ones.
He even pipes in at the last minute, "yeah you can use a lighter do this too, while he uses a hot air gun or something.

Then I get the product and try it out and then test a soldered joint and it kind of "makes crunchy sound when you squeeze the joint with pliers" then I do a few more and test them and both joints pull apart in my hands without much effort. Then I think about it FINALLY and of course it is crap because every joint is cold soldered, the wires you are trying to join never get hot enough for them to really meld in with the solder like a normal hot soldered joint is.
When the solder does finally get hot enough to "melt" the insulation is also so hot that it melts and burns leaving the cold soldered joint un insulated and "cold soldered" At least it was only 20 bucks for 120 pc box of them. So lesson learned .

title: A lot of extra effort for marginal results
text:
I have used solder seal type butt connectors for years now, this isn't new technology. So when I was getting low i ordered these I'm September 2020 but looked at them and didn't really need to use them for a couple months until my previous supply was exhausted
Immediately I was dissapointed in the heat shrink. The melt temp is not correct and you can get burn through if not watching carefully. You can achieve solder melt by very slowly heating the joint. Very slowly. Only to still be dissapointed in the fact that you have no insulation and you need to add heat shrink to protect the joint. What insulation they talk about in thier product description for this didn't make it to production. It is actually faster to solder the old fashioned way and you wind up with a solder joint you can inspect prior to heat shrinking.

I challenge you to cut a few of these in half after you have done them at the solder to see what you are really getting. You may save yourself frustrating failures or possibly even fires down the road. I can vouch for other manufacturer's, including the original that the product when made correctly works fantastic.

Lastly all of the red 18-22 in the kit I received were of correct size on one end but the other side the heat shrink was already reduced significantly and therefore all of them were useless on the gauge they were intended.

The bottom line is be careful that you are not just accepting unwittingly a joint that is not as well joined as it looks. And for safety sake add extra heat shrink over the joint if you just must use these. Because you can get the solder to flow plan on going very slowly and try as you might it is almost impossible to get a good joint without burning through so be ready to heat shrink every joint. And please buy a good heat shrink and not a paper thin brand.

title: As pictured and described.  Work as expected.
text:
Briefly: I think this tubing would work well in most places where heat shrink tubing is used. The sizes included should fit the needs of most people. It seems abrasion resistant. The glue seemed to form a tight seal.

The 1/2", 5/8" and 3/4" pieces slipped easily on their respective sized rod.

I tested the 5/8" tubing with a 4.7 mm (3/16") dowel connected to a piece of 5.74 mm (~15/64") OD tube (see picture). It shrank to create a tight fit that did not leak when I blew hard into the tube. I presume that this is a watertight seal for rain, underground etc. The tubing is some what flexible after shrinking. The tubing length remained approximately 2.4" after shrinking the diameter. I did not have any way to measure the temperature from my heat gun on low setting which worked well to shrink the tubing.

It was hard to but possible cut away part of the tubing to separate the parts that were covered. The glue left no residue on the parts that were joined. I think that a wire splice might have had glue residue.

I found the count of the 1/8, 3/16, 1/4, 5/8 and ¾ inch tubes to be accurate. I presume the remaining are too.

title: it's a sure sign the start capacitor is bad or going bad
text:
Save yourself a lot of $$$. When your lights dim as your heat pump cycles on, it's a sure sign the start capacitor is bad or going bad. Remove power from the heat pump (there's a little pull-out "circuit breaker" where the heat pump is located), open the access panel (usually two hex head screws) and look at the capacitor to determine its specs. Replace the access panel, plug in the "circuit breaker", order the capacitor and wait a few days.

After receiving the new capacitor, turn off your thermostat, go back outside, remove the "circuit breaker", open the access panel, note which colored wire goes where on the capacitor. Using RUBBER HANDLED pliers, remove the wires from the old capacitor and do NOT short between the terminals of the old capacitor. Remove the old capacitor from its clamp, and insert the new capacitor. Using the RUBBER HANDLED pliers, attached the colored wires to the new capacitor's terminals, replace the access panel, plug in the "circuit breaker". Carefully put the old capacitor into a large plastic baggie to protect the terminals from shorting, and dispose of it in an outside garbage container (not inside!) in case it shorts out and throws some sparks.

For the cost of <$30 you've avoided at least a $130 service call.

title: Looks to be Good Quality - Install Suggestions
text:
[[VIDEOID:9dc4b734cb9a7dcd05a67bebf2f91cf0]] I purchased this to protect my elderly dogs feet on a Harbor Freight aluminum ramp. The install was easy and the edge protector seems to be snug. I will follow up later if that changes. Here are a few install suggestions from what I learned:
* Use trauma sheers to make cuts. I wanted to make a right angle bend on one end and taper the other. Trauma sheers easily cut through both the PVC and aluminum. I had no success with a hack saw, tin snips, or bolt cutters. They cut through the PVC but not the thin aluminum. A razor knife works great on right angle cuts but also will not cut the aluminum inside.
* Don't use a mallet or rubber hammer to speed the installation. In my case this caused the aluminum to splay out on the install and become loose. I had much better luck with pushing the trim on by hand.

This was an easy install and seems to hold tight to my 1/16" aluminum edge on the ramp. (See photos and video)

title: Good Enough
text:
I am an analytical chemist with 10 years of experience specializing in mass spectrometry in regulatory, medical device and drug discovery. First, this review is based on at home use, so I’m not considering any of the factors I would if I were thinking of a GLP/GMO/ISO lab. That said it works, it’s easy to read and it comes with clear concise instructions.

My criticism is for the price, I would add pH 10 calibration fluid. Even at home it’s important to calibrate 3 points. I work with potassium or ate as a preservative in beauty products and eventually I would like to sell products which means I need a meter that I can calibrate to pH 10. It would be nice to have a lower pH too but in the lab that’s not a requirement and I don’t expect it. I’m in experimental phase. This device is alright but I’m not sure it will be sufficient to take to the next level. The other major critique I have is the packaging on the calibration fluid is not possible to peel off. I had to cut the seal and I’m concerned it may have contaminated the solutions. It’s not a huge problem since I measured the solutions I’m working with today and will be working with these concentrations for a few months. I’ll know if something is off if my measurements begin to vary.

In spite of those concerns, the device is worth purchasing if you’re interested in something to give you a relatively accurate reading for experiments at home. If the precision fluctuates I’ll mention that in the future.

title: This former water plant operator gives this pH meter 5 STARS without being paid or bribed.
text:
In the 90's I had over 10 years experience in lab instruments as a municipal water plant operator in Florida, so I think I have some experience with pH meters. As I became aware of the health benefits of ionized, alkaline drinking water, I wanted to know EXACTLY what the pH of my well water is, from raw, tap, and after the RO system. I tried pH strips and found them not accurate enough due to the difficulty in reading the color scales accurately, so I then got a pool pH kit using Phenol Red drops, and also found them not accurate enough for my needs. So I decided I needed an electronic pH meter, and the search began. There are dozens and dozens of cheap sub-$20 meters, most with poor to mediocre reviews (or free product reviews with 5 stars), and then there are the "lab quality" meters that run from $200 on up. I wanted something in the middle, like a tradesman type pH meter, with good quality and accurate readings. There are also many in this area, in the $50 range, but the Apera AI209 PH20 pH Meter immediately jumped out as a QUALITY meter. It looked well designed, had great reviews, and came with a box, calibration solutions, and accessories, so I chose this one.
I am pleased I did! The unit feels solid and the glass bulb of the pH meter, the part that actually measures the pH, was also well designed. The case is very nice and comes with a very nice plastic-laminated instruction sheet, as well as a paper instruction booklet. The calibration using the supplied 7.0 and 4.0 pH standards was simple and fast. The meter gave the ACCURATE results I was looking for, very quickly. It verified my suspicions: that my RO system makes very LOW 5.6 pH, UNHEALTHY drinking water! To think I thought I was doing my family a HEALTHY thing by using an RO system. How ignorant I was! I will be using this pH meter for my side business as a Tyent authorized dealer of water ionizers at GenesisHealthy_dot_com and I expect it to be just what I needed to share my pH discoveries and what it means to the human body. I highly recommend this pH meter!

The instructions for calibration are not written clearly so I recommend checking youtube for a video that walks you through the process. You can also purchase pH 7 and pH 4 or pH 10 buffers to use for calibration. The quantity of buffers than come with the meter won't last indefinetly. You can also make your own probe storege solution (3 Molar Kcl). Dissolve 225 grams of KCl in 1 liter of water or half that amount in 1 pint of water. Always use distilled or deionized water. If you are looking at pH range of 7 to 4 use those two buffers for a two point calibration. For a range of 7 to 10 use those buffers. title: Good value, indoor or light duty outdoor use, not as directional as 3M conspicuity tape
text:
Seems a good value retroreflective tape, especially for indoor applications.

I'd bought some 3M conspicuity tape (3M 913-10) 12" long samples from another source, so some observations and photos in comparing the two products (comparative photos have 3M on right, Smalloo tape on left):
- The 913 series 3M tape is much more directional and highly retroreflective IF the light source is right next to your eyes. This can be a good or bad thing depending on the need/application: Viewed with my car lights on at 30' distance, the Smalloo tape is actually brighter (see photo with tapes on board in front of glass door) because my car headlights are below my eye/camera level by a couple feet. At very long range, the 3M will likely be superior.
-Smalloo tape is whiter; 3M has slight blue-ish reflection
-Smalloo tape has a stacked structure consisting of smooth plasticized front layer and a thinner white backing layer. The 3M tape seems to be a single film with shiny metallic backing layer. Its possible to peel back the top layer from the white backing tape on the Smalloo; see photo showing laminates and the tape backing layer (which is tossed before placing the tape), but some effort is required. If its going to be on a surface needing lots of cleaning over time, the 3M may be more durable.
-Smalloo tape is slightly transparent (when backlit). 3M is completely opaque.
-Smalloo tape is 0.012" thick x 1.974" wide. 3M is thinner at only 0.004"
-Smalloo tape is easy to place and sticks well. It can be peeled off without leaving goo (at least for the little time it was on a plastic surface. I'd seen video of removal of 3M tape requiring a heat gun and pliers. However on my black plastic test surface, both peeled off with some effort (3M a bit stickier).
-Smalloo tape, because of the stacked layer, seems more susceptible to mechanical or water damage over time. Out of the box, the first couple feet had some slight visibible imperfections (following feet seemed fine so probably due to movement within the box during shipping damaging some of the retro lenses). I soaked the tape in water as I guessed the laminate structure might allow some water in affecting the optical performance. In horizontal tape photo on black backing board using camera flash, the defects can be seen by stripes and where I'd peeled a bit of the laminate apart at the corner also. Along the edges, a couple of the retrorefelctive triangles where water had seeped in were visiblly less reflective. Not sure these are obvious from photos. The water did NOT seem to seep deeper than a few points along the edges, but I only soaked in water for 15 minutes or so. The manufacturing looks like the individual triangles are isolate so probably will be fine for decent time in outdoor use.
- Both tapes have DOT-C2 marking, but I've not verified compliance to that.

Cost:
3M tape cost me about $15 for ten 12" pieces, so $1.50/foot
The Smaloo tape was only $0.15/foot at time of review.

So, for most uses indoor and moderate outdoor use, the Smalloo tape seems a great value. If you need a very long-term durable/scrubbable outdoor use, very long range & super-highly retroreflective tape, you may prefer the expensive 3M tape. Especially for indoor use at moderate distances of use, I'd choose this Smalloo brand as it'd probably be brighter in normal lighting use and be far cheaper.

title: Very disappointed in both quality and performance - AGAIN!
text:
This is going to be a bit of a rant, because both of the Apera meters Amazon sent me are basically garbage-quality. Apparently, Amazon decided not to post my previous 1-star review for the first unit they sent me that was clearly already bought, used and returned by someone else for being defective. F-U, Amazon. Any company who blocks negative feedback should probably be avoided. Not to mention the sheer incompetence required to send out a defective unit that had already been returned at least once.

So, they send me out a replacement right away. This one arrives clearly brand-spankin-new. Awesome, I thought. It was reading within .1 of the calibration solutions, but I went ahead and calibrated it anyway, wanting it to be as precise as possible when I'd be needing it in a few days.

So, here we are today. I mix up my nutrient solution, add enough acid to get me relatively close to where my pH should be and then I break out the new meter. It's telling me the solution is 7.2. Seemed a little higher than I'd expected, but didn't sound entirely unreasonable, so I add another mL of pH Down and I'm fairly confident that that should put me right around 6.2 or so. Well, the meter tells me it's now 7.0. That seems odd, so I break out the General Hydroponics pH indicator solution I've been using for the past year. When added to a small sample, it turns a nice bright urine-yellow, telling me it's right around 6.0.

I decide that I should calibrate again, even though it seems utterly nonsensical that it would jump so far out of calibration from sitting unused for a few days. Yes, I'd left several drops of tap water in the cap to keep it nice and moist, as the instructions tell you to do. So I put it in Cal mode and get to it. The instructions are fairly poorly worded, but the process is clear enough. When put in the included 7.0 solution, it reads 7.5, so I hit Cal and set that parameter.

When I put it in the 4.0 solution, that's when it started to get really wonky. At first, it acted like it couldn't tell if it were in 4 or 10 buffer solution - 4 and 10 kept alternating constantly - but after a few tries I do get both parameters calibrated.

So, when I go measure my nutrient solution again, it's telling me 6.7. Meanwhile, my indicator drops are still giving me a reading right at 6-ish.

If the best I can hope for is "close enough" out of this meter, I may as well just stick with the General Hydroponics test solution. Gonna mull it over for a few days, but I'll probably end up just sending this junk back.

I noticed that Apera reps like to troll the comment section, pretending to care about customer satisfaction. Well, if you guys are reading this: Nothing short of sending me an entirely free UPGRADED meter would convince me to ever own another Apera product again. You wanna do that, I'll gladly give your product line another shot. Otherwise, don't waste your time posting the same song and dance you give most of the other negative reviews.

title: Great selection of copper sealing rings
text:
This review is for the “360 pieces 15 sizes” selection of copper rings. First I’m going to list the sizes and quantities, since I haven’t seen that in the description. ID/OD (qty)
5/9 (52), 6/10 (20), 6/12 (31), 8/12 (20), 8/14 (30), 10/14 (31), 12/16 (31), 14/18 (32), 10/16 (20) All of these are .036” thick.
12/18 (20), 14/20 (15), 16/22 (15), 18/24 (10), 20/26 (10), 22/28 (10) All of these are .055” thick.
The 6mm ID actually measure about 6.3mm, so they’ll work with 1/4”. All the others measure pretty much dead on to the specified ID.
These come packaged in a compact plastic case, a layer of foam keeps the washers from migrating out of their bins. Unfortunately my case came broken, a crack on the back and two dividers broken out. These were delivered in a soft pouch mailer which failed to protect the case. There are no markings anywhere on the case, no indication of sizes or of the manufacturer.
Quality of the rings is excellent. Both sides have a smooth surface finish, the ID is concentric with the OD, and the rings are flat. These will work well as seal rings in general auto applications. Finding copper seal rings can be tricky, and this set not only has an wide range of sizes but also has generous quantities of each. 5 stars for this comprehensive assortment.

title: A Nice Replacement Casters Set for Roll-Out/Trundle Bed
text:
Our kids' rollout bed has a bad set of casters wheels set and needed replacement. This replacement set is great but we needed to be creative in using it. First, this set is much bigger than the standard low profile that came with the trundle set because of the locking mechanism as well as the larger size frame to house its double ball bearing seal. The drawbacks are as follow:
1) Due to the limited size of our trundle bottom frame, we could not take advantage of the 360 swivel of the wheel but only about 30% rotation but that's adequate for our need for the rolling in and out of the trundle.
2) This wheel set is really quiet and well made. The locking mechanism is amazing because our wooden floor is not level due to our old foundation so this wheel locking mechanism helps prevent the trundle bed from moving itself out of place.
3) The height of this set is about 1/2" taller than the standard trundle casters so the top of the trundle mattress has barely enough space to roll-in the frame of the trundle.

The bottom line is this set is perfect fit for our need as a replacemet caster set for our rollout bed because all we need is rolling in and out AND we needed a wheel locking mechanism because our standard trundle wheels set has no wheel locking capability. If you want to use this set for your rollout bed, you better have extra drill bit to drill another set of hole to install this casters wheels set. Furthermore, it does not come with any screws so you need to order a set of large wood screws because the screws for the standard rollout bed is too small for this casters set. If you have the right tool and the right screws, then this caster set is a nice replacement for your rollout bed, especially if your house has a bad foundation like ours.

text:
I just started doing 3D printing, using a XYZ DaVinci 1.0 Pro. After using up most of the spool that came with it (ABS), I ordered several different brands/colors/types to try out. This was my first one to try since it was white and I am printing a cabinet in my shop for organizing my resistors. I needed tiny (and I mean TINY) drawers because there's so many different standard values. I have rarely found a commercial cabinet that worked well; most are just too big and cumbersome.

Anyway, I started out with the white ABS roll in the Jayo 5-pack. A little trouble initially with warpage but that's expected (the DaVinci 1.0 Pro bed only goes up to 90 degrees). Once I got that solved, this thing is printing like a maniac! The filament from Jayo is smooth, precise, and seems to flow well. It is performing at least as good as the XYZ filament that I had. It is also repeatable, which I like. I get one good print and I can repeat that unattended, just recalibrate the bed every few prints.

5 stars, will definitely consider buying again. This 5-pack is a good deal as well, averaging only $14 a roll.

These are perfectly fine, but they don't compare well to the Dixie polycoated food trays, which are also available on Amazon. These SC trays don't stand up nearly so well to greasy food and they're actually smaller for the same poundage. The reason is that the Dixie trays draw a three-pound line well below the top of the tray, while these SC trays apparently hold three pounds of food only if you fill them right up to the brim. The Dixie trays are also made from a heavier weight of paper and I think they're more attractive than these brown SC trays.

I will note that on the date I'm posting this review, these SC paper trays are a lot cheaper than the Dixie trays, so if price is a priority for you, these SC trays are OK.

title: A good, solid and well-designed pH meter with reasonable accuracy and true temperature compensation.
text:
This pH meter is made by Apera Instruments which is known for high end pH meters that are used in research laboratories. This instrument is value priced, but has electronics that are competitive with higher end pH meters. I checked the accuracy of this instrument using a series of standards and found that it is indeed accurate to 0.1 pH unit when measurements are made with 2 pH units of one of the calibration standards. I further verified that temperature compensation is accurate. There are many inexpensive pH meters for sale on Amazon which claim temperature compensation, but actually have none. This meter is nearly perfect for checking the pH of a pool prior to adding chemicals to control the pH. Two-point calibration is adequate for this application, but this meter will do 3-point calibration for those who feel they need it. (One needs a pH=10 standard to do that. Only pH=4 and pH=7 solutions are included in this bundle.) This meter also reports the temperature, which is very nice.

Apera provides a useful video showing the two-point calibration process [...]
This is a good, solid instrument. I took off one star for lacking a backlight which for me is a critical component of any pH meter, and a feature that should have been included for the price. That said, I would recommend that anyone who plans to use a pH meter in a non-hobby application where accuracy is important to step up to the Apera PH60 instrument which is far more accurate (+/- 0.01 pH unit), includes a backlight, and is only about $30 more.

So far so good. If things change I'll come back and update but as of now, I love this thing!

text:

If you're stacking plastic hangers or the thin "huggable" hangers, you'd definitely be able to fit way more than I currently have on here. I think it's a good buy for the price.

title: Good reflectivity but NOT a strong adhesive bond.
text:
While the reflectivity of this tape is good its adhesive strength is not.

Before committing the tape to a project I'm working on, I decided to do an adhesive test to make sure the tape would hold for my particular purpose. I used alcohol to pre-clean a painted metal cabinet I was using for my test. I put two pieces of tape on the pre-cleaned surface: one of them was a clean sample where nothing touched the adhesive side of the tape before pressing it into place; the second piece was attached and repositioned several times as well as my fingers touching the adhesive surface of the tape several times before adhering the tape to a freshly cleaned area.

The tape was left undisturbed for 6 days at room temperature. The manufacturer claimed the tape could take up to 72 hours to fully cure and reach its maximum adhesive strength.

The results after seven days of curing is that both pieces of tape peeled off easily (without much effort) leading me to believe this tape isn't a good choice if your are looking for a strong permanent bond. If on the other hand your needs are only temporary, this tape will probably work fine as long as the tape won't need to undergo any severe weather conditions.

title: Critical Design and Operating Flaws
text:
The first problem with Eibos dryers is actually not the worst. I have ordered several of this dryer and also their Cyclopes dryer. I am not exaggerating: the DOA rate for both was 50%. Fortunately, one can just return them.

The more serious issue, also reported by others, is the off or uneven temperature control inside the box. It needs to have a temperature gauge/display. The first 3 spools of Prusa PETG run on 2 different dryers have all fused together in the last half of the spool. We are talking about more than 1" of material left from the center core. The filament becomes very brittle and fusing together like a giant brick. After the first one, I was very careful to have the printer dialed to lowest range. In fact, I have kept it just below the PETG range for several prints, and it still happens. So, either the temperature control is terribly off, or there is a significant temperature gradient from the heater element to the temperature sensor. I suspect it is the latter. The heat is blown out from the central holder, and I think it is getting far too hot in the center of the spool.

This problem is very significant, because it causes significant pull on the mechanics during print. It caused many prints to fail, but my bigger concern is causing damage to the printer. So, I have taken them out of service, and they are now taking up space in a cabinet.

I compared this pH pen to the Abbott Architect ci8200 (laboratory analyzer for human testing) and found the pH to be off by about 0.3. That being said, I am confident that the pH pen will get you numbers that are in the ballpark but the advertised accuracy may be a bit of a stretch. Also, I was caught off guard that there is not a recommended calibration schedule. Instructions pretty much say to calibrate as needed or after not using for a long time. title: Check your Home Brew tap water
text:
I purchased this as an addition to by LaMotte BrewLab kit to measure pH to improve my home brew beers. I worked in a chem lab along time ago where our analog pH meters were continuously soaking and we calibrated before each use. You also had to measure the temperature of your sample and manually correct readings.

I chose the PH20 due to its size and the company's reputation. The calibration procedure is easy enough: rehydrate initially in the 4.0 buffer for 15 min, rinse with demin water, calibrate with the 7.0 buffer until it indicates it's done, and you're all set. You can also do a 2-pt calibration with the 4.0 and 7.0 solutions provided or a 3-pt calibration, but you will need to purchase the optional 10.0 solution. Since I'm only measuring tap water, this kit was fine for my use. It even does the temperature corrections automatically. Nice. Overall, I'm very happy with the unit and am looking forward to see if my home brews improve.

text:
Just received my Apera AI209 and all I can say is "I`m thoroughly impressed"!! Meter came packaged in a protective carrying & storage case with a foam insert with cutouts for the meter, solutions, lanyard and batteries,, something you`d expect from high end manufacturers. Pen feels sturdy and well built and LED reads well and easy functionality of the 2 buttons,,, a far cry from my first meter which came in a cardboard box, instructions and 2 packs of buffering solutions and no "faux" leather pouch. Additionally meter came with batteries installed and factory calibrated with certificate and an easy to read laminated instruction card enclosed.
I`m relatively new to the ph world and have learned the hard way of the importance of monitoring your ph levels and frequent maintenance and care of your ph meter through the lack of knowledge and inexperience.
I am no longer on the bottom of the learning curve but still have a long way to go.
To conclude, this is my initial response to the Apera AI209 and I`m confident that I`ve made the right choice but only time and usage will tell and believe me,, if I have anything negative or contrary to say,, I wont be shy!!!
UPDATE 11/05/2019. After 13 months of use, meter still works fine and accurate. I only have 1 issue as the meter takes some time to get a final reading after the "smiley face ' appears but well worth the wait for an accurate reading. I`m so satisfied with this meter that I`ve just purchased the Apera EC60 replacing my EZ TDS meter which was impossible for me to calibrate plus I`m not a fan of button batteries.

title: So far not great
text:
I used the unit twice before it would no longer read correctly. First time I used it was to check calibration with provided solutions (they were sealed and leak-free unlike some other reviews), so I could test my samples. First day of use was a success, everything measured correctly. Followed the manufacturer's recommended storage method and put the unit away. 2 days later, rinsed the probe off before testing my samples and the unit was reading 5.0. My tap water is 7.3 and the unit also reads it as 5.0. Ph 4.0 solution reads 3.8, but 7.0 reads 5.0. Unit would not recalibrate, even after making sure the probe was clean and there were no air bubbles inside.

I'm a bit disappointed as of right now. The case and everything included made the product look promising, and Apera seems like a quality company just by the packaging and laminated instructions card. I know defects happen, and I will give Apera one more chance to make it right. I spent hours researching before choosing Apera for my next handheld, as I wanted to make sure it would last a while.

title: A wider variety of butt connectors than any other kit I own
text:
[[VIDEOID:a0a6e69ee44bbaae5af42b12f2ab57cf]] I'm a mechanic that fixes everything and I have a customer who bought a boat that, among other things, needs a partial wiring harness to be replaced. Replacing part of the wiring harness means that I'm building a new part of a wiring harness from scratch. Since this boat is carpeted and now has new upholstery, I don't want to risk dripping solder on it. As such, I brought in this large variety pack of heat-gun style butt connectors made by Haisstronica.

The case the butt connectors comes in is nice, closing with two snap-clips with the case halves lining up easily and thereby securing the butt connectors within from becoming a yard sale inside the case. Moreover, each type of butt connector sits in its own tray within the case and those trays can be removed and brought over to your work area. Well thought out, Haisstronica. See my video for more!

title: First Impression: Easy to Use, Appears to Work Consistently.
text:
This meter is easy to use. The instructions are clear and come on a laminated card.

1. Stir vigorously when calibrating and testing. Even though the smiley face appeared, it continued changing for a while. Don’t think of this as an “instant read” pH sensor. Give it a bit of time to settle.
2. My degree is in chemistry and biology. I’ve worked in several labs and used pH meters before. I know how to care for lab equipment. (Yeah, I dropped a quartz cuvette. Oops.) I’ve seen reports on here that the meter has problems after 60 days. I’ve had that problem with previous meters. I will come back in 90 days and give an update review. I’ll use it a lot in that time period as I have two aquariums that have a high pH due to local tap water. So this pH meter will get a workout.
3. The videos were helpful. It won’t hurt to watch them.

text:
This meter is great, it's got clear instructions, allows you to calibrate to +/- 0.1pH For the low and medium sections of the pH scale using the included 4.00 pH buffer solution and the 7.00 pH buffer solution. title: I'm sure there are brands that work well; this is NOT one of them
text:
Two stars, only because the shrink tubing is VERY nice, and the adhesive KINDA works, sort of...

I had high, high hopes for this version of the "self-soldering, waterproof, butt joint connector" that so many companies offer. The reviews looked quite good. This was my first time buying a product that does this. This one is a fail, BIG TIME.

I used an SMD heat gun to concentrate hot air ranging from 120°C all the way to 165°C to try to get the "low temperature" solder to melt. It never did. Not on the tiny, 24 AWG size, nor the 12 AWG. They would KIND of soften, I guess, a little. But they would never flow. Not even close. The typical melting point for this type of solder is 125°C to 140°C. I started to get nervous about damaging the shrink tubing, or at the very least, the insulation on the existing wire.

I even tried applying flux to the wires first. I went as far as to take the little solder ring out of a tube, put it on my workbench, and heat it at 165°C with DIRECT heat, and it just kind of softened into an ugly, misshapen blob-ring. It did not do what solder is supposed to do, i.e., liquefy and run a bit. The joints are probably OK in the connections I made, but only do to the squeezing pressure of the shrink-tube and the little bit of softening that probably makes a decent contact. But it's not "soldered" properly. Not by a long shot.

title: High quality meter, with reliable and verifiable results
text: There are other, cheaper meters - and several that cost much, much more. However, for most people, this is the one you need. If you calibrate it (and that was a must for me), store it correctly (moist, but not actually in water), and give it a little TLC from time to time (soaking it in the 3M KCL fluid to restore its ionic balance), it will serve you well. I use it for my hot tub, and when calibrated weekly, it matches the Taylor kit drop test exactly - just with greater precision, and it gives you a nearly unlimited number of daily uses - which is helpful if you're adding acid to your hot tub and want to prevent any hot spotting and over dosing.  BUT, one critique is that they didn't include the high pH calibration solution in the kit I purchased. If you want to reliably test over a pH of 8, you need to buy that fluid separately. (There are actually 3 total calibration fluids you need - and they only gave me 2 of them.) Still, even if you have to buy it separately, this is the best meter you can get for the price point.

title: This one’s a winner
text:
The black material is prusament pc-cf blend, the chain machine is black pls+, prisa galaxy gray, and some dual color pls.
So, as usual let’s start with the cons, some spools fit in this dryer better than others. I’ve only come across one spool that didn’t quite fit properly. All the rest have including my favorite, prusament (love their carbon fiber polycarbonate blend). You’re not going to be able to stuff a 2kg spool in it and the display that comes with it only shows humidity not temperature. Now the pros: It’s works great!. The temp can be adjusted from pretty low for pla and much higher for polymers like polycarbonate and nylon. It fits a pretty wide range of spools. I find that spools with openings in the sides dry more quickly than spools that have solid sides. The fan makes all the difference. Some other dryers just heat your filament. That’s great and all but we want to remove moisture content so air circulation is key. Where I live relative humidity is quite high and inside the house it’s rarely below 55%. Not quite optimal for storing filament especially without a dry box. A few rolls I have purchased have come in “wet”. This puppy dried them right out, and after into a dry box they went. Many times I will print right out of the dryer, even if the filament was in a dry box. I feel like the little bit of moisture the filament carry’s into the extruder can be mitigated and give a better print. I’ve even used this “off label” to cure prints. Put four glasses down, one under each corner. This raised the fan inlet and air outlet up away from my print table. Toss a few parts inside and them bake over night. I’ve ran this dryer for hundreds of hours and have let it run continuously for days on end for very large prints, it has worked perfectly. I don’t think it would work well for storing filament even with desiccant in the holders as there are a few openings and no gasket on the door so I usually just turn the temp to the lowest setting and let it run until my next print which is usually not long. Per the review prompts I will mention that wet filament usually has issues with stringing or issues bridging due to bubbles caused by moisture. Drying your filament will mitigate that. So far this has been a great little machine and hopefully continues to be.

title: if your AC is tripping the breaker on startup, consider this
text:
installed on a goodman GSX130481BC

our central AC kept tripping the breaker on startup, so i did some research and arrived at the possibility that the capacitor could be causing this (the cap can't supply enough power when the AC kicks on). read numerous guides and watched numerous videos about how to test/replace, and eventually worked up enough guts to turn off the power and try it myself.

disconnected the old cap and verified with a capacitance meter that it was fried (the 45 uF side was only registering about 19-20 uF). took pictures with my phone of the wiring, picked up a new mounting strap at lowes (since this one is smaller in diameter than my old one was), and installed this new capacitor. once i committed to making the swap, it only took about 15 minutes from start to finish. turned the power back on, and the AC started right up. going to be picking up another one of these to keep on hand, since my research also suggested they fail often.

tips for installation:

1) make sure you discharge the old cap first (there are plenty of videos showing many methods to accomplish this). it may already be discharged (it was in my case), but better safe than sorry. don't zap yourself when disconnecting the old cap.

2) take lots of pictures of the wiring before disconnecting the old cap, so you know how to install the new one and what wires go where.

3) if the new capacitor isn't the same size as your old one, go to the hardware store and buy pluming hanger strap for about a dollar and use that to mount the new one, rather than trying to mess around with bending the old strap. this is optional but i figured it was a good idea.

title: Buy This Instead of a Cheapo pH Meter!!
text:
I use this for mead making to maintain a pH of 3.8 throughout primary fermentation and have a few things to say.

First of all, buy this and not one of those cheap pH meters. There is a HUGE difference. Those cheapo pH meters will stop working the first time you accidentally dip them too far into your sanitizer bucket. They'll also automatically shut off while you're waiting for your reading.

Now, on to why this is worth the money. Not only is this pH meter waterproof and comes with calibration solutions, but it is extremely accurate and gives a temperature reading as well. Probably the most convenient aspect of this meter is that it doesn't automatically shut off while you're waiting for the reading to balance out.

One last invaluable feature. Instead of having to fill a small cup with must and then setting the pH meter into the cup, the cap of this pH meter IS the cup. You take off the cap, fill it up, set it down, then push the pH meter down into it and it snaps back on and gives you your reading. It's incredibly easy to do with one hand too. Man, what an upgrade!!

title: It’s an ok product
text:
At the very beginning it was very difficult to make this work... I used a lighter, heatgun, torch, soldering iron, and nothing seamed to work .. it will shrink the tube and seal it but the metal wouldn’t melt unless if you would melt the plastic with it .... meaning the tube Burt to an extreme that it became useless.... so after practicing with half of the quantities that arrived in the box I learned that using a lighter is way better than using anything else I mentioned above, but you still have to put the tip of the lighter flame about 2”-3” away from the middle part and eventually it will do it’s job, be patient and rotate the wire only after the first stage of the shrink tube actually shrinks to distribute the heat all around and you will notice the solder to begin melting and spreading out ... once it begins spreading out give it maybe another 5 seconds on the flame while rotating and if everything didn’t melt and you still see a part of the metal formed as a ring leave it as you will never get that to melt unless if the plastic starts burning or worse the actual wire.. then your toast!! So if you see that the shrink is getting black using a lighter that only means that you have the flame touching the shrink tube and your way to close... don’t let the flame touch the plastic keep away from it ... if you use that lighter and place your finger 1 feet above that flame you probably won’t feel the heat but the lower you get the hotter it gets... 2-3” away from the plastic is enough to melt the plastic first and then the metal.... it takes practice like everything else ...

To the guy that compared this to a carpenter hammering finishing nails with a mag light .... it’s not the proper tool for the job and I get that....but it can be done if that’s all you have available.....man when I was younger like 10-12 yrs old and couldn’t afford anything, I would hammer nails with my moms heels and a spoon for more hammering area... so anything is possible ..... the key is not to loose patience and don’t let the world close on you ....🤦‍♂️🤦‍♂️🤦‍♂️🤦‍♂️

title: Bed seems to heat fine, hole measurements in specs are NOT correct
text:
Ok, so the bed seems to work fine. However, I designed and laser cut a custom bracket for the bed based on the assumption that the holes were 214mm apart, as stated in the description:

"Product Size: 220mm * 220mm * 3mm hole spacing 214mm"

This was not correct, rendering my beautiful custom laser cut bracket to be subjected to hacky fixes using a drill. I wasted a lot of acrylic on this! For any future people, the holes are actually 208.2 mm from center to center (and 205 from side to side) with 3.2 mm diameter holes.

If you are going to put a specification in your product description, put the correct specification in it. Otherwise, just don't bother.

title: Not water proof!
text: A PH meter or anything else that fails this fast it NOT WORTH the money it cost to own it. I received the Aspera PH20 less than a month ago. I was EXTREMELY careful not to submerge the PH20 into the medium (water) beyond the 1/3 mark as I had already seen reviews warning against doing so. I needed to water the roses two days ago so As I turned on the ph meter, it was 'glitching out'. I opened up the sealed, pressure fit, cap at the top-end and both tops of the batteries (+sides facing up on them both. Strangest thing ever) where wet and rusting! I let it set out in my room at 77° with 45% RH to dry. Instaled no batteries today and It will not Calibrate or read anything but 7.0-7.2 ph. So- now I have $200 worth of plants that I'm in fear will not make it out of this without taking a big hit! PH it a big deal in growing and Its not like this was a cheap freakin' PH meter. People in the real world have to save 2-3 weeks for something like this just to have it FAIL! I've looked and looked on my Amazon orders to find a way to get a hold of the seller to no avail. I hope they see this and make this right. Its not as if I have another $55 floating around to blow on another worthless buy. I'll try to call apera on Monday but we all know how that will go. "You need to contact the Amazon seller, your warranty is through them". I'm sure I'm F'd but I'll update if/when this is resolved.

title: A bit tricky to install, but so worth it!
text:
I recently purchased this BLTouch sensor for my Crealtiy Ender 3 Pro. It arrived quickly and well packaged. It appears to be a genuine BLTouch 3.1 in a genuine Creality kit. The kit has all necessary hardware for installation and straightforward but not helpful-to-me instructions(see below).
After haunting youtube and FB for advice and tutorials, I took the plunge and installed the thing. It took about 45 minutes for the physical install and a couple of hours to work through the software changes. I didn't use the included firmware flasher, as I had previously installed a bootloader and Marlin 2.0.1. Just needed to make some changes in the Marlin config files and flash the new firmware. Simple enough, once I had updated the IDE and libraries. Could do it much quicker next time.
Once I had it working and calibrated, I couldn't believe the difference in my prints! Perfect adhesion and flat, smooth bottoms. No more bed leveling! Now I cant imagine doing without it. It's definitely my favorite mod so far.

title: Expensive meter for such a short lifespan
text:
This meter works very well. It is easy to use, is very accurate, and well built.

But, mine only lasted 18 months before the probe went bad. Notice that the warranty on the probe is only for 6 months. The probe is NOT replaceable and the manufacturer clearly states that the probe will only last for 1-2 years. Which means the meter is only good for 1-2 years.

There are much cheaper meters that are good enough If you only need to use it occasionally and are okay with a throw away meter or more expensive meters that have replaceable probes that would be cheaper to own in the long run. This meter seems to fill a spot in-between those two where it is too expensive to just throw it away once a year and it doesn't last long enough to warrant the high price tag.

title: Accuracy?
text:
The meter is packed really well. Instructions are somewhat confusing. It appears my unit was already calibrated because I had the smiley face and LM when I turned it on. I tested the same water multiple times with very different results. I cleaned and dried the head with distilled water before initial and subsequent testings. I refreshed the distilled water each time also. First reading in my water sample was 7.5, then I turned it off and cleaned it and got a second sample from the same water source and it was 6.5. Did the same procedure a 3rd time and it was 6.2. Each time I tested it showed that the unit was calibrated with smiley face and LM. When I put it in the PH 7.0 calibration solution is read 6.9 consistently but kept changing when I put it in my water sample which was from the same source so not sure why it jumped around so much?
Returning this unit and going to try PH testing solution instead.

Seller- I made sure my shapeoko XXL grbl software was the latest and greatest and I also made sure my Carbide Motion was up to date. Just an FYI, the Carbide Touch probe ($120) actually uses a different header (3-pin - as it has an LED and needs 5v). I used the header that is shown in your picture and is labeled 'probe'. Maybe this older probe header is disabled on the newest Shapeoko XXL. Since i don't know the pinout of the new header, I didn't want to chance plugging your touch probe in it. This is the only thing I can think of because all this thing does is toggle a bit.

Also note, the 120 dollar Carbide touch probe only works with the latest carbide motion (416) and latest GRBL firmware (1.1), so makes me think, the old header has been disabled in software.

title: The BLTouch is making my prints come out great!
text:
I installed this kit on my Ender 3. I followed the directions found on Teaching Tech's YouTube video. The installation of the BLTouch is very easy to do. The included mounting bracket is great so you don't have to print something that will work. I installed Marlin as suggested in the video so it's easier to adjust the BLTouch. The Capricorn tubing that comes with the kit and the springs are a big upgrade from the stock bowden tube and springs that come with the ender.

A few side notes about installation. As far as I could find you need a PC to flash the printer. I wasn't able to find anything that would work on a Mac. Because of the limited memory size of the Ender 3 the Marlin version has to have a lot of the LCD menu options turned off. Most of them aren't anything I ever needed except for one. After installing everything I went to calibrate my e steps and the menu for changing it wasn't there. I was able to hook up octoprint to the ender and with a plugin change the e steps to what I needed.

Overall I'm very happy with this kit. It did take a little while to fine tune everything but now it's printing like a charm.

title: Wow. Customer service!
text:
I had a major issue when I first received the device... The readings were all over the place. I reached out to the Apera Instument customer service desk on their website. Tyler responded to me within the hour. Unbelievable customer service for a $40 product!

The problem was that I had a tiny bubble of air in the glass sensor bulb. The fix is to the hold the device like a wand (sensor away from your body) and wave your arm down in a fast motion… Kind of like you’re trying to get the water out of the end. The bubble disappeared and the device works perfectly.

Another plus with this device is that you don’t have to leave it soaking in storage solution… That said, if you do notice that the accuracy is starting to fade, you can stick it in storage solution for 24-48 hours to restore the sensor. As a note, the storage solution is available on Amazon.

title: Very poor product, just use real kitchen spoons
text:
I am teaching all of my children to play something as part of their musical education. I let each kid choose what they want to learn to play. I was getting these for my 12yr old daughter who wanted to learn to play spoons. Bad idea. We ended up not using them because they are so bad. These things are VERY cheaply made. The metal is very thin & weak and bends way too easily. They also sound tinny, weak and pathetic. If you are looking for a kid's toy, these might be fun for a toddler or something, but probably not.

After seeing how bad these are, I searched Youtube for "Spoons" and found some great tutorials on how to use regular old kitchen spoons. Regular kitchen spoons are solidly made, sound great, are very easy to hold, easy to learn to play and cost nothing. If you don't want to beat up your good stuff, go to the store and buy 2 spoons for $1. The difference in sound is very noticable. These Trophy things sound horrible, are hard to play, and really aren't worth buying. We have found that playing real spoons is enjoyable for kids/adults of any age. Trying to play these is not fun at all, and can be downright frustrating trying to get them to work like real spoons, they just don't compare.

The point is, if you want to use these as a rhythm instrument, or for elementary education, and not just as a toy, don't use these. Put in the extra 2minutes for a youtube search and see the difference real spoons make and then just use those.

title: Spectacular sound
text:
I'm a musician and do a lot of recording, and therefore need headphones which provide an accurate representation of the music I'm playing - you don't want to record something using headphones which artificially enhance the bass, because you'll think it has nice bass but someone else will listen back to it and it will be woefully short of bass, as they're not listening to it on something which boosts that aspect of the sound. These HD 300 Pro's seem to have very accurate sound reproduction - solid yet accurate bass, wonderfully detailed midrange, and highs which are crisp but not unpleasant.

I've got some Sennheiser HD 280 Pro's and these of course cost more, but I think they're certainly worth it. Bass is more solid and midrange is more detailed. I also have some 1MORE Triple Driver Headphones and although they're wonderful for casual listening, the frequency response isn't flat enough for studio monitoring. So these will be my go-to headphones for studio work from now on. And of course they're fantastic for casual listening as well.

As far as included accessories, there aren't any. The cord is of sufficient length for my purposes, but in this price range you usually expect a short cord, a long one, and a coiled cord. These only have one cord of medium length. There is also no bag or any other fancy goodies. Just the headphones in a cardboard box.

Comfort-wise these are fine for me, a bit tight and the foam feels a bit firm, but just like my 280's I'm sure these will break-in given time.

Overall I'm very happy with these; some additional cords and a storage bag would have been appreciated, but for pure sound quality, I'm totally satisfied.

title: Does Exactly As It Says : Takes any XLR signal and gives you a USB interface (max quality:16/48kHz)
text:
This device takes the headache out of trying to connect an XLR mic to a PC or from an XLR pre-amp (or other XLR devices) to your PC. I am using Windows 10 Pro x64 which was plug and play with this cable/USB audio interface.

I even had all of the correct hooks ups to deliver RCA line-in through my Creative ZXr from my Rolls Mini-Mic Preamp output, but for whatever reason, the quality was bad or simply had no sound output when using a Seismic Audio - SA-Y5 XLR (to RCA) Y-splitter to my line-in.

This cable fixed all my troubles with getting this to work and it couldn't have been any easier! I have the cable between my Rolls Preamp to the PC, due to the fact my Nady CM-100 needs phantom power. If not I could have connected the mic directly to the PC, but I do like having the additional volume control that comes with using a preamp.

I highly recommend this cable to anyone trying to hook XLR up to their PC. Your only other real option is to get a mixer which would allow you to take XLR and output through RCA or 3.5mm TRRS to the PC. Only trouble is that would cost you at least 6x more than this cable!

title: I went to my local dealer and tried out this P255 and loved it. The feel of the keys is true ...
text:
I play as a hobby. I had an old Baldwin RP1, about 20 years old, and the keys started failing.

So I decided to up for a keyboard instead of a console this time.
After some research, I went to my local dealer and tried out this P255 and loved it. The feel of the keys is true weighted piano feel. It doesn't have a whole lot of voices and I personally don't care, I use the grand piano voices most of the time anyway. I liked the fact that this keyboard has good polyphony and better speakers built into it.

I don't have an ipad yet for the p255 controller app, however the settings on the piano are fairly easy and consistent to get familiar with.

I must say, when I use headphones I think the high end of the keyboard has a slight tinny/tinkly sound, but using the regular audible piano speakers it sounds just fine. Could be a foible of my headphones I guess.

All in all I'm very pleased, and my local dealer matched the price here.
I also bought the Yamaha YKA7500 high-end double-brace keyboard stand, which I really like.

The one downside I found is that the sustain pedal won’t stay put on my hardwood floor, and slides away from my foot. I finally decided to anchor it with four small screws, two in the front end on either side of the cord, and two more on either side of the pedal. title: The Grand Experience...this is it!
text:
I don't have a $45,000 Grand piano sitting around my apartment and my neighbors love me for it. When I was trying out the different products, I had no reference to what a true Grand piano "feels" like. I trusted Yamaha and bought the P105 first ($600). Two weeks later exchanged it for the P 255. During those two weeks between, I spent A LOT of time with acoustic pianos in stores. I bought sheet music just so they wouldn't call the cops and throw me out.
To me, the P105 sounds as good as any competitor of the P 255. This is where the P 255 comes in. None of the competitors, including the P105, sounds as real and rich as the P255! Having the experience of touching the keys on a Yamaha true Grand C3, I discovered a few things between "the competitors".
The surface feel of the P255 keys feels EXACTLY like the Yamaha Grands I've touched. There's a porous quality. The black keys on the real Grands, whether wax, polish or materials were "stickier" than the P255. I like the P255 better on the black keys, although they are the ever most slightly thinner.
The touch, the most important issue next to sound, is EXACTLY the same as the Grands. You'll think I'm crazy but, go try one for yourself. I didn't find this result to be true of the Casio, whose sound I totally don't like, or the Roland touch, which was "weird". It terms of tough touch, Casio was the "thickest" although other more "Hanon" types might love it. I found it make sound too loud for the lightest tough. It didn't feel like the acoustic Grand whereas the P255 was exactly the same, even to when the sound occurred.
The store manager brought up a valid point, saying the Grand piano gives the player "sympathetic vibrations" which the digital piano cannot. That's true out of the box. I got a gentleman at George's Music to plug in the Peavey stereo 12" monitors and the sympathetic vibration I felt in my fingers with the Grand, I could now feel all over my arms, face and hands! It wasn't loud, it was FULL--as if I stuck my head under the hood of the Grand and the strings were vibrating inches away.
As an experience, the stereo monitors were "more authentically warm" than the acoustic piano. What was totally cool was hearing the digital recording of the hammers striking the strings, the degree of gentleness the sustain pedal was able to attain. I listened so hard for any notice of "fake" or distinction which would let me know it was not a real Grand and heard only...a Grand piano.
I listened without contribution to several shoppers talking about each keyboard. Casio. "Man, don't buy that. People will laugh at you. Casio makes toys." That's not true but, it's perception so, why do that to yourself. Me, personally, I think the Casio sounds like an acoustic piano but, not a Grand. It's missing something and I don't pretend to know what. Maybe it's "too upright" sounding. I think Ragtime would sound better on the Casio but I want something which can play Chopin, Liszt, Mozart...
The Roland? Just no. It did NOT sound like a Grand but in fact, had an electric boost, as if the strings were intentionally placed out of tune to "fatten" the sound. Kind of like the Kawai pianos sound. I'd hands down say, it might not be what everyone is looking for but, the Yamaha was the "most serious" sounding Grand piano doppelganger. I thoroughly LOVE my P255. It is a Grand Piano TO ME. I play several hours a day because I love the music and the device. It's too expensive. It doesn't have enough voices. It should be compatible with android devices. The metronome is not loud enough and STILL...it gets a five star review from me. It's about the Grand experience!

What pushed this forward as poor advertising is the fact that there is no mention of it 'not' being compatible with certain mics.

To follow up with this, the team representative I talked to assured me it works that it is my USB port that was the issue. Furthermore, I mentioned that the LED light blinks when plugged. He then mentioned that their technician said it does not support enough power. And to conclude, I asked if condenser mics were supported, they said yes. To elaborate, I replied once more to ask the technician if it doesn't provide phantom power to mics that needed it, and instead I was prompted a refund for a return.

2-stars are merited to cable quality and prompt customer service.

title: Decent guitar cable for practice, with one issue
text:
This looks and feels like a well built guitar cable. I have been using it for several weeks and overall it has worked well with most of my guitars (more on that later). The sheath looks nice and is very durable, but a little less flexible than some of my other cables.

I opened up the connector (see photo #3), which is more of an old style connector that allows you to unscrew the cover and see how it attaches to the plug. Inside was very simple, but the connection was well soldered, the wire gauge seemed thick enough, and the whole thing was encapsulated with a plastic cover to prevent stress on the soldered connection. This is more than I've seen on other budget cables.

The issue I have with this cable is that for some reason, it fits loosely in some of my guitars when plugged in. In most cases, this resulted in decreased volume that I did not even attribute to the cable until one of them also crackled, which caused me to look at the cable fit. Usually, looseness in the connection indicates an issue with the guitar jack, not the cable. But in this case, other cables worked fine, whereas this cable was looser. I'm still working through how big of an issue this is and why this would be the case.

So, overall a decent budget cable. The build quality is better than most cables I have seen in this price range. If you have 1-2 guitars and this cable fits well in the guitar jack, this makes a great practice cable - definitely not for serious live performances. However, if you have several guitars (in my case over 50) you will likely have some number of them where this cable will be unusable due to fit issues with the jack. With Amazon's return policy, it may be worth the gamble to give these a try.

title: Fantastic Pedal Value
text:
If I had access to inexpensive pedals like this in the 80's, musical history might be different, at least my personal music history, lol.

I was building my first pedal board in 20 years, as I had been using multi-effect boards from Boss (Me-80), an old A.R.T. multi-ffects, as well as the presets on my Fender Mustang III and Marshal Code amps. I had tried a handful of el-cheapo pedals from Don*** and Cal*** and was sorely disappointed.

I had a Strymon Blue Sky and EH Canyon and Proco Rat to start with, and this was the 4th piece of the puzzle.

The Proco Rat is a vintage one I got from my late father in laws estate, but it was too harsh to my ears...it seemed brittle, angry and unpleasant, and frankly, unusable. I had never stacked pedals before, but on a whim, I put this right after another inexpensive purchase I made at the same time, a Joyo JF-10 compressor then into the Rat.

Holy schnikes...I was about to dump the Rat on the market, but pairing this pedal with it gave it new life. I can go from dirty to the umpteenth level to just a slight breakup for some searing blues work. That's cool, but how does it stand alone? Well...

I turned off the Rat, and just played with the Orange Burst, and and fell in love with it. Dropping the gain all the way down and using it for just a signal booster for lead sections is effortless and just what I needed. Cranking the gain to 70% or so gives me close to what I had with my old Tubescreamer 808 in the mid-80's. I remember saving every penny I earned for 2 months at my part time job to buy my first pedal, the ill-fate TS that took a header off the stage and busted. The tones I was wringing out of this were just what I hoped for. She's a beaut.

It would be a bargain at double the price for me. Were it stolen/lost/damaged, I'd buy another without thinking about it. I'm thinking about going on a Joyo pedal buying binge, actually. When I kick the bucket in 20 years or so, my poor wife is going to discover boxes stuffed with pedals like this. I hope like hell they don't end up in a yard sale, but if they do, well, they served me handsomely.

text:
As soon as you pick it up, you can tell that this microphone is well constructed. It is heavy, solid and strong. The shock mount is similarly of good quality.

You do need to connect this to a device that provides +48V phantom power. One such device I tried failed to work with a laptop, as the laptop said there was too much power draw from the usb port that powers it AND carries the signal. Just something to be aware of.

Even as a relative recording novice, I was able to get crisp and clear sound. The included mic cover muffled the sound more than I liked so I decided it is better not to use it. I don't think this mic is as biased towards close sounds as some, so you may pick up noises in the room.

Where this microphone comes up a little short is that many cheaper microphones include a tripod or other stand and a pop screen. With this, you'll have to get those yourself. It will take 5/8" mount or a longer 3/8" mount male attachment (nested inside the 5/8"). It does include a nice, long XLR cable.

title: High expectations riding on the HD 300 PRO. Mostly achieved.
text:
There's a lot riding on the reputation of this HD 300 PRO. For one, it indirectly replaces the HD 250 LINEAR but with design cues of the HD 280 PRO.

I had the original HD 280 PRO and loved it for the price and performance. It was used to death and I stupidly chucked it once the ear pads and headbands of the faux leather started peeling without thinking I could have just ordered replacement parts.

My go to for everyday listening was the Audio Technica ATH-M50x. When connecting directly to a device, I find it a good balance between an over equalized set (paging those two hyped and over-marketed brands that begin with a "B") or a linear headset for critical listening and mixing. This is due to the low impedance of the M50x which portable devices are able to power.

Enter the HD 300 PRO.

With a frequency response of 6 Hz - 25kHz and a maximum SPL of 123db at 1 kHz, this will theoretically put other headphones within this price range to shame. At an impedance of 64 ohms, again another happy medium between headphones that perform well with portable devices versus high impedance headphones exclusively for home/studio amplification.

So my advice when listening to these HD 300 PROs is you'll need to crank up the volume slightly higher to wake the drivers up.

PROS:
1. Awesome linear response. Not for the usual listener expecting artificial highs and lows.
2. Mind blowing frequency response down to 6 Hz.
3. Generous ear pad sizing.
4. Overall fit is comfortable over time.

CONS:
1. Clamping on the sides is a bit disappointingly tight. Probably needs more break in.
2. Cable is secured by two Torx screws and provides a big inconvenience in portability. I'd love to be able to break down and remove the cable to prevent snagging and twisting while in transport.
3. No provided bag.
4. No other cables provided - coiled, various length.
5. Typical simple German low-key design.

Here's the thing, to truly appreciate the HD 300 PRO, you'll want to use a portable DAC/amp like the Apogee Groove. The 64 ohm impedance is not too bad, but they will sound more dull unless you crank up the volume. But inserting an amp in between will make you realise how awesome these truly sound such that switching back to your others headsets will just irritate your ears including going back to the ATH-M50x.

I'd love to make this my go to for everyday listening and not just for critical mixing, but the tad higher impedance makes this not the most ideal for portable devices. And with the lack of included accessories for travel including a bag and replaceable cable of various length, this stays at my desk.

For a product billed for professionals on the road, this would be a miss. The performance is there. Sennheiser needs to re-think how they can re-package the headphones to cater to both professionals and prosumers on the go. They need to learn the marketing achievement of their rival Audio-Technica which has less than optimal performance and durability, but the included accessories alone has won the hearts of plenty.

Hoping they wake up and find their footing.

title: Great headphone, but only a few small differences from the HD280
text:
I've been using these at my home and work desks for over a week, mostly for music listening, and I've been impressed by the immersion and the overall comfort when wearing them for hours. These do take my similar, old Sennheiser HD280s a level up, but are they worth the extra cost? It depends.

While I have a soft spot for closed-back headphones, the immersion/field of sound at times does remind me of an open headphone. I'm listening to a mix of pop, dance, electronic, which a bit of classical mixed in and it all sounds pleasant to me with this pair. While I've tried many headphones, I do prefer a balanced sound (like monitoring headphones are supposed to provide) that doesn't go too heavy on bass. Compared to the HD280 Pro, of which I've owned a pair for nearly 20 years, the new HD300 Pro sounds a bit clearer and a tad less muddy on mids and lows. The headpad, compared to my old HD280, is more comfortable with a nice split in the middle (though the new version of the HD280 also has a different adaptation). While I don't call myself a true audiophile, I currently own nearly 10 pairs of headphones (several from Sennheiser) to fit my own mood and surroundings, so I've definitely tried many models over the years.

Note there's a line in the manual warning not to use these on portable devices as you may damage your hearing -- a bit extreme, but nonetheless, remember these can get pretty loud (132dB SPL) so use caution with volume. They're 64 ohm impedance, which means they should be easy to drive with a portable device (and I've hooked them into my iPhone 8 and had no trouble driving them or issues with sound quality) as well as a mixer or other professional audio source.

In terms of actual features: the cord is thinner than the HD280 coiled cord with just a slight coil on the top, but the rest is straight, it's also lighter with less pull on the left earcup. It seems less heavy duty, but I think I prefer it over the coiled version on the 280 that often just gets in the way and can you weigh you down. It's replaceable with a purchase from Sennheiser and a torx screwdriver. Both models fold up in a similar manner, but the 300 just gets a bit more compact (though that is not a scientific observation). The only included accessories are a 1/4" screw-on adapter, a brief pictorial getting started guide, warranty/safety booklet, and a velcro cable tie. Overall, the construction seems quite durable and that I can throw these around (lightly) without any significant damage.

The isolation on these is quite good. I'd say it's just slightly below the attenuation of a pair of hearting protection earmuffs (keeping in mind these also have no anti-noise circuitry like a Bose headphone). More or less the same level of passive sound blocking as the HD280. The ear cushions are softer and have a bit more of a gel feel than the 280, but not significantly different. On the other hand, I've worn these for longer periods of time than most headphones (3-4 hours) and my ears don't get as hot as other closed models, so this is personally a win for me, though your mileage may vary.

Is the 2x price worth it? If you'll be wearing your headphones for several hours daily, want that extra bit of sound clarity with a good closed headphone, and perhaps doing some monitoring, then yes. If you're a casual listener that wants a good "desktop" closed headphone with the occasional "pro" project, the HD280 will still fit your bill nicely. But the difference is quite subtle, and for someone looking for a decent isolating closed headphone and only wants to spend a hundred bucks, the HD280 is the better choice.

title: nice mic, good shock mount
text:
This is a very nice cardioid condenser mic setup with XLR cable and shock mount. With the mic being directional, it reduces background noise to focus on the sound in front of it. This does require a phantom power supply or if you have a sound board, even better.

The sound is good. It’s solid and clear. It’s strongly put together and well built. The mic is mostly metal and has a nice, weighty feel to it. It connects to a cable firmly and securely.

I do like the design of the mic with the interesting hole design in the middle. Not sure it really helps with the sound but it makes it stand out. It also comes with a little handy foam windscreen.

It comes with a shock mount that I quite like. It’s plastic but the set screw is steel. This will hold up under regular and irregular use. It does not come with a mic stand other than the shock mount. For mounting to a mic stand, it has what appears to be a brass connector. I always like seeing brass rather than steel.

It’s supplied with a short XLR cable with metal ends that is good for desktop use. The cable locks in tightly and securely. I would describe this as a basic cable which is fine but if you plan on using it with a larger stand, you will be looking at longer cables.

XLR has been around for several years and has remained favored because it works. The cables are usually heavy duty and made to swap out. XLR can be used fully analog (if you have the proper equipment) which some people believe gives a richer, warmer sound than digital can.

This does require a mic stand of some sort, a phantom power supply and while it comes with an XLR cable you will likely want a longer one if you do much with it.

title: Excellent build, more low end than I’d like
text:
Cool looking microphone. Design reminds me of JZ mics vintage series. Will look nice on camera if creating visual content.

Metal construction, weighty and solid. Feels great. No concerns about build quality. Shock mount is plastic but does the job well and holds the mic securely. Foam windshield is decent and improves plosive rejection noticeably.

Included cable is cheap but works fine. Used it for all my testing without issue.

My immediate thoughts on the sounds are that the low end is a little prominent.

Talking up close on the mic (3”), proximity Effect is noticeable and things can get boomy real quick. A high pass filter can be handy here, which is easy post in the DAW but for live use you might need some hardware (my audio interface has a low cut / hi pass switch).

From further away, bass is lessened but still kinda noticeable. I was happy with the mid range and top end but always wanted to EQ some low end out.

With louder, sung vocals, happy with the end result, suits my voice rather well.

Acoustic guitar sounded pleasant and natural. Again, a little EQ doesn’t hurt but VERY usable recordings.

As a room mic for electric guitar, does ok. Didn’t test as a close mic.

Overall, it’s a fair price for a capable mic but there are a LOT of capable mics in this price range, some of which have a more controlled low end (Worker Bee II for example).

I like it but rating it 4 stars due to the low end issues mentioned above.
