title: Impressive booster with EQ cut-boost capabilities and better-than-expected durability
text:
I'm new to the Caline brand, but based on this experience for a very modest investment of around $30, I may be looking at one or two others. Caline is brand of Chinese clones/copies/impersonations of popular boutique pedals that usually cost between $150 and $300. I've used a fair number of clones, most of them Joyo, and had very positive experiences all around. I had heard that the Caline pedals were built similarly to the early Joyos, so I thought I would take a (pretty modest) risk on one.

The CP-18 Orange Burst appears to be a clone of the Xotic BB Preamp, which was actually a pedal I had barely heard of before I came across this one. I have not played the Xotic model, but the basic functionality of the Orange Burst is the same, and I'm pleased to say that it's quite good. More importantly, it offers something a bit different that the boosters and light overdrive pedals I already have, which is terrific in a 30-dollar purchase.

The Orange Burst, fundamentally, is a booster. There's a lot of debate over the technical difference between boost, overdrive, and distortion (my unit actually says "OVERDRIVE" across the bottom, but the cliff notes version of that is that by boosting the input gain of a guitar signal, you can create an overdriven sound.

Boosters, therefore, are relatively straightforward effects, and I would certain never pay close to $200 for one, as I am a hobbyist, not a professional, working musician. But the Orange Burst has two features that I find useful and a unique. First, it has independent volume and gain controls, which means that it operates more or less as a transparent clean boost with the Gain at "0" and the Volume turned up. This is a nice feature, since other boosters (like my EHX LPB-1) may have only a single level or gain control, so you can only really add gain/saturation, as opposed to just boosting your level.

Second, The Bass and Treble controls are independent +/-15dB boost/cut controls for high and low frequencies. What this means is that if you are using the Orange Burst as a fairly transparent booster, but your resulting sound it too bright (or dark), you can boost or cut the highs or lows without completely changing the overall tone. I know that EQ control on boosters has expanded in recent years (notably in the MXR Micro Plus), but I'm not sure that some of the other options give as much control as this pedal does at shaping your sound.

Plug this pedal alone into a relatively clean tube amp, and you get a pretty amazing range of tonal options - everything from pure clean boost, to bassy Bluesbreaker crunch, to "gainier" sounds you would associate with a more traditional OD or Distortion pedal.

Oh, and the build quality? I'm actually quite impressed so far. The early run Joyo pedals (JF-01 to JF-17) are a fair comparison, though I think the footswitch on this one might "feel" even a bit more reliable. There is a 9V adapter jack on the left side below the output jack. And while assume there was a ton of cost savings done on the circuit board and pots, the 4 pots have a good resistance to them, and, frankly, feel more comparable to my Wampler than some of the other "cheap" pedals I have played. Having said that, I do think that budget pedals like this are an "either/or" proposition: In most cases, you will get a perfectly functioning unit that will suit the needs of players who don't abuse their gear, but there is always the risk of a defective unit or some component failing that is some unknown percentage more likely than it would be on a unit from an establish company with better quality control. At $30, I feel that's a worthwhile risk, and I'm really enjoying the Orange Burst.

title: Fantastic pedal! Sound like what I feel a Maxon 808 clone should
text:
If low to mid-rangy overdrive is what you're looking for then this is a fantastic pedal with a great tone (especially if you play blues). I've had a Maxon OD808 for sometime and I've always felt it lacking and thin and just not powerful enough to really 'hit' me. THIS PEDAL? Different story. This thing hits and hits just right. The sound is (for lack of a better term) thin-ish, but in a full and striking way (you really FEEL this thing when you kick it on and there's body to it). If Blues is your thing, then this pedal can really kick a clean or on-the-brink-of-breakup amp into the danger zone and get you some killer tones--BTW, the controls on this thing are (as I prefer) VERY sensitive and have a very wide range to them (much experimentation is possible).

If you get this thing, it's loud, it's forceful and it's capable of a wide pallet of tone in the low to mid overdrive arena and is built quite solidly, as well. For the price--it's a STEAL. Get it.

title: Outstanding Guitar For Any Style....
text:
I originally purchased this as a back-up electric guitar. I am a busker, and it's not a good idea to play a $2000.00 Gibson ES Series outside in the weather. I discovered very quickly that this guitar is by no means a cheap back-up, and it has become my main weapon.

I am a little surprised that everyone rates this as a Metal-Only guitar. I play everything from jazz, blues, country, oldies, and easy listening on my Dinky and it performs splendidly, from a setting-your-teeth-on-edge Tele-like twang, to smooth jazz that rivals my Gibson ES 135. I have even used it as an acoustic, by adjusting the compression and EQ. It's all in the EQ, and sound mods. The Dinky will do anything you want t to if you just have a little patience.

I replaced the light gauge strings with Jazz mediums and changed the Floyd Rose springs over to the red Heavy Duty models. It required a re-adjustment of the Floyd Rose Trem, but it only took a few minutes. Now it can hang with a Tele on twang, or be smooth and creamy on the mid and neck pickups. I hardly ever use distortion, and the only effects I use are a little reverb and maybe some slight delay. When played clean, the sound of the Dinky falls somewhere between a Stratocaster, and a Gibson SG. I actually think it is superior to both.

The hard finish on this guitar makes it feel bomb-proof. Mine has been knocked off its guitar stand on concrete several times (it happens when you busk...), and all that happened was a few small scuffs that were easily repaired with white nail polish. The neck was fine even though it was smacked very hard, and it never even went out of tune.

If you want something to hang on the wall and impress your friends with, stick with a Strat or Les Paul. If you want a real tool that will go into the trenches with you and do what needs to be done, you need to look no further than the Dinky. Great job, Jackson.

title: Good little pre-load here, might need a few pilot holes
text:
Not really a 4 or 5 but I'll lean toward 5 stars. It's made pretty solid and a good deal for price.

For me, pickguards rarely come perfectly fitted and usually require at least a few pilot holes. Aside from that, the pickup sounds good and . The parts and wiring are decent enough, you get what you pay for in most cases. Didn't have any scratching sounds adjusting the pot. Whatever pickup height is set at the factory is just to get it out the door and like all others that are pre-loaded, it won't sound its best until adjusted. Set it too high and I can't get a decent clean, and too low I can't get a good breakup . I was able to adjust the height where I can roll off the volume to about 7 and clean it up while still getting the desired breakup at 10.

I only needed one or I'd get another one. I have no regrets about buying it and would recommend this pickguard.

title: This bass is so good!
text:
My boys are starting out on the upright bass and they showed interest in the electric bass. However I have a 6-string bass which is not really suitable for smaller hands. After much searching and YouTube research I found many people who said this bass was very good to great. Many said that the price point as compared to an American made Fender made it an easy choice. I have seen Mexican J-basses starting around $800 and American J-basses over $1000. So without even trying it I ordered it from Amazon. It comes in a cardboard box and is well protected inside. Out of the box, the setup was spot-on and the action was great. One review here stated that he didn't like Fender strings. They are not my favorite either but these strings were good. I borrowed it to play out one night and after 3 hours with the strings I thought they were a little too light for my touch but they are still good. They sound just fine.
Another reviewer said that the electronics were not good. I totally disagree. This is a passive bass so there is no pre-amp boost. I you expect that your expectations are not valid. The tone is that of an authentic Fender Jazz and the front, or rear, or both, pickup combinations all sound great. As it is passive you may need to rely on your amp or an preamp device to equalize the sound to you tastes but the source sound is pure. At my gig, I used a Fishman Bass pre-amp with it into some gigantic amplifier of unknown vintage and it was a great sound. I've also played it through my own amplifier at home without the pre-amp and it sounded great. When I plugged it in at my gig the other band members faces lit up when the heard the sound and they all thought it was a great looking bass.
The natural maple looks great and the finish on both the neck and body was perfect and very glossy. I know some don't like the neck very glossy but a little sanding will fix that. The seams of the 3-piece body were so good I had to look very closely to see that it was 3 pieces of wood. The pickguard is sturdy and the chrome knobs and cover have a good finish. The bridge is of the super-thin Fender type. Fully adjustable and there is plenty of sustain. As with Fenders of the past there are many options on the market if you wish to change the bridge. The tuning keys are typical thin chrome Fender keys. No concerns there. The neck pattern is not black paint it is truly set in the fretboard as is the black binding around the neck. It's well done and there are no gaps.
The balance of the bass is surprisingly neck-heavy considering the weight of the body but it is not a problem when playing it sitting down. It feels great to play this bass. The action is perfect and it is easy to play.
As it is a Fender shape it should take any upgrades that you may want to apply to it including pickups, pickup cover, bridge cover, tuning keys, nut, pickguard, etc. It's not really mine to modify but I did put Schaller strap-locks on it. That's all it needed in my opinion.

After having this one, I bought an additional one so my boys won't have to fight over it later.

My only complaint is that if they had basses of this quality when I started playing I would still have it and be playing it. I remember a bad period in the early '90s when the Fender J-bass was not as good as this bass is. I know that Squier has the reputation of being a bad imitation of a real Fender but this bass is good quality and should last a long, long time.
As a side note, I have recently played a Squier Affinity P-J bass at a price point of about $180 dollars and made in China. I was absolutely astounded at the quality of that bass. Same complaint, where was this stuff when I was starting? If this bass is too much money for your situation, get the Affinity. It's not as fully featured but the sound, action and feel are perfect, Fender really has top quality control. Get one while they are good or before the price goes up.

title: USB is one way only
text:
Works as expected. Input ONLY.

This is exactly what you'd expect, but you have to know to expect it. Many USB interfaces are two-way: input and output. This one is INPUT only. Mic to USB port. Don't expect to be able to send output to speakers.

title: This pedal captures medium bore OD tone perfectly
text:
This pedal is everything I had hoped it would be. The boost side of it will send a close-to-the-edge valve amp into clear-as-a-bell overdriven tone. No surprise there. When adding drive from 9 o'clock to 12 o'clock it -once again- provides the clearest, most focused OD tones without harshness. I run it with treb and bass at 12 o'clock.

The CALINE Orange Burst is capable of more drive than I typically use and it sounds really clear and crisp at higher OD levels...think: Billy Gibbons ZZ Top Tone when dialed past 12 O'clock. Tone knobs are sensitive and easily adjustable to get your tone profile set. Plays well with most other OD pedals.

Now for a surprise: The Orange Burst in front of my ZOOM G1x on is really fun. The ZOOM has some excellent 'verbs, delays and compressors as well as some good amp sims. Having the Orange Burst pedal in front moves clean patches into mild OD / volume boosts for soloing or just crunchy rhythm playing. I am shocked at how well it plays with digital processor partners fronting valve amps. Bottom line? Getcha one.

My advice is, if you think you are buying a good alternative to your amp, your not.  The Iridium does not react like an amp at all and it works even worse if you plug an overdrive or distortion into it.  So no, the Iridium is not a good alternative to an amplifier.  What a waste of money!  If I could return it I would but it will cost me $80 to return it.  Buyer be ware, not everything sold on Amazon is sold by Amazon and you could be subject to restocking fees to the tune of 20%.

title: Very good 'Marshall in a box' pedal
text:
Allegedly the Caline Orange Burst is a clone of an Xotic BB Preamp pedal, which is a 'Marshall in a box' (aka MIAB) pedal. I had this on the wish list for some time, and at this price I thought I'd better snag one and see if it's a good value.

I own a lot of MIAB pedals. A couple of them are Calines--the English Man sounds like a Super Lead Plexi, and the Rock Face has a JTM/Bluesbreaker kind of sound. Both are excellent Marshall style pedals, and I enjoy them both.

The Orange Burst fits in the middle of those pedals, I suppose. It's similar to the Rock Face in that it's voiced like a mid 60s Marshall. You can crank the gain and get to, say, JTM45/100 territory, but its sweet spot is a little cleaner. I currently have the gain on my Orange Burst a little above 12 noon. That gives me a desirable tone similar to some of Jimi Hendrix's slightly overdriven sounds on Axis: Bold as Love.

A word of caution regarding the pedal's volume control. It's a bit tricky to dial in, because it's not a simple level control where you just find unity gain. The tone is colored a bit by where the level is. Set higher than 1 o'clock, and the low frequencies become woolly and overbearing; set lower than 10 o'clock, and the low frequencies start to disappear and become like an AM radio. I have mine set to about 12:30--that gives me a good balance between a present bass and a normal treble. Then, with treble and bass set to my liking, I can find a number of good overdrive sounds just by dialing the gain like a throttle.

I like that the pedal has separate bass and treble controls. Many of my MIAB pedals have just the unified tone knob, which is usually adequate, if a bit limiting. The Orange Burst's dedicated bass control allows me to add a little warmer bass as I like, so it sounds a little like a Marshall Super Bass, if you want that. Or dial it back and it can sound more like a JTM. I think the bass knob sets this pedal apart from other pedals in its class.

A pleasant surprise. The Caline Orange Burst is a well-voiced Marshall style pedal, and I'm enjoying it very much.

title: Should never have been sent from the factory.
text:
Really disappointed. I found out why my Jackson Dinky was having trouble keeping tune. I decided to upgrade the tremelo and I put a floyd rose original on it. The problem turned out not to be the stock tremelo, instead they had mis- and over-drilled both holes for the locking nut, and only the lower screw had any bite into wood at all (~1/3 turn, just barely holding the nut on). Very disappointed in the quality of this guitar, and I won't be buying another one. It arrived with multiple blemishes on the face paint, also had drops of over-paint run that were never sanded down. Two of the tuners lost their plastic washers within a week. Also, it has cheap brass frets that leave slivers galore in your fingertips. I was always walking around with tweezers in my pocket so I could pull the metal slivers out of my left hand. I got sick of it so I decided to refret it, and that's when I found the root problems with the neck/nut mount. If you are planning on actually playing it, you will have to refret it. I did mine with silver nickel jumbo's and it's much, much better. IT's SOOOO worth it to save and get a guitar that doesn't have brass frets. They are aweful, unless you're a complete massochist.

I ended up completely re-doing my guitar out of disgust (and some boredom). I straightened the mis-aligned neck to body joint, ripped out the crappy electronics and wired in a set of Duncan Blackouts (AHB-1). I re-fretted it, put in Grover tuners and patched the old holes (had a set of black mini rotomatics that were burning a hole in my toolbox), reconstructed the neck wood and re-drilled the nut holes, properly this time. Put on the Floyd Rose original and a 32mm big brass block and it's now very playable and quite enjoyable, but it's definitely not a Dinky DKA-M any more. (Oh yeah, they also over-drilled the floyd rose body mounting holes, so they were consistently screwing everything up that required a power tool.)

One side note: For many, myself included, the volume knob is mounted in a postion that my hand hits it when strumming, which eventually causes damage to the pot, but also can have you accidentally changing the volume frequently. When I decided to put in the Blackouts , I moved the volume pot back to a hole that I drilled and routed an inch closer to the tone knob, and it's fantastic, not in the way at all. I did have to reconstruct the wood where the old hole was but after the paint job it's completely invisible now.

I have more hours in to this than I care to attempt to quantify, but looking back it wasn't worth it. Granted, it looks, plays and sounds great now, but I'll never get all those hours back. Save your money, get a nicer guitar that has these things done right, you'll surely thank yourself. It'll also have a higher resale value than a souped up chinese jobber like mine.

In short, it should never have left the factory.

title: Incredibly light and small; very bright, sharply defined projection spot; works well with mirror balls
text:
I have little experience with LED pin spots, having been trained using the big aluminum cans with fuses that easily blow out and heavy glass lamps that attach to positive and negative terminals and are secured with screw-tight caps that also house thick plastic gels and burn so hot that they cause serious burns and heat up a room.

The TSSS® Pin spot I received was so small and lightweight that I was amazed that it worked as well as it did. This pin spot projects a light through a small hole in the lens which results in a very sharply defined spot, similar to a film or video projector. The light reflects amazingly well from a mirror ball to create a clean, sharp reflection rather than the soft, round spots seen with conventional halogen pin spots. The reflections were a bit smaller and uniformly square-shaped; bright, but very clean and almost structured.

PROS
- Very easy to use and position
- Extremely portable and lightweight
- Long lasting, LED bulb
- Bright, sharply defined spot
- LED bulb stays cool
- No fuses or heat issues to worry about when setting up

CONS
- White light only
- No way to replace bulb or lens from what I can see

Despite the cons, this is a good light for a home enthusiast or party thrower. I was able to use a piece of red plastic film and an elastic to change the color of the light from white to red. Although it was easy to rig up, I would prefer a way to use a good fitting gel or lens that spins so several colors could be included. I especially appreciate the light weight, lack of fuses and cool temperature the light maintains, which allows it a great deal of flexibility when positioning the light and makes it very versatile and portable. I definitely plan on purchasing more.

Bottom line this means the cable will pick up a lot of extra noise - especially if it's a long cable. On the positive side this does work plug-and-play with an android phone.

The best part is that they make you feel like you sound in your head. This is what I wanted for my radio cans, this affects performance by giving you a positive fidelity between speaking and hearing yourself speak. That makes me better at my job. No lie. I am probably not going to use these for music gigs, Blue makes a great headphone with in-ear amps for that, but I’ll grind my daily on these any day.

title: Good, ergonomic harmonica (when you get it with a deal)
text:
Before I review the instrument I'm going to let you know that I'm not a Hohner fan, mostly I don't like their product... and their company, I bought this because it was at a lower price than usual (I paid almost 43USD for this brand new Rocket, key of C).

The good

Holes are big... really big, easier to pucker and to tongue block, overall the harmonica feels really ergonomic in the mouth, the most out of any harmonica I've tried. It looks and feels like good quality, cover plates are really comfortable in the hand and they seem to be crush proof with that thick middle support while allowing the harmonica to be open in every way, the back, the sides, the cover plates even protrudes a bit, like a trumpet and yet, it's air tight. Finally that zipper case is excellent, sturdy, protective, much better than the thin leather pouch Seydels come with.

The Bad

Regular price, I wouldn't pay 60USD for this knowing that I could get a Seydel Session Steel or a Suzuki Promaster. Tone is brighter than it should for a harmonica at this price, not as 'fat' and 'full' as other harmonicas I own.

The ugly

Not at this point, but will bet the reeds are going to be out of tune way before my other harmonicas, plus Hohner's screws wear out quicker being made from brass

But for close to 43USD, I now can get myself some Special 20, Progressive series, when they are at a discount, remove the reedplates and put them in my Rocket to have a nicer harmonica.

title: Able to lower my gain settings when using this mic.  Nice to have the headroom available to do that.
text:
Review of an XLR Microphone Cardioid Condenser Microphone XLR with 32mm Large Diaphragm for Computer PC Metal Professional Studio Microphone for Recording Podcasting Streaming Gaming ASMR Voice Over Vocals.

I plugged this in after removing a Donner Condenser Mic and I left all the settings the same as they were for a little voice over recording I did last night. When I started the USB interface to provide the +48V phantom power and connect to the voice over software again, there was hissing, which I recognized as too much gain. I was able to back the gain down from 9 to 6 and the hiss went completely away. I haven’t got another mic that gives me that kind of gain headroom on the interface controls. All my other mics (including the Donner, which is not too bad) are nearly maxed to get enough gain. This one does have twice the diaphragm size, which may explain it at least in part.

Nice quality metal shell, good looking mic, decent shock mount. The shock mount is the only option that comes with the mic for mounting it, which is a little disturbing since it is an unusual shape and may be hard to find another mount type is wanted.

I did some recording and in the process I turned away from the mic and got a noticeable drop in volume, then intentionally got right up in front of it and the volume swelled accordingly, but not obnoxiously.

Very happy with it. Nice microphone.

title: Good studio monitors, not a huge upgrade over older models
text:
I've been using Sennheiser HD 380 PRO monitoring headphones for about 5 years now. For the price, the they are comfortable for long mixing/recording sessions and sound really good. A nice flat response which is what you want from a monitoring headphone. I actually use the 380's for listening to music as well, I just like how they sound.

These HD 300 PRO are a newer model and sell for a little more than the time tested HD 380 PRO. Sennheiser has been a great professional brand over the years but it seems like they keep raising prices and giving less value for money. These headphones do not come with a case, and you cannot quickly remove the audio cable like with the 380 PROs. That said, the sound quality is excellent on the HD 300's. It's very even and sounds great from low end all the way up to the highest audible frequencies. They fit fine on my head, but the earcups aren't as comfortable to me as the 380s, and certainly not as comfortable as monitoring classics like the ATH-M50 and MDR7506. That said, they aren't terrible and I'm starting to warm up to how they feel on my ears the more I use them.

I'd say the best thing about these headphones is how they sound, but it's been hard for me to prove they sound any better than the excellent HD 380 PRO headphones, which are an older design, but are high quality and sound great. I do want to mention that these 300 PRO are also high quality construction, but I wish they ear cups were more comfortable when wearing them for long periods of time. Monitoring headphones are different from other audio gear because it doesn't seem they get better sounding over the years. It seems like audio quality stays about the same for a certain price point and overall quality goes down as companies try to maximize profits. I do like these HD 300 Pro headphones, they are definitely above average, but not perfect. The earcups do a fairly good job of blocking outside sound, so they are somewhat usable for front of house or monitor mixing, depending on how loud the venue is. I'm using these for studio mixing and recording. I'm happy with how they sound.

I don't want to come off too negative because these are great sounding headphones for monitoring audio, but it would be nice if they included a case and made it easier to remove the cable like if I wanted to easily switch between a coiled or straight cable for different uses. The cable is removable though, you just need to remove a couple screws. So that's nice if the cable does wear out over time. Studio monitors can last a long time, and once you find ones you like, you tend to use them until they fail. I have been using these along with my DT 990 PRO headphones which are a lot different than these but are some of my favorites. Those are open back but are in the same price range as these and another great option if it's ok to have sound bleeding out from the headphones when listening back. The Sennheiser HD 300 PRO are closed back and keep most of the sound inside, which is nice if you are using these in a place late at night when other people may be sleeping.

title: I used 150 at first and switched to 220 for fine tuning. I have a workshop so I also ...
text: Bought these to replace the originals on my two MIM Strats. The quality is there but you'll need to do some shaping and/or filing to get it to fit and function properly. Also, it is about an 1/8th inch short overall so you'll have a 1/16th on each side when done. In order to get the fit right I laid the nut on the fretboard right below the slot and used a sharp pencil resting ever so slightly on the board to trace the radius. Once I had that I got to sanding. Be warned, Bone is a slow sand. I used 150 at first and switched to 220 for fine tuning. I have a workshop so I also utilized my belt and disc sander to speed things up. You will also need a razor blade to score the finish around the old nut before removing. Once old one is off, keep dry-fitting until it's snug and the ends are seated in the bottom of the slot. Make sure the height above the fretboard is ok before installing it with tite-bond. My first run changed the action on my guitar drastically. I had to make some changes before I felt it was going to work. All in all, I'm very pleased with the quality and the improved sound. Would buy again.

title: Try the next level up just so you're informed
text:
In one day, I tried this, the Yamaha CP4 (NW action, their best action), the Kawai MP11, the Casio PX360, the Roland RD800, and a 7ft Kawai grand piano (I visited several local music stores). I'm not the greatest pianist, but I was serious in high-school/college and played pieces like Rachmaninoff's C# minor prelude, Beethoven's "Pathétique" Sonata on my teacher's Steinway model B quite a bit. I also play various Jazz standards.

None felt/sounded as good as the real thing of course (I'm not just saying that to sound elitist and cliche, it's simply true), but the Yamaha CP4 and the MP11 action felt the best. The P255B, the Casio, and the Roland all felt plastic-y to me, non-authentic. The action just didn't feel like a real piano at all to me, and switching between these left me feeling like I could never settle for the Roland, Casio, or lower end Yamahas. The MP11 seems to be the gold standard for feel with their "Grand feel" action. But the MP11 is certainly not really portable at 70lbs.

Anyway the CP4/MP11 are obviously much more expensive than this, but I just wanted to let prospective buyers know that if they want something as close to the real thing as possible, there are other more expensive options available that are still a fraction of the real thing's cost.

Disclaimer: I paid less attention to the actual sound vs. the feel because you can hook these up to a computer and get the best, massive samples of amazing grand pianos for pretty reasonable prices. If you're not willing to do that with a cheap computer/monitor/laptop, then maybe you're not that serious about getting a great piano sound. In 5 year a standard computer/display will just be integrated into the keyboard. It's troubling watching all of these youtube videos discussing the sound differences between $2k pianos. If you're spending $2k on a keyboard I don't see the point in locking yourself into the samples they baked into the keyboard. Not in 2015.

I'm always looking for tone shaping and "a bit of character" between the tele and the tubes, and this fits right in. The tone controls aren't harsh and (in my case) cleaning up some bottom end and adding a bit of sparkle was easy to do. As others have noted, the gain control isn't extreme -- more in the "just a bit of grit" range. I was pleased with the sensitivity of the pedal when switching from single notes to chords -- not a one trick pony.

In the mix and match category - I'd say that this one pairs well with the Pure Sky-- similar control set but with harder drive available.

Construction wise - it is a solid orange box with knobs. Quite happy with a Pedal Power iso supply, and it seems quite happy with the other pedals on the board.

title: Not sure what others are hearing that I'm not...
text:
I actually bought this twice and sent it back both times. I bought it when it first came out; couldn't get a sound I liked out of it. 2 years later was thinking about an amp modeller again (for recording), and all the positive Iridium reviews sucked me back in. Figured maybe I didn't give it a fair shake the first time.
But, the second time was just the same.

I played a clean tele through it, into an audio interface. Headphones were plugged into the audio interface. No matter the settings, I just could't get a full, well-rounded, balanced tone out of the thing. It sounds either too muffled or harsh and brittle. The best way I could describe it is: the tone sounds like it's put through a band pass filter. Like there's this crucial band of frequencies missing. It almost has a shrill "telephone" like quality. I'm not sure what other people are hearing that I'm not, but this thing just sounds bad to me. I actually liked the default AMP plugin in Ableton Live better.

THAT said, tone aside, it does have some interesting amp-like nuances happening with the attack transients. I liked the drive/saturation on the chime setting. I admire Strymon as a company and have the Flint and love it. Bummed the Iridium didn't work out for me (again).

title: Heavy, high quality mic delivers.
text:
This heavy duty XLR microphone has a simple design and is made very well. The weight of it will surprise you, it is solid and uses mass to help dampen vibrations. No tinny sound from this mic, as the gold plated diaphragm picks up everything though the wire cage. The wind cover is beefy, and sprung back into shape from being in the box in under an hour. There is no off/mute switch, but that means less opportunity for making noise in your recording as you touch the mic to hit the switch. Better to use the mixer to control the mic mute.

A slight weakness was with the shock mount. Mine was leaning to the left every so slightly, and I tried to straighten it which helped some. Nothing serious and certainly not worth taking a star, but it did ruffle my fastidious nature.

For the sound test, I ran the mic to my Mackie mixer, which has 48V phantom power, and the mixer into my Native Instruments A/D converter, and then into Reaper. Sounded Great! I also recorded a bit of acoustic guitar, and that also sounded great.

Big mic sound, for mid mic prices. Five Star XLR Pro-level Microphone.

title: Stick to the HD 280 Pro
text:
So, I've owned a pair for Seinheiser HD 280 Pro for around 14 years. They are still great, but have been falling apart. So when I got the chance to "upgrade" to these 300 pro headphone that cost more than twice as much, I was very excited.
These go for $200, the HD 280 pro go for $80 like once a month, but you can find them at retail of $99 any day. I wore them for 4 hours a day for those 14 years - my "work" headphones, so I am very familiar with them (and possibly biased, because I really like them)

That is the main problem with these headphones. They look similar and sound virtually identical. That means, they both sound great, and non-audiophiles can pickup noticeable differences between these and the earbuds included with cellphones (or any cheap pair of headphones/earbuds).

These headphones are more bass heavy than expected - not too terrible like other brands that crank up the bass, but not natural bass like I would have expected with "monitoring" headphones, or the HD 280 pro.

Overall, I listened to the HD 280 pro and the HD 300 pro back and forth the same songs, and there is virtually no difference in the sound quality or the noise isolation. The HD 300 pro are definitely heavier on the bass though, more punch - so if you like heavy bass you will probably prefer these. If you like more natural/neutral bass, the HD 280 pro are the winner there. They both put pressure on your head after an hour or so, but it's not terrible, and you get used to it, and can wear them for 4-5 hours a day.

So... these are good quality headphones. But do yourself a favor and spend half the money and go for the HD 280 pro. You'd be hard pressed to notice any difference (other than heavier bass) and save $100+ dollars.

If I didn't know the HD 280 pro existed I might have given these 4 stars, but knowing that you can get almost the same quality for half price cost them an extra star. The only way I could maybe recommend these, is if you love heavy bass in your headphones.

Quick overview of the good things/bad things that this shares with the 280 pro:
- Great sound quality
- Adjustable/foldable
- padded headed
- Expensive replacement ear cuffs (they will start going bad after a year or two if heavy usage).
- Not the most comfortable, since they "seal / put pressure" on your head to isolate sound, but you get used to them

Good headphones, but priced too high when compared to the HD 280 pro.

title: Not bad.....can't wait to see V2!
text:
I'm using this device differently than most. I have deployed it for gigging because I wanted to find a way to reduce the size and weight of my setup. I'm just tired of moving 100 pounds worth of head and cabs around to small/med sized clubs. Had a friend who let me borrow his Iridium for a couple of days. My thoughts follow.

Sound is decent. I'm more of a hard rock/metal guy. Just like a real amp......the Iridium rock tones are "just OK". However, just like a real amp, fronted with a Timmy (volume 100%, gain 0%) on the Marshall setting this little wonder sounds phenomenal and goes easily into metal territory. Cleans up decently (but not as much as I would like) with the guitar's volume knob. Sounds good with IEMS, and sounds even better into a PA speaker (or into my case, a Headrush 108 floor wedge). Clean and edge of clean tones on the Fender channel are excellent.

Running it very early in my chain, with chorus, delays, and a volume boost after it seems to work really well. Only pedals I have in front of it are tuner, and Wah. No problems running it this way.

Cons:

1. The "favorite" feature is nice. It lets you switch back and forth between 1 preset, and whatever the unit is set to. IMO it needs 3 favorite buttons built in, instead of just one........essentially making it a three channel amp. The on/off button should at the very least be replaced with a switch on the back .....at least freeing up space for a second favorite button.

2. The reverb to me is just horrible. Needs a complete re-work for live use imho....... I just don't use it.

3. Didn't care for the AC-30 channel tbh.......but some may find a use for it.

4. The controls, while analog are still very much "digital", with discreet increments. As an example if I move the volume from 7 o'clock to 8 o'clock I might not hear a volume increase, move it a slight bit more to cross the threshold, and there it is. Sadly, the increments are too wide for my particular application (stage use).

5. Spurious noises (lots of them on high gain). Doesn't affect me too much in a live situation, but I can't imagine using this in a recording environment tbh.

6. Sometimes when letting the high strings ring, the low strings are not loud enough (in high gain mode). For example, play the high strings on an Open E chord, then starting chugging the low E string. While the high notes are ringing the low chugging is greatly subdued. As the high notes decay the lower E chugging becomes vastly more prominent. It's almost as if there isn't enough polyphony capability in the unit. This is the biggest problem with this unit, and it was apparent on both units I tried. I'm hoping this will be addressed in a future update, because it's very distracting.

So even with the listed shortcomings, I went ahead and purchased one of these for myself because I really do love what it can do. It's just more "amp-like" than any other digital modelers I have tried (most of them). If you are looking for a simplistic solution that works with your existing pedals (like a regular amp does), this is the best out there.

title: A Worthy Successor To HD 280 Pro
text:
***** If you have not used circumaural headphones like these, make sure to adjust the earcups down to a comfortable level! Most people can wear these without adjusting them, but they will be very uncomfortable! *****

As a user of the HD 280 since 2008, I've been a fervent believer in Sennheiser. I was therefore quite upset when I discovered that they had stopped manufacturing and selling replacement components for the HD 280 for the last several years. I was even more annoyed when I discovered that the HD 280s being sold for the last 5-6 years have been entirely made in China and not in Ireland like mine were. Much to my surprise, when the headband on my pair of 280s broke, I found that Sennheiser had finally developed a successor to the HD 280: the HD 300 Pro.

I have to preface this by saying that I am by no means an audiophile user, nor a professional. I recognize full well that these are designed for sound engineers and other audio professionals. That said, I've tried a great number of high-end consumer-grade headphones over the years and they all sound *wrong*. The bass is overblown, the highs are muted or out of proportion, or the mid is muddled and lost. Just like with the HD 280, the 300 faithfully reproduces sound with crystal clarity, and the closed-back design ensures that nothing will disturb that reproduction.

This is a generally flat set of headphones - no one part of the spectrum overpowers any other. The mids might be a little quieter in the mix than the highs and lows, but not by a significant margin. If you're not familiar with studio monitors, don't mistake a flat profile for boring - these things will knock your socks off. These things attenuate a significant amount of external noise. You won't hear much of anything unless you're listening to very quiet audio. Positional recreation is perfect - you can pick out each instrument in a small ensemble and where they are in position to the microphones (also great for games). The definition is similarly excellent; you can clearly hear the vibration in string instruments and the impacts on drums. The range in volume is also spectacular. You can clearly hear instruments as they go from pianissimo to fortissimo (Edward Grieg's Hall of the Mountain King or Klaus Badelt's Fog Bound are great examples of this). These sound great listening to orchestral pieces, rock and roll, hip hop, metal, and house. All in all, the HD 300s are close enough the HD 280s that I'm not disappointed in the slightest.

Now, there are a few departures in design from the HD 280s, mainly to do with the cord and headband. The weird-looking headband cushions seem to do their job well, keeping the weight off the softest part of your skull - something that would occasionally cause some pain and discomfort with the HD 280s after several hours if worn incorrectly. So far the headband has been very comfortable. The earcups are perhaps a little tighter than I'm used to, but seeing as the headband broke on my HD 280s, it's more likely that I've forgotten what they felt like originally. They are still very comfortable - and as someone who wears headphones for 8-16 hours per day, both at work and home, I have no doubt that these will remain comfortable throughout the day for a long time.

The other major (visible) difference between the HD 280s and the HD 300s is the cord. For the most part, I really like the change to a mostly straight cable from a mostly coiled cable. It's maybe about a foot shorter than I would like it to be, but it's about the same length as the HD 280s was coiled. The major improvement is the coil at the earcup. Not only does this act as a small amount of give and resistance before you reach the end of the cable, it also dampens the vibrations that travel through the cord. The one thing that annoyed me about the HD 280's cable was that the coil stopped about a foot and a half away from the earcup, which meant that any movement from the cable in that space transmitted the noise directly into your headphones. So any time the cable moved on or brushed your shoulder or chest you would hear it loud and clear. With the new cable design you really have to smack that thing around to really hear it.

Speaking of cables, the HD 300 offer some hope for those of us who will want these things to live forever. The cable is now terminated in a connector that is screwed into the earcup - meaning no more soldering to replace a cable. The headband cushion appears to have the same zip-lock-esque attachment as the cushion on the HD 280s. The bad news is that I don't see how (without disassembling the ear cups) you would replace the ear cup cushions. I also don't see a headband replacement being in the cards - the earcups are essentially one piece and without removing the cushions I don't see a way to disassemble them. The other bad news is that Sennheiser has not yet listed any replacement parts other than the cable. That said, these have only been on the market for 3-4 months at the time of this review. It's entirely possible they simply haven't made any spare cushions yet.

Overall, I'm extremely pleased with the HD 300 Pro. The HD 300 Pro claims to trace its electrical design to the older HD 250 Linear model; I have not listened to those, nor have I examined the electrical design of the HD 300s so I cannot make any judgement to that claim. But I've spent the last ten years listening to HD 280 Pros, and, despite the loss of that pair, I'm as pleased as punch with the HD 300 Pro. This is very much a worthy successor to the HD 280 Pro.

title: A brilliant pedal that goes from a warm boost to killer overdrive.
text:
I built a pedalboard for my home studio using mainly the inexpensive pedals that have popped up on Amazon, etc. over the past few years. Like the Squier Classic Vibe series, the value & bang for buck is insane with some of these pedals. This one is definitely one of those head scratchers: HOW can this sound so good?!

It's no secret that this Orange Burst pedal is a BB Preamp clone. In fact most of the Caline, Azor, Joyo, etc Chinese made pedals are heavily based on the circuits of well known (and more expensive) "name" brand pedals. The BB Preamp is known to be an excellent warm boost that can push tube amps into a nice breakup. You can crank the gain and use it as an overdrive in and of it self of course, which sounds quite good, but it really shines when used in conjunction with an overdrive placed after it running together.

I am running the Orange Burst into the Joyo Ultimate Drive, an OCD clone. I used to have a Fulltone OCD and A-B'd it with the Joyo which I got it in 2016 (I was an early victim of the "cheap" pedal GAS strain.) I sold the Fulltone to fund more budget pedals based off of how great the Ultimate Drive is. When used together the overdrive I was getting made me break out in goosebumps, no B.S. I am keeping it set up on my board for the foreseeable future, it's an incredible combo. Highly recommended.

title: A fantastic product that solves a very expensive problem for just $10
text:
First of all, if you're going to use this product directly with a non-powered microphone without a microphone amplifier, it may not work. Note that most XLR microphones belong to this category. (Someone posted a video to initially say it does work, but later specifically warned that he no longer recommended doing that. It's completely surprising to me that it would work in any occasion at all. All this cable does is to convert microphone output signals to USB audio signal. There is no amplification in this cable. What most people don't know is that the vast majority of professional microphones do not have built-in amplification and therefore need a microphone amplifier, while most consumer microphones have built-in amplification and therefore do not need a microphone amplifier. The reason is very simple: professional microphones need versatility of preamplification, often very expensive ones. Having a built-in preamplification in a microphone deprives that versatility. Cheap built-in microphone amplifiers would create crappy signals, which once happens cannot be cured by any downstream amplification.)

BUT BACK TO WHAT THIS PRODUCT IS DESIGNED FOR,

if you do have a pre-amplified microphone or a proper combination of a microphone and an amplifier, this product works. And it does a fantastic job. I have tested it on Audacity and also with speech recognition software, and both show very clean and high quality sound input for recording or speech recognition.

You might ask why would anyone need this product when you already have both a microphone and amplifier?

The answer is simple: you want to use the USB sound, bypassing the business of interfacing between the amplifier and a computer soundcard, which can be extremely problematic.

If you are interested in why, read along.

THE BACKGROUND BEFORE I BOUGHT THIS PRODUCT:

I use a professional grade condenser mic, along with a quite good dedicated stand alone microphone preamplifier. But all this great equipment does not work with the computer very well. The reason: poor compatibility between professional grade microphone output with the built-in soundcard's microphone input. Sometimes it simply does not work. When it works a little, the sound quality is poor, and to make it even worse, it is often unreliable, and prone to interferences due to poor shielding of built-in computer components. In the past, I had bought numerous equipment to solve this problem, including several USB sound interfaces which tend to be quite expensive and also would render my high quality standalone microphone pre-amplifier useless. I ended up buying a very expensive soundcard to be installed on the computer, and used its line input to receive the output signal from the microphone preamplifier. It worked well, but when I got a new computer recently, the soundcard could not be installed because the new computer lacked a proper interface slot.

It seemed the only solution was to buy another expensive high-end soundcard.

But before I did that, I found this cable and gave it a try. I didn't really have much confidence that it would work, but decided to give it a try anyway because it was so cheap.

It worked. And it does a fantastic job. I couldn't be happier.

title: I'm a pianist and this is THE BEST digital I've owned!
text:
I got the Yamaha P-255 as a graduation gift and I can't be more happy with it. I previously owned the Yamaha P95 digital (which didn't have the graded hammer keys like the P255 does), and this digital blows that and even the brand Casio out of the water. I'm a musician (pianist) and not only does this digital produce phenomenal sound, has a natural feel, but it's also trustworthy to perform during recitals and other live performances. Every single sound (4 grand piano sounds, two strings, guitar, harpsichord, etc.) has quality.
There's also four reverb options to accommodate the setting you're in; whether you're playing in the comfort of your own home or on a stage platform, the reverb brings the quality sound to life. In addition, there's three EQ sliders which allows you to give your specific song just the right depth and sound.
The recording options are exceptional and trustworthy as well, and you can even insert a memory card into the recording slot if you're the type of musician who likes to record covers straight-from-piano. The outcomes sound just like a real symphony you'd hear at The Kennedy Centre. There's buttons to adjust the transposition, select two instruments at once, speed adjustment, and even several beats to go along with your song! You can use these beats as either background music or a metronome.

I can't say nothing but positive and joyful things about the Yamaha P255. It's a quality, trustworthy digital that I'd recommend to any aspiring AND professional pianist who's looking for the entire package. Take it from a professional pianist. I've had it for little over two years and it's still as good as I first played it! Good luck.

text:
The Rocket Lives Up to it's name, ROCKET!

While $70.00 is a little pricey, it is a top quality and extremely nice playing harp, that is more like a custom harp out of the box.

As it plays very Lively, and it plays well on very little breath, it is so active in playing that for someone coming from a Hohner Blues Harp which needs to be played with considerably more breath, you will need to adjust Down, so that you dont abuse your new harp.

The comb is Nice and smooth with recessed reed plates like a Special 20, Rockets Hole size is larger.

Covers; Back is wide Open, sides are open as well.

It is a loud playing harp that requires much less breath to play, than some others do, so adjust accordingly.

It is a Very nice playing Instrument, similar to the Crossover, as far as playing goes and sound.

Hohner has a winner with the Rocket.

I like it!!

No dead holes, all reeds play well,

The Rocket is a little larger than the Crossover, The Rocket is slightly longer, it is also wider, thicker and the comb is also thicker.

The Rocket is a Very Comfortable playing instrument, That has very active Reeds, that i am sure will be a big Hit.

The rocket is mustache friendly, when you see the special 20, the Rocket is similar, only the Rockets covers are more closed, and Rounded Very Nicely at the front corners, adding to over all comfort, and Making the Rocket more comfortable than the Special 20 as the special 20 has Sharper Corners and Gaps in the front corners of the covers this is a mustache catcher/lip beater on the Special 20, like i said the Rocket is very comfortable to play, one of the most comfortable i have played.

The Rockets Covers, Comb, & Reed Plates, should be what Hohner uses for all their Harp lineup.

That being said, i cannot answer to durability, with the Rocket being this active of a harp, I hope it does not have a short life span.

In Conclusion;

The Rocket, while Not my Favorite, is one fine instrument, that is in the running for second place, First place goes to the Seydel 1847 Noble Steel, Matte chrome finish, it is the clear Winner.

title: Buy cheap equipment, Get cheap audio
text:
So I initially bought this when I was still figuring out how to stream and how to make audio do its thing, and I figured "oh, its just a cable, how complicated does it get"
Not knowing better, I got the cheapest cable I could have shipped in a 2 day period, and the result was a hissy, high sound-floor sound that i didnt really notice until I learned how to analyze my sound quality and started doing VO work.
It has a nasty, white noise hiss around the -30 to -45db range and I thought for the longest time that it was my mic, (an MXL 990 Midnight edition). Unplugged the mic, and the sound persisted.
"okay then it must be my mixing deck right?" (a Yamaha MG06X), Unplug the output cable from the mixer expecting it to go away.
NOPE. With nothing more than the electricity afforded to this cable by the USB port, this cable, somehow, is responsible for independently generating this weird, constant hissing noise.
Now that I know better than to trust Amazon for audio equipment, I'll be taking my business to sweetwater and finding a cable made by a brand of better reputation.
Now if you'll excuse me, I now have Vods full of annoying hissing to have to slog through in Vegas.

title: Sounds EXACTLY like a grand, 11/10
text:
[[VIDEOID:302a453e987d34744ab08f7dddb6bd09]] I remember when I was you. Sitting here reading all of the reviews for digital pianos trying to find the one that was right for me. I love the portability of a digital piano, while at the same time I wanted something that would sound just as crisp and clear as a grand piano. I read each and every one of these reviews, probably just like you're doing now... and I could not be more happier with my decision. THIS, folks... THIS is quality.

PROS:
- This piano comes fully equipped with some more than capable speakers (be sure to use sound boost when you don't have headphones attached - it really brings out the crispness in the upper ranges).
- The piano sounds so freaking fantastic, I was expecting greatness when I read some of these fantastic reviews, and boy did it deliver. The piano also sounds really good with headphones attached (make sure to buy a 6.35mm adapter for the headphone jack - only like 3 dollars on amazon).
- The feel of the keys are amazing. The weighting of the keys is graded down the piano so it mimics the exact feel of piano keys on a grand, and the keys themselves are made from synthetic ivory so it's so smooth to play and just feels overall great.
- The piano also includes plenty of sounds to have fun and play around with (and they are all top notch quality!) I think it was mentioned before, but no joke the choir sound is just so on-point it is absolutely insane. You also have the ability to do two sounds at once (so like piano and violin together) which is great for dramatic effect, or trying to get just the right sound for a song.
- The price, while many complain, is more of a pro than a con in my opinion, because you get what you pay for, in all honesty. Plus, there is no other digital piano on the market that offers this type of sound for a better price - the p255 is number one on all charts in its class, and for good reason.
- You can record lossless audio straight to your flashdrive! Recordings sound fantastic, just like you'd expect. I attached a video of me playing part of Yiruma's "River Flows in You" on this piano. The audio was recorded directly with a flashdrive and synced up with the video.

CONS:
- I sort of expected there to be a micro headphone jack that could be used with your average headphones, but you actually need to buy a 6.35mm adapter like this: [[ASIN:B005E2Y0KK Monoprice 107139 6.35mm Stereo Plug to 3.5mm Stereo Jack Adaptor, Gold Plated]] but it's no big deal when it's only 3 dollars.
- The Yamaha X-Stand is probably the best in terms of portability for this piano. And yeah, while it's very stable and sturdy, it just makes a very slight creaking noise when playing hard (not really a problem with headphones but idk) its just a tiny little thing that bugs me a bit.
- You need to have sound boost turned on to get the most out of the piano when using the onboard speakers. It's literally a must, because without it the piano sound is overwhelmed with bass. Again, once you turn sound boost on, it sounds absolutely fantastic just like an actual piano. From my experience the piano sounds great either way with headphones on, but sound boost is a necessity for playing without headphones. Again, I feel like I'm making this seem like more of an issue than it actually is, because it's a simple touch-of-a-button, but I just wanted to let you know.
- Price of accessories. Sure, this piano costs $1300, but with the bench, the stand, the pedal, etc etc, it can cost up to about $1500. So, I what I did was buy a package that includes all the accessories. I myself bought [[ASIN:B016FWP4L6 Yamaha P255 Yamaha Digital Piano + X Stand + X Bench + Carrying Bag]] and was very pleased with the purchase.

A fair warning to everyone: buy the piano from new from Amazon. Not eBay, or any other site where people sell them used, because you lose your warranty coverage altogether when you buy from third-party unlicensed Yamaha sellers. Personally, your best bet is to buy a package that includes the stand, seat, pedal, etc. from a licensed Yamaha seller like I mentioned above. Best of luck to whoever you are trying to find a piano for, but for an aspiring advanced/intermediate player such as myself, there was no better option than the p255. 11/10 would buy again, thanks for reading this review.

This black knob fits the MPC ONE quite well. You do have to hold up the knob roughly 2mm-3mm when installing so that the encoder has room to click, but there is no risk of scuffing your MPC while doing this. It looks big in photos but it's width is the same as the base of AKAI's included plastic POS. This feels good in the hand, and you screw it onto the flat side of the pot, so it stays on real well (ie, I'm not going to pull hard on it, would probably rip the pot out before I got this knob off).

My only disappointment is that "the wobble" I had in my original knob is still present, as I tested and verified that is part of the pot, and not the knob. The blame for this falls on AKAI, as the Q-Links are perfect, so shame on you AKAI, give us better Encoder Knob pots. This product still feels 50x better than what AKAI gives you.

On the subject of Q-Link, you'll notice I've got metal ones as well, this is a 4-pack on Amazon also from mxuteuk. There are AKAI 3rd party vendors selling these knobs for the cost of a whole 4-pack on Amazon, so I recommend you find them on here. They work great, the touch sensitivity is still there, and they look rugged as hell - because they are.

All in all I think it's a great upgrade for an MPC owner, you want the product to feel like it should at the pricepoint AKAI is selling it at, I take no issue with the Q-Links that are provided (but still prefer metal) but the encoder is something AKAI really needs to think long and hard about. For the Encoder Knob, this is the best it gets, and I highly recommend the mxuteuk knobs. I may try them out on my other gear and see how it fares, some measuring of the pots and you can probably fit their knobs on all kinds of equipment.

title: Wonderful tube tone!
text: I bought this because I wanted real tube tone.  This is the second all-tube amp I've ever owned.  The first one was a Fender Hot Rod Deville 60 watt combo that I eventually got rid of because it was so loud it was impractical for me.  But in the years since I have been pining away for that glorious tube tone.  I finally decided to get a tube amp again.  I have some home-made speaker cabinets I made and put a 12" Eminence "The Governor" in one and a 10" Jensen in the other.  So I got the Bugera V22 Infinium HD (head).  The price was right when compared to equivalent name brand amps.  I have a 3 year warranty, so no worries there.  But the best thing about it is TUBE TONE for days!  I haven't even run any pedals through it yet, it sounds so good by itself.  I play a HSS strat style guitar.  The neck pickup on the clean channel and the neck/middle on the clean channel is glorious.  the reverb is fantastic.  I can feel the tone through the floor.  This is what I've been missing!  There is a ton of headroom on the clean channel, very little breakup - but that's what I wanted.  If I want dirt I can add a pedal or use the drive channel.  And speaking of the drive channel - very nice crunchy tone so far with a decent amount of variation.  I haven't played with the drive channel a whole lot yet, because I'm so in love with the clean.  I like to use the boost on the drive channel but no boost on the clean.  I'm so happy with this amp and I know I've just scratched the surface.  And by the way - the volume issues I had with my Deville are not an issue with this amp - there is a switch that cuts the power if you desire, plus it is "only" 22 watts, so while it can get loud enough to be painful, (and certainly gig-able) the volume control is gradual enough that I can dial it back when in my house to where my wife doesn't want to kill me and still have the tone I like.  I couldn't give this amp a higher endorsement - I really love it.

title: Great OD and boost,  transparent and wide tone range
text:
I never give five stars until now. And since I've only had it a few months I cannot speak to durability though it feels very solid. Most of my years I played tube screamers or a sansamp or tube screamer and other drives on an ME-50. I've been getting back into individual pedals. I love Xotic. I just had to try this .
The gain ranges from pretty clean to transparent drive all the way to medium overdrive some say similar to Marshall. You could probably get away with hard rock but a little short of Heavy OD. I have played the AC booster with the comp (which I love) and also the SL Drive. This is no slouch .
Even at no gain the tone controls are very responsive. Turn up the bass and it sounds like a seven string or octaver in a good way. The treble can provide crystal clarity. I often play Strats so I like to turn the treble just a little back to 11 o'clock and the tone is so warm I just have to play and that's what it's all about.
The first 20% of gain keeps you in the clean area with some serious tone options. The gain starts early about 8:00. There is a wide range from warm tube sound to not quite the full gain of a tube screamer. The overdrive is different from a tube screamer though. I have too many pedals and fear I will probably always use my multi effect. But I could see adding this pedal even in front of a multi effect to get boost, tone control, and smooth overdrive. This pedal might work well before or after another overdrive.
I am considering the mini version of this but I doubt it will have the same range. For me the only con is that I can't seem to put a battery inside a Caline but it will take a Battery lead with a 9 V. Most people will just plug it in but I like a battery option as sometime I may just take this with me to a jam to have a wide range of tones. This may not be the original upon which it is based but it is an amazing pedal on its own. Even though I have overlapping options I just don't see getting rid of this. I'm sure I'll use it and already use it at home.

title: Fantastic Dirt Pedal for Dirt Cheap
text:
First off, let's get this right off the bat: it's a clone of the Xotic BB Preamp pedal. The only real difference is in the tone section; on the BB, the bass and treble knobs are powered so you can boost or cut by up to 15dB. In the Caline Orange Burst, the tone knobs are not powered and only cut, so maxing them out gets you a completely transparent signal. If you want to hear a demo of this, feel free to listen to demos for the BB, too.

That said, the drive section sounds really good, and the tone controls are perfectly functional in a way most other OD's I've played are not. Setting them both a hair under max evens out the too sharp treble and too deep bass out of the signal, resulting in a really amazing sound, especially for a $30 pedal. It's all metal and just as solid as any American made pedal I've played, too.

This pedal is well worth your time and money if you're in the market for a good, low to medium gain, stackable overdrive pedal. It won't shred, but pairs well if every dirt pedal I've put after it in my chain. This and a Joyo Ultimate Drive, sounds amazing. The Caline Orange Burst overdrive now has a permanent place on my board.

title: Well built, great sounding, overdrive pedal on a budget price!
text: This pedal is supposedly based on the Xotic BB preamp. This Item arrived quickly from this seller, and was new in its original box. There was no manual included, but operation is pretty straightforward and self explanatory, so not a huge deal. This pedal is solidly built. The chassis is heavy duty metal, the knobs and switches feel heavy and well built. The footswitch is a bit tight, but also feels well built. The four knobs adjust the Volume, Gain, Bass and Treble. With the gain turned down and the volume up you get a very nice clean boost. As you add gain, the tone gets very dirty, very quickly. At full gain, it gives you a very crunchy, fuzzy overdriven tube sound. The bass and treble pots noticeably boost (or cut) the EQ mix; I can really feel a difference in the low end when rolling that bass knob up. This pedal is true bypass, as listed in the item description. This pedal sucked the life out of a fresh battery when turned off and left overnight. I have not opened the chassis, and am not a tech type person anyways...so, I cannot speak on the quality of the solders or the guts on the inside of the pedal. I do think that one of the drawbacks of these Caline pedals is that rather than a dedicated battery compartment, you have to unscrew the entire rear of the chassis in order to change the battery. Mine had a 9V battery adaptor included inside of the box as a pleasant surprise, problem solved! This pedal feels well built, and sounds great, but I have only had it for a week or so...we will see how it holds up over the long haul. This really makes me want to try out more of the Caline pedals...It seems that for the price, you just cannot beat this Caline Orange Burst overdrive pedal!

title: Absolutely fantastic headphones
text:
I recently found myself needing to replace my decades old over the ear headphones that I used with my gaming PC. I began my search by trying a number of different headsets, thinking that with how popular they are they must be good.

I was wrong. Every gaming headset I tried had terrible, tinny sound quality. A friend suggested I might be looking for high quality headphones, and he was right. I've used Sennheiser studio headphones in the past and figured they were worth a look. So far I could not be happier with the HD 300 headphones. They sound great whether you're listening to music or playing games. I was worried with how light they are that they wouldn't have good bass response, but they absolutely do. Headphone tech has come quite a long ways in the last 10 years!

I had a giftcard and went with the HD 300s because they had slightly higher reviews compared to the HD 280s. I highly doubt 90% of people would be able to tell a difference between the headphones, so if you're worried about the price just get the 280s.

title: CHEAP PARTS! DO NOT BUY WITHOUT PLANNING ON MAKING MODIFICATIONS!
text: Fast shipping but I was very unimpressed by the quality of this cable, mainly the female XLR connector. The terminals were mishapen and spread open (due to being a very thin material) so they wouldn't make a solid contact with the pins on my mic resulting in static and connection loss. It almost looked like a return/used item. Also the latch has 1/8" of play resulting in a loose connection and further allowing the terminals to spread open. After disassembling the end I found a frayed shield wire crossing other contacts and a broken solder joint on one of the pins. I was able to fix the issues by resoldering the connection and putting a wedge (cut/broke bobby pin into pieces) in each hole outside of each terminal which made a very tight fit for the pins on the mic. Everything is now tight and functioning properly but if you receive a working one this cable, due to the quality of the components and the soldering, will not last very long at all with regular use. Best solution other than the one I found is to buy a new female XLR connector and splice it onto this cable. Otherwise plan on frequently ordering replacement cables. Hopefully you were luckier than I was.

title: Great but overpriced
text:
Great amp/cab sim in one. It's def for people that want to use their pedals and not totally change over to processors.

I normally use a tube amp with a 4x12 cab but due to a broken back this year I'm going direct into an insanely loud Headrush FRFR108 speaker that weights 19lbs. This will keep up with a metal drummer.

Anyway, the Strymon sounds really good, not as good as the amps on the Fractal FM3 I had and that's where I'm going with my point. For $400 I think it's over priced. Should be $300. It's limited on high gain, so you'll need a boost if you play anything that is extremely high gain or if you want to tighten your sound.

I use a boss SD1 overdriver with the volume on that up all the way, eq to taste and the driver all the way down and it tightens the Strymon Marshall and Strymon Vox settings. I also went in and changed the Cab IR's to get me what I was looking for.

My favorite setting is the Marshall on the stock Cab A setting with my SD1 fed into my Headrush FRFR 108 speaker. It sounds good, not perfect but really good.

I'd be quick to jump ship if I could go to another amp/cab IR pedal that offered more of what I wanted for high gain. Would like to see Neural DSP offer the same thing without having to buy an entire processor (quad cortex).

title: Solid all around. Jack of all trades master of none.
text:
tl;dr: This headphone doesn't have any glaring weaknesses. Overall, its a well built, good sounding headphone. It does a solid job as a studio monitoring headphone, it does a decent job as not being too boring to the point to where you can't use it as a casual headphone. Its biggest weakness if it has any, is the cord that it comes with. I Would have liked to see a longer cord, its a bit on the short side. Also, the cord is attached to the headphone via one ear cup and secured via torx type screw.

Sound:
One differentiating quality between this and other headphones in the same range is the resolution in the highs, midrange, and also the solid low end. It actually goes pretty low, lower than many headphones. As one could expect, Sennheiser knows how to present the frequencies in the mids. However, unlike the HD650, this headphone doesn't have a strong veil, and unlike the HD600, this headphone has more low end body without compromising the mids or highs, and without sounding artificial. The headphone overall has an "warm" character, but only slightly.

Comfort:
Tight fitting, but the cups and headband are very comfortable and they mold very nicely to your head.

Other features:
They have good passive sound isolation, which works effectively in louder environments. These block out sound almost as good (80-90%) as my Bose QC35 but without any added noise cancellation effect nor without any degradation in sound quality.

Conclusion:
Bottom line, although there is heavy competition in the studio monitor headphone segment, and good competition, I can't think of another headphone that sort of ticks all the boxes as evenly as this headphone does, at least in the same price range. Build quality, sound, comfort. Most others skew heavily in one area over the other, but this headphone seems to do the majority of things well but nothing really super great. At the end of the day, what else do you want from a studio headphone?

title: Side by side sounds nearly identical to the BB Pre
text:
I compared the Orange Burst side by side with the BB Preamp in a controlled studio setting. Really put them through the paces. Bottom line is that they are really, really close. Almost identical. Sonically they are a close enough match that in a live situation (on stage or in rehearsal) you probably couldn't tell the difference. If I had to describe the difference with gun-to-head I'd say the Celine is a hair brighter and the BB is just a hair darker or thicker... barely. The Caline is just as transparent as the BB Preamp and stacks with other dirt boxes and boost pedals just as well. I am impressed.

You may be concerned about quality and road worthiness of components, switches, jacks etc. it is a cheap Chinese clone after all. But this pedal is quite solid. And for the price you can afford to buy a spare. You can get a spare for your spare and still spend under a hundred bucks.

If you are already a fan of the BB Preamp, or you want to experiment with the sound of a transparent mid-gain boost pedal I recommend it. You can always upgrade to the real deal and keep The Orange Burst as a spare. I'm keeping the BB Pre on my board forever but this one will live in my gig bag and I may get another one for my "fly-in" board. Like the BB Preamp the Orange Burst is a great sounding pedal. For the price it's a no-brainer.

/*--- Edit: April 19 ---*/

Wanted to add -I also picked up a Caline Pure Sky. A similar pedal (lower gain) for about the same price. Stacked in front of the Orange Burst they sound incredible together. The Pure Sky is supposedly a "Timmy clone." Not sure about that as I don't have one to compare it with. But to me the Pure Sky seems to be very much like the Xotic AC Boost. Which makes sense as the Orange Burst is so close to the BB Pre... For around $65 The Orange Burst and the Pure Sky are two great sounding pedals that sound even better together.

title: Great deal
text: Just received this head from Zzounds today. I purchased it there to take advantage of there awesome pay as you play plan. I own a blackstar ht club 50 that needed retubing, so I ordered this as I needed something quick for upcoming gigs. I was worried about the power being enough at 22 watts for playing over a drummer. This thing is plenty loud, probably even loud enough to drowned out your drummer. Now I do have this running through a 412 cabinet so it helps with the volume. My next concern was having enough gain, no worries, its not quite saturated enough for metal but a boost pedal like a ts9 will take you there. Finally the tone, the tones great. The clean is super clean and close to a fender. The gain channel is brighter than my blackstar but super clear. The boost switch is a little much, I dont think i'll use it. The features are also great. Led lights to tell you when tubes are bad, a switch to cut power in half for bedroom jamming and a 4,8, or 16 ohm impedance switch for handling any speaker. The reverb is digital but it sounds good for being digital. I cant say anything about reliability yet but it seems solid. The included footswitch is made out of metal as well. This amp far exceeded my expectations especially for the price. Honestly it may get more playing time than my blackstar. Dont hesitate to buy this

title: Make the right decision, buy this today.
text:
I am very rarely impressed by the complete quality of lower end PRICED guitars. While I feel like I am a good guitarist, I am a softy. I own a Gibson SG, Fender American strat (cool rails) mexi-tele, and two Gretsch guitars (one with P90s). I needed power.

I GOT POWER.

Neck feels amazing, and the cutouts allow easy access to the upper frets. All the electronics are solid with no wiggles, as well as the Floyd Rose type system. Setup was near perfect when the guitar arrived. One thing I found shocking was its' weight, being a little heavier than I expect. Not a drawback by any means. Sidebar to the Floyd Rose, if you do not intend to use this system, upgrade your tuners. If you do not use the nut locks, this guitar goes out of tune in a hurry. If you do use the full term system and locks, rock on.

title: Best Harmonica I've Ever Played
text:
I've bought many harmonicas recently, Golden Melodies, Special 20s, Blues Harps, and Crossovers and I can easily say, the Rocket is by far my favorite harmonica yet. It's so comfortable, so responsive, and so LOUD.

The channels are tad wider than a normal diatonic so it's easier to play and wrap your mouth around (I use pucker embouchure so that was nice.) The Rocket sounds fuller, louder, and generally more pleasing to the ear, the reeds are easy to bend and you hardly have to give it any air at all for those notes to come ringing out so sweetly. With the lack of reviews I was skeptical spending $80 on this harmonica (I payed for express shipping, I'm impatient.) but after seeing, feeling, and playing this next to my Special 20. I couldn't be more pleased. I would recommend this harp to ANYONE. In my eyes, it's perfect.

Beautiful harmonica with a beautiful case: I thought I wouldn't like the new zipper cases but they're actually a lot nicer than the boxes they use on the other harps because the harp has no room to bounce around in your pocket, it also has an elastic band to put on your belt if that's what you're looking for.

Amazing Purchase. If you're looking for a harp. Get this one.

title: Great beginner guitar for the money
text:
I bought this guitar way back almost 10 years ago, and have played it frequently since. For a hobbyist or a student player, it is hard to beat this price. Could you get a better acoustic guitar for slightly more money, or find one if you hunted around for a deal? Sure. But you could do much, much worse.

It has a strong, booming resonance, and doesn't take long to break in. Once there, it stays well in tune. There's a little more fret buzzing than I would ideally like, but hey, we are talking about a sub $150 guitar here. I would say the biggest negative is that the top is laminate instead of solid wood, and therefore doesn't have the same richness or "matures with age" quality that a decent solid top will give you. But this little guitar has served me very well and I can't complain.
