title: Great fight pad and great for VC games
text:
This is a Wii Classic Controller made to look like a GameCube controller. It plugs into a Wii Remote and can be used with both the Wii and Wii U on the menu and in games (assuming the game in question is compatible). Naturally, the designs are designed around Smash Bros. characters, and this controller definitely feels right in that game, as it has since Melee.

The build quality is top-notch, but if you've ever bought a HORI controller, that's kind of old news to you. The plastic on the controller is matte finished, rather than the glossy finish of real GameCube controllers. It makes the controller feel slightly different than a real GC controller, but it still feels great. The ZL and ZR buttons are actual buttons, not triggers like the L and R buttons were on the GameCube, which could be a bit of a downer for some. That said, an L button was added to even out the controller.

The controller has a turbo function, but I've never really gotten into using turbo for games. The sticks are tight and pleasant to use, with little resistance. They, as with the plastic on the controller, are a different material, but still feel good. The buttons go down easily and seem to use a mechanism identical to the old GC pads - so it's not likely to stick. Finally, the D-pad blows the real GameCube's D-pad out of the water. It's much larger than a GameCube D-pad and feels an awful lot like the D-pad you can find on the Wii U GamePad, but smoother. Since the GamePad has one of my favorite D-pads, this is a very good thing.

It is more versatile than the Wii U Pro Controller at half the price - as a Classic Controller, not only can it be used with compatible Wii U games, it can also play games through the Wii Menu and can be used with actual original Wii hardware without extra setup - I've used this controller for playing Super Smash Bros. Brawl and it feels just as great as it does in Super Smash Bros. for Wii U.

Overall, there's nothing negative I can say about this controller. It exceeds expectations, it feels great, and it brings a familiar controller layout to a new generation of games.

title: Even better than the original
text:
After finishing the 30 Day Challenge on the Wii Active: Personal Trainer, I decided to give "More Workouts" a shot, and I'm glad that I did. The warm up and cool down stations are a welcome addition, although it's annoying that the trainer insists that you watch him do the movements each time, as they are not that complicated that I need constant reminders. However, it is easy enough to throw in a few extra reps while the guy is needlessly showing me how to do the warm up or cool down yet again. However, just having a cool down that is more than "walk ten steps" is a vast improvement.

The ab exercises, although few in number, are also a nice addition. The island location is a bit hokey at times but is pleasant to look at, and the island-themed sports are pretty engaging. Doing squats to get through the water skiing course is much more interesting than just doing dozens of squats while staring at the trainer; likewise for lunges with squash, and the ability to choose left or right handed is nice, even if moving the leg band isn't especially nice. The cardio boxing is much better than in the first version, and I have made a cardio workout on my own with a large portion of cardio boxing.

There are of course the occasional issue where the game doesn't read your movement correctly, and it's unfortunate that the "1" button tells you what song is playing and you have to hit the button again to continue, as I seem to hit the "1" with annoying frequency while doing arm exercises with the resistance band. I also wish there were a way to swap in an exercise of a similar type for one you don't want to do, as there are some that are too hard on my knees, and the running ones make the downstairs neighbors mad; it would be nice to be able to do a different exercise in place of the one I don't want to do, rather than getting rid of the exercise entirely.

With the addition of 1-lb gloves and a much stronger resistance band, I feel like I am getting a fairly decent workout, and the variety of workouts is keeping me engaged. I look forward to working my way through the 6-week challenge, and trying a few of the recipes in the included booklet.

title: Love The Sims 3: World Adventures
text:
World Adventures has to be one of my favorite expansion packs. WA brings so much to the game in terms of content. There is new furniture, hair styles, clothing, and traits for your sims. It breaks up some of the monotony of everyday life for your sims. I enjoy sending my newlywed sims on honeymoons or sending the whole family (children and up can go on trips) to bond with each other.

When your sims go on a trip time freezes back home so everything is as they left it. There are 3 locations: Champs Les Sims in France, Al Simhara in Egypt, and Shang Simla in China. When your sims first go on vacation they can only stay at each location for 3 days until they improve their visa level. There are 3 visa levels and for each location you must build the visa level.For example if your sims has a level 3 visa in Shang Simla it doesn't carry over to the other 2 locations.To improve their visa levels sims must complete adventures (hence the name World Adventures) for local sims. They can range from bringing that sim metals to exploring tombs to find a lost object.Once your sim reaches visa level 3 they can buy a vacation home in that location.

This game is one of my favorites in the Sims 3 franchise. I love it and would recommend you buy it.

title: EA Sports Active is Great
text:
I have been using Sports Active for three weeks. It is very motivating using the 30 day challenge. I sometimes am eager enough to use the system that I skip the rest days that it recommends! I have used Wii Fit for over a year and enjoy some of the activities (I still use Yoga almost daily) but I dreaded using the strength exercises. With Sports Active the exercise routines are varied and filled with many short segments of different exercises. If I do not enjoy one exercise in the routine, I know that I will quickly be done with it and on to another that I like more. The system tells you how many calories you are burning, which I find motivating.
I have not lost weight since using Sports Active but I am in pretty good shape already. I think that perhaps I have built a few muscles using the system though and this may explain the lack of weight loss. The Wii Fit never made me build up a sweat but Sports Active routinely has me perspire with exertion.
I would recommend that you buy a heavier resistance band to use with the system unless you are an absolute beginner to strength training.

title: Experience LOTR in this glorious game...
text:
This game is the best, with a good mix of fighting and time-oriented puzzle levels. The graphics are wonderful, far better even than the Two Towers, and the levels are excellent. I would not have minded having a few more chequepoints in some of the more difficult levels as it can be extremely frustrating to be sent back to the beginning of a hard-played level when one fails at the very end. If you were unable to be a part of Peter Jackson's incredible film, this is the next best thing, although the plot is a bit different from the film that was released in the cinemas. I suspect that Frodo's 'shiny shirt' may turn up in the extended version of ROTR, however as it is an important part of the original story by Tolkien. The gameplay is more sophisticated than Two Towers: there are opportunities in this game to interact with different items, allowing a character to climb ropes, use catapults, overturn vats filled with burning oil, cast spears and so on. I rather wish that the secret levels, which are really training levels, would have been available BEFORE one wins the game, but they are given only as a reward after one beats every level. It is similar to the Two Towers in this respect.
I have to say that I found some of the characters to be inferior to others in their fighting abilities, no matter how many upgrades they have. In particular, poor Pippin always has a more difficult time of it than the others. Gimli, albeit very slow, is a powerhouse of strength and has a wonderful tumbling combination move, but the sheer joy of being Legolas, who is the fastest and most graceful of all players, cannot be equalled.

With respect to LOTR games, I actually recommend the GBA version of ROTR above all others, as it is incredibly detailed, extremely beautiful and one can play six different characters, including Eowyn. (I would have liked to have seen her in the PS2 version.) The GBA version has more to it than fighting, as one can spend time searching for ancient artifacts and finding valuable weapons and armour can be fun as well.

title: Hope you don't need to transfer your save data anywhere
text:
Bought a new console? Sucks to be you.
Old console broken and needs to be replaced? Tough.
Paid for that online membership to get access to cloud saves? Nope.

Ignoring the issues with the "one island per console" thing, there is literally no way of moving your data to a new Switch, regardless if it is 100% your own data with no additional player information in it. For a company that likes to keep putting out new custom versions of its consoles, this is at best an extremely short sighted decision.

title: You will get your $40 worth
text: Having completed the first EA Active 30 day challenge, I decided to try out the "More Workouts" version. EA did address many of the issues I had with the first one such as making the routines a little more balanced, adding warm up and cool down exercises plus exercises targeting abs. However, there is only one warm up and one cool down segment and only 3 ab exercises, this gets a bit old after a couple of times. Also, this game is hard on the knees and upper front leg muscles, EA needs to hire developers who know that there are other lower body exercises than lunges, squats, and jumps. Another feature I would like is the ability to switch out an exercise before you begin the daily challenge, right now it only lets you delete it not replace it. Another issue, though no real fault of EA, is using the WII remotes, they can actually making some of the exercices near impossible to do since the tether cord gets in the way or there are times when they are just not responsive enough for the activity at hand. title: Wow what a workout!!
text:
Ok, so I was hesitant about spending $60 on a workout game when I already owned three of them - all exclusively for the Wii. After my first 50 minute workout though I can truthfully say that this trumps all of them. It is like Gold's Gym, the Wii Fit, and My Fitness Coach all rolled into one. After my workout, which included everything from boxing to dancing to running to shooting hoops, I was sweating profusely and feeling great!

What I liked:
- Like the Wii Fit, it incorporates the Balance Board.
- I get to pick my exercises - unlike on the My Fitness Coach
- The graphics were good, the track, courts, etc. actually made me feel a little like I was actually there.
- The running was everything the Wii Fit running was not. It counted my calories and seemed a little more responsive that the Fit.
- I appreciated the feedback I received when doing the stretching exercises... This I missed in the My Fitness Coach- there was no sensor to tell me if I was squatting to high, not jumping in the right rhythm, etc. With EA SA the control that was strapped to my thigh was able to tell the game when I was not doing something right - giving me the opportunity to correct my form.

- I also like the fact that you can work out with a friend.

Cons:
The resistant band is weak - for me anyway but that can be easily corrected with a inexpensive trip to Wal-mart.

I discovered that I may also be buying a wireless nunchuck... the wire was constantly in my way.

It doesn't track my weight loss.

It's not really a con but I wish there were step aerobics. It could have easily been worked in.

Overall impression: I'm glad I broke down and paid the $$$ for this game. It far surpasses My Fitness Coach, the Wii Fit, and Gold's Gym (though I will probably continue to use Gold's Gym for the boxing routines and the wii fit to track my weight loss). It's hard core, but I feel it will definitely give me my desired results.

title: Works fine with a little effort
text:
Short Review: Reccommend this with up to a 4 TB HDD. The Data Bank works ok so far with my 4 TB WD Green HDD. Data Bank looks nice enough, seems halfway sturdy. Instructions that come with the Data Bank are very nice, but I think you may need to follow them step by step because I didn't and ran into issues. Maybe you actually do need to install the OS in safe mode. You get to the safe mode by holding down the power button until the second beep.

Whole Story:
I bought the Data Bank and a 4 TB WD My Book since it was cheaper than any other 4 TB hard drive I've ever seen (it was $96) and decided that I'd just remove it and stick it in the Data Bank. Removing the hard drive from the enclosure wasn't too hard, there are probably even videos on how to do it. Regardless of that, whether you decide to buy an external drive and remove it or just get an internal hard drive, I HIGHLY recommend downloading the software to your USB drive first before you get to work on anything else since it takes the most time out of the whole process. Also, I recommend downloading all of your save data to a USB drive prior to swapping out the hard drives. You don't necessarily need to do this as much if you're a PS Plus member, but it's not too bad of an idea to be on the safe side. When I first booted up my PS4 with the new HDD in it, everything worked well for a while. Once I put in a physical disk though, it said the data was corrupted and asked me to delete it and reinstall it. I did this, and it said the same thing again and again for a few times. Used the "rebuild database" option on the PS4 a time or two, nothing worked. The games would install, but I couldn't play them, and I always got the same "data is corrupted, delete and reinstall" message. I had to initialize my PS4 again, and once I did my games started working. The first time I transferred the OS onto my PS4 HDD I did NOT do so in Safe Mode, and I think this may have been the reason for my aforementioned troubles. I haven't imported my previous save data to the new hard drive yet, I just installed and booted up a game to make sure it actually worked. I'm going to install the rest of my games and import my save data and hope everything continues to work, either way I'll update this post with more information.

Four stars so far, five if I can come back to this in a week or so and still say I recommend it and everything works.

Update: Might not have been my non safe mode OS install that made my hard drive not recognize any games. I did however get the hard drive to recognize some games once I reinstalled the OS under safe mode, but there was still one game that wouldn't launch after the update file for it installed. I then took the hard drive out and reformatted it to exFAT and that seems to have solved my problems. Since I reformatted my hard drive to exFAT haven't had the usual "corrupt data" or "disk unreadable" messages, nor have I gotten the error codes 30012 or 30034 to come up when launching my games. Still using the same WD Green 4TB hard drive that I pulled out of a 4TB WD My Book. So far I'm happy with both the Data Bank and the WD 4TB Green hard drive, even though it takes a little bit of effort to make it work properly.

title: The best SimCity ever
text:
SC4 is the best in the series. A few caveats, if you have a system that is more than a year or two old and wasn't at the higher end even back then, your game play experience will be significantly affected. Don't pay attention to Maxis' minimum requirements; instead look at their recommended requirements. I have a 1.7GHz Dell w/ 64Mb Nvidia video card and even then it seems like the game runs slower than it should. The graphics are spectacular, as is the amount of detail rendered. But the game is also different in many subtle and important ways that make it more satisfying to play.
SC4 is the hardest game in the series. In SC2K and SC3K you could plop down a couple parks, a good mix of zoning and have a beautiful, successful city. Not so here. For a while I was actually very frustrated with SC4, even though I fancied myself something of a SimCity expert. My cities were spread out and not tall; they did not seem to grow past a certain point; I seemed to be losing money left and right. I highly recommend visiting fansites for help (my favorite: simtropolis.com) or getting the Prima guide. After I did that I got a better understanding of how the internal dynamics of the game worked and how to begin thinking about planning a region rather than simply planning a city. (SC4 cities are interconnected with other cities you build around them in a large region.) I currently have one central city with most of the wealthy commerce, citizens, high tech industry and a large university. To make it successful, I needed two other cities: an industrial city to the south and a bedroom community to the west. I recently started a new bedroom community to the southwest that I hope to transform into a wealthier suburb.
Within cities themselves much has changed. Educational, health, and safety buildings have a specific effect on the neighborhoods around them (think big halo around each of the buildings) and you can adjust their level of funding accordingly. Also, rich apartment buildings coexist next to low income tenements. Traffic takes on a more important meaning. The initially-buggy "My Sim" feature which allows you to move in your sims from The Sims or use SC4-supplied sims into your city is also a huge plus and adds an element of human drama into the game play. If your sim lives in a poor area, but one with good services, you could see him move from a job flipping burgers to becoming a school administrator to becoming CEO of a downtown financial services company. If bad traffic prevents a sim from getting to work, he tells you. This helps you think about how it is that people live in your cities and what kind of services and support they need from you as Mayor to live the good life.
Sims aren't real, of course. But as many SimCity Mayors have discovered for themselves, playing SimCity gives you an appreciation of the demands placed on local governments as they try to meet the needs of the people in their areas and the balancing they have to do to meet those needs. SC4 takes this all to a whole new level and initially does not make it easy--but after you get one city going it's amazing how much fun it can be to develop it and the region around it.

title: Great Workout: Sometimes VERY Frustrating Experience
text:
First of all, I've had this game for over 3 months now: I feel good about giving an honest review. Some of the highest rated reviews include lines like "I just finished my second workout" which, to be honest, are NOT SUFFICIENT. This product requires MUCH more in depth use before a proper review can be presented!

Overall, this game is great for people who want a Wii fitness regime. If you want a game, go somewhere else. If you want a good weight program, go somewhere else. But if you want a daily workout (anywhere from 10 minutes to an hour) then this is a great product.

There are two aspects to this product:

1 - Does it give you a good workout? HELL YEAH! I really feel it, I'm a big fan of the product from this perspective, because it has many MANY individual exercises and you can tailor your workout around several of them, or use the provided workouts, do a 30 day workout "challenge", etc. Bravo to EA for really thinking about how people do their workouts and providing a great management interface!

2 - Some of the exercises work wonderfully, but others ARE THE MOST FRUSTRATING THING IN THE WORLD! Specifically, despite comments from other reviewers, there is NO FEEDBACK on your movement. After two months of using this, you will simply skip several of the exercises because they just exercise your temper, not your body.

Let me explain:

Picture lifting a dumbbell: you hold your arm with the weight down (at "rest" : point A) and you use your bicep to curl the weight up to your chest (point B). Then you finish the exercise by lowering the weight back down.

The Wii has no way of telling if you are holding the nunchuck at waist height or over your head. Instead, the product pretends to track your movement: if you are holding the nunchuk down at your waist (in position A above) and then you curl your bicep up, you end up "moving" the nunchuck. EA Active detects that movement and responds by making your character move (it does an animation: it doesn't actually move your arm in the same way that you moved it. In other words, if you do ANY nunchuck movement, it assumes you are curling your biceps.) After after it stops detecting movement, EA Active waits for you to stop moving (to "hold" the curl at position B) before you can continue. Lastly, you do the reverse movement, leaving your arm at position A again.

So, what's the problem? You have to hold the nunchuck/controller (depending on the movement) _STILL_ at position A to start, position B, and then again at position A when done each rep. If you wiggle the nunchuck/controller, then it will not think you have "finished" moving and will not let you continue.

This is complicated by the fact that some exercises have very brief/short "hold" times, while others have longer times. Additionally, some exercises expect hold times that are short at position A, but longer at position B! It's EXTREMELY frustrating at times when it's telling "you didn't do that rep properly!" when you're yelling at the TV "YES I DID! YOU JUST DIDN'T NOTICE!!!!"

Example: I can do lunges with my right leg no problem, but when I lunge with my left leg, my bad knee makes it hard for me to keep still: I end up wiggling a bit. Well, EA Active HATES this and yells at me all the time: it's enough to drive me crazy! Fortunately, I can switch those lunges to be side lunges instead (where I don't have the same problem.)

ARGH!

Other things of note:
- The rubber band it comes with is horrible. Buy your own resistance strap, you'll be happier
- Doing some of the exercises (tricep kickbacks notably) with a wired Wii Controller/nunchuck can be difficult: the wire makes it hard to get full extension.
- Some of the "sport" games are not very active. Tennis, volleyball, baseball: they are more of a distraction than actual exercise because they are SLLLOOOOOWWWWWW.
- The squats work very very well! Easy to see what's going on with a bar showing the position read from the nunchuk! Awesome! And the ONLY exercise with such feedback: even the squats with calf raises don't do it :( EVERY exercise should have this!!!!!
- The game makes you create your own character which is NOT your Mii. I wish it would have used Miis instead.

Anyways, I give the game 4 stars because it really does let you manage your workouts effectively. I just wish it wasn't so frustrating to do some of the exercises.

title: Great game, faulty equipment
text:
First I would like to say, I love this game. I bought the Wii Fit, and after using it actively for a month, I got no results. I've tried going to the gym everyday, burning 700 calories everyday on an elliptical, and lost no weight. I'm tried low calorie diets and lost no weight. After using the Active for eleven workouts I'm actually seeing a decline in my weight. I can actually feel the exercises getting easier because I'm getting stronger. My only two gripes with this game is that my leg strap is tearing. I want to keep on playing this game, I actually want to play it more, just because it's that effective, and it would be a shame if I had to stop playing it just because of some faulty equipment. I would like to give this game a five star rating, but unfortunately I can't because the equipment given to me is faulty. The other gripe I have is that sometimes I'll do an exercises and it won't detect my movements, and it will chastise me for that. This fortunately only happens with the biceps curls w/ shoulder presses exercise. I would recommend this game, but I don't think I can until EA recalls the leg straps and replaces them with something that is not as weak.

Edit: After buying a new resistance band from Theraband, I'd have to knock this down a little more, the resistance band provided here is pretty weak.

title: Get Lost in the Charming World of Animal Crossing: New Horizons
text:
Animal Crossing: New Horizons is a game that's hard to describe. On the surface, it may seem like a simple life simulation game, but in reality, it's so much more than that. It's a game that's full of charm, personality, and endless possibilities, and it's easily one of the best games available on Nintendo Switch.

The premise of the game is simple: you move to a deserted island and must build it up into a thriving community. But the beauty of Animal Crossing: New Horizons lies in the details. The game is full of little touches and surprises that make the world feel alive and dynamic. From the changing seasons to the daily events and interactions with the game's cast of lovable characters, there's always something new and exciting to discover.

But what really makes Animal Crossing: New Horizons stand out is the level of customization it offers. You can decorate your house and island with a wide range of furniture, decorations, and other items. You can even create your own designs and patterns to use on clothes, furniture, and more. And with the ability to play with friends both locally and online, there's no shortage of creative opportunities.

One of the things I love most about Animal Crossing: New Horizons is how it encourages you to slow down and take things at your own pace. There are no strict objectives or time limits, and the game's gentle, relaxing atmosphere makes it the perfect way to unwind after a long day.

Overall, I can't recommend Animal Crossing: New Horizons enough. It's a game that's full of heart and charm, and it's sure to keep you entertained for hours on end. So if you're looking for a game that's both relaxing and engaging, look no further than Animal Crossing: New Horizons on Nintendo Switch.

title: Outstanding Option for Smash Bros. and Beyond
text:
This is, economically and ergonomically, the best 3rd party controller you can buy for the Wii U. It’s a near perfect recreation of the Gamecube controller, with some minor tweaks: the controller is lighter (due to lack of rumble motor) and the top buttons are akin to that of the (original) Wii Classic Pro, which this particular controller is designed to mimic. It also plugs right into the a Wiimote and is compatible with nearly every Virtual Console game and many (but not all) Wii U games.

If you’re dead set on using a GCN controller for Smash Bros. but don’t want to wait around for the special controller and adapter (which have been nigh impossible to find for a reasonable price), this is the one to get. And the bonus is that it’ll work for so many other games as well. You’re getting a much better deal with this. And it also doesn’t hurt that this controller is officially licensed by Nintendo.

text:
My hubby bought me this game because he knows how much I like to workout and thought that this would be a great supplement to my workout regimine.

i think you get out of this game what you put into it. There are definitely ways to cheat and not get as good of a workout, but why bother doing it then?

This is definitely NOT a substitute for hitting the gym or going for a run, but it is a fun way to sneak in a little extra calorie burn while having some fun.

However, someone who is a complete beginner would definetely benefit from this program.

The guns & other items you have in the game are nice. I wish they had a more diverse collection of weapons though. They have 4 distint types of grenades. I wish they had more distint firearms. The most frustating part of the game is your freeze meter. If your body tempture gets too low you die.. You must constanty go back & forth into building to rejuvinate yourself.. This gets repetitive fast & is very tedious & boring. I found this game to be unsuspenseful in most accounts. The game does a good job of picking up the pace the middle parts & will keep your interest during the more tame beginning of the game. Not knowing who is infected is pretty cool, but lacks in suspense too, cause you know your NPC teammates are going to be infected. Thats a no brainer. There really aren't any suprises. Only a few minor ohh's & Ahh's.. If you have a weekend to kick back & relax, rent it.. Just don't expect it to be a great horror survival experience..

title: Better then Wii Fit?  Please!
text:
First, let's look at the value provided in EA Sports Active. For your 60 bucks you get a joke of a resistance band, the leg strap, and the game disc. If you like to wear nylon gym shorts you will be disappointed in the leg strap. It won't stay in place because Sports Active is very much high impact. Lots of jumping, and more jumping, and running in place, with high knees or it won't register properly. Then deep knee bends, not squats, as they're mislabed. In four episodes of using the prepared workouts you'll earn a trophy.... for over 100 deep knee bends.
Second, as several reviewers have already pointed out, the "game" locks up frequently. No rhyme or reason to either the lockups or what you'll have to do to recover. Other reviewers have also noted the lack of any pushups or situps, but there are lots and lots of lunges and deep knee bends, mislabeled as squats.
Third, holding the numchuk and wiimote while corded together and doing some of these exercises will have the cord flying all around your face.
Fourth, for all of you complaining about the time it takes to do a workout with Wii Fit, the pre-assembled so-called 30 minute workout with EA Sports Active takes 45 minutes by my clock! (The twenty minute ones take about 35 minutes by the clock, even skipping all videos.) I can do the entire Strength, Yoga, Rhythm Boxing - Expert from Wii Fit in one and one-half hours and get credit for one hour and twenty-one minutes of exercise.
Fifth, prepare to do the same things over and over in each workout. Deep knee bends, running in place, bent over rows are all repeated at least twice in each of the pre-assembled workouts.
Sixth, you'll spend an inordinate amout of time putting the numchuk in the leg strap, taking it out for the next exercixe, putting it back in for the one after that, holding it with the resistance band next, etc. I find that much more aggravating than clicking through the Wii Fit menus.
In conclusion, I don't know how this got such good ratings. It isn't a fun workout, flows less well than Wii Fit, and since you're constantly fixing either the leg strap or resistance band, this game is downright aggravating.

title: Fun and getting better, but was hoping for more ....
text:
I first discovered SimCity with SimCity2000 and played it religiously for a long time, I loved that game! I was a bit disappointed with SimCity3000 and had high hopes (based on previews) for this version. Unfortunately, it only realized some of those.
First off, the game is beautiful. The buildings are rich in color, texture, and style. The options are many and the concept of regional play is a good one (although isn't quite as fulfilling, see below). Your sims can commute from one place to another, power lines can be strung and freeways can lead from your city out to the city with the airport. The interface is fairly clean and most things can be made to go away in case you just want to sit back and stare at what you've built. Another neat thing is the day/night mode. It seems to be mainly for visual effects (I haven't detected different sim behavior patterns or anything) but it is impressive looking. The usual fun disasters are there.
That said, there were some elements that were flawed. First off, the cities that came with the game were small and paltry things. SimCity3000 came with many different types of cities, ranging from 0 to well over 1,000,000 people. Some were paradises, others ghettos, but each was unique. SimCity4 comes with 6-7 regions, two with very small cities started. It's a personal thing, but I don't really enjoy the process of taking nothing and building all the way up, sometimes I want to start with a big (and perhaps flawed) city and try and solve it's problems like crime, homelessness, decay, etc. At least they could've provided us with more variety in city types than they did.
Another gripe is laying out the zones. In the old days you just painted the terrain a particular color and watched whatever was supposed to happen, happen. In SimCity4 you still do this but the computer also lays out lots. Still you have little control over which direction these lots are and often they have minimum dimensions, which aren't apparent when first placing them. Furthermore, try to zone a parcel bigger than say 5x5 tiles and the program will immediately try to add roads into the mix, even if you've already built roads to frame your zones! It doesn't even place the roads in the right places half the time, leading to wierd angles and lots that aren't buildable. Finally, there's no way to turn this thing off! It's nice when you're zoning lots of completely empty space, but a real drag when you're trying to rezone a few blocks.
One gripe about the regions is that they really aren't regions. They tend to just become boroughs (but with their own budgets!) of a city. The New York region shows this as Manhattan is cut into multiple regions. You could develop one as all Residential and another as say commercial I suppose but I was hoping for true regional play where you have actual separate cities cooperating with or competeing against each other.
Still, it's getting better. The game has been patched a couple of times to weed out the bugs and a new region has been posted to the main site (with a large population to start with) with more promised. Further patches will help make the game more playable and I am enjoying it more every day so who knows? If I wrote this one month from now it might've been 4 or 5 stars. One can hope.

Funny thing, the 20-minutes actually get your heart rate up and even the Light intensity level had me sweating and feeling good aches the next day. Only minor drawback is the nunchuck holder (upper thigh) which slipped off of me the first two workouts, but it works better when not over pants (so wear shorts) and when you use both buckles. I'm admittedly klutzy and uncoordinated, but the workouts were easy to learn with the video directions and easy to carry out, though the music is a little cheesey it is a fun way to workout and a different exercise routine that works with the wii fit package. I am pleased with the value for the price.

title: Great way to switch up your workout!
text: I received this Wii workout about two weeks ago and love it. At first when I used it , it took me a little bit to get used to holding onto the Wii remote and working out at the same time, but once I mastered that, it was really enjoyable... and FUN! There are different levels to workout at, so if you're a beginner to intermediate, they have workouts just for you. You can also target the things you want to work out on any given day; upper body, abs, lower body , cardio and you have the choice of being able to workout by yourself or with a friend. The scenery is set on an island and you can choose a male or female trainer. The variety of workouts is what I like the most. You can raft, cardio-box, participate in an obstacle course, race against other runners, waterski, or workout with bungee straps (not included), and there is much more!  The best part is the Wii balance board is NOT mandatory! For example on your obstacle course, or when you are running, you are not doing it on the Wii balance board so you don't have to worry about twisting your ankle and staying in one spot! The Wii balance board is required for some of the activities, but they are activities that don't require a lot of physical movement of your feet, just moreso leaning your weight and working on balance exercises. When you have completed your workout it will give you a graphic image that shows the intensity of your workout based on the time you completed the necessary task. I was a little "iffy" as to whether or not this workout was going to actually work you out, or whether it was going to be a fun way to pass your time and make you think that you worked out, however, I was pleasantly pleased when the next day, my muscles were "feeling" the challenge from the day before! The downside to this type of workout, as I touched on before, is that you have to make aure you are holding the Wii remote in the right position so the monitor can read your movements and you are not holding your position in a squat lunge any longer than you have to! All in all I would say that if you are getting bored with the same routine workout, Ea Sports Active-More Workouts is a great way to keep you motivated and keep that momentum going.

title: This is not your best option...
text:
I bought this for my Wii and I thought it was a pretty cool idea using the nunchuk in a leg strap the way they do in this. I was wrong.

The problem with the leg strap is that whoever engineered the design had no business doing so. I'm not terribly out of shape and my legs are the normal "circumfrence". However, when I put this leg strap onto ANY sort of clothing/fabric, it always slipped down during the exercises. I tried running shorts, jogging pants, jeans, casual shorts, anything and everything that would just stop the damned thing from slipping. NOTHING worked. It always slips and you can feel it slipping and it makes you really distracted from the exercise which is TERRIBLE for a good, focused workout. I highly reccomend waiting until they possibly improve the leg strap.

Also, the mechanics of the game are TERRIBLY flawed. On several of the exercises, I was doing EXACTLY what was asked of me by the game, but the trainer kept insisting that I wasn't doing it right and implored me to try again REPEATEDLY ad nauseum. You will become so frustrated that, if you're anything like me, you'll end up screaming to the TV "BUT THAT'S EXACTLY WHAT I'M DOING, YOU PIECE OF..." Well you get it.

The most difficult workouts to deal with are any of the ones involving lunges. It NEVER picks up on your movements, and then blames YOU for it. I recall one time a member of my family spent 5+ minutes simply trying to get it to recognize that she was doing the correct movements. It takes an act of god for this game to recognize and understand your movements. I wouldn't give this game the money or the time of day required to use it.

Buy any Wii workout game but this one and you'll be much better off.

title: An Amazing Movie, An Amazing Game
text:
This game is beyond words. The levels are so complex and detailed it's a wonder it was made by computer animation, rather than filmed live from the sets! The characters are exact replicas of their actor counterparts, and the voiceovers by the actors make it all that more realistic!
The complexity of the different battle techniques one can use are awesome. This is not a "press alt to kill" type game, it requires some thinking through and getting used to different attacks and parries. You will definitely not get bored with it. Also, the game is not going to be done in one day. The cool thing about it is that it stretches itself out. You're not going to defeat the whole game in one sitting and then wonder what to do next. It's a challenge, though not too difficult to handle. It's an addicting game that will bring you back every day to keep going.
Once you're done, you unlock cheats, interviews, new levels, and new characters! Also, you can repeat the whole game using characters that were locked before. For instance, you can try and see how Aragorn would fare getting the Ring to Mount Doom, or how Pippin would have survived the Paths of the Dead.
Amazing game, make sure to get this one! You'll be so glad you did!

title: Great Workout!
text:
So far, I have really enjoyed EA Active. I don't enjoy working out, so it's hard for me to find something to stick with. I was also nervous that this workout was goign to be boring, but that has not been the case. I have stuck with this workout longer than most. I realy enjoy the 30 day preset workouts. It's something a bit different each day, yet it still doesn't feel overwhelming. I'm pretty out of shape, but I leave each work out feeling like I've done something which is usually followed by a day being pretty sore. My past work outs were strictly aerobic, but this one works everything.

I do have a few complaints though...

1. I'm a pretty tall and lanky person, so the leg strap does not stay very well. I've found that I've needed to wear leggings or somtehing tighter to my skin instead of my preferred sweat pants.

2. During arm exercises involving both remotes and the resistance band, I often feel like the game reads the wii remote too sensitively and it often gets "stuck." It doesn't want to register my crunches so I find myself redoing them more times than needed. I think the game is too picky about how the wii remote is held for each exercise.

I own 4 or 5 wii workout games and this one is definitey my favorite. I think it has given me the most results and is easiest to stick to.

title: An Improved Sequel!!!
text:
The previous reviews convinced me to give EA: More Workouts a shot and I'm glad I did. I'm just completing my initial 20 workouts from the previous disk and this one is not only a welcome addition, I'm currently using it in unision with its predecessor for an awesome workout! They take more advantage of the fitness board (if you own one) and the pushups using the board was a pleasant surprise (but I still hate pushups!). It seems more focused on abdominal exercises which is one area I thought the previous game was lacking. The obstacle course combines a lot of jumping, hopping and movement and is much superior to the old track exercises. A few subtle changes you may not notice right away, but the calorie counter is now with four digits (and a comma) so you could do 9,999 calories if you are so inclined (that was a joke, you shouldn't come close to that level in a single workout)UPDATE: I went back and reviewed the original cartridge and it also has four calorie digits (just no comma) so this is a wash, you still don't need this many. Someone had mentioned the skiing was tricky and it seemed that way at first but now I am a veteran skiier and the trick seems to be the getting the legs to register your moves properly. Same with Squash, if you really accentuate the lunge it registers the movement every time.

The one thing I wish either cartridge would do is to just pick and play an activity of your choice. I know you can program custom workouts but most other cartridges (Wii fit, Wii resort, etc.) let you just go directly to an exercise and flail away. A small complaint but not a killer. EA Sports really has it together and except for the original boxing game on Wii Sports these are the only ones that make me sweat (literally). Excellent workout games!

title: Not a More Cardio Wii Fit, Rather a Disaster of a Product
text:
I am very enthusiastic about this category of product. I have used the Wii Fit at least weekly for over a year. The Wii Fit is great fun and is a superb stress management system, but is a poor cardio workout. So when I read reviews of EA Active as a more cardio Wii Fit, I bought it.

I have used Active almost daily for over a month and it is a very disappointing product. Active has many, many problems but the biggest is that Active does not deal with data coming from the nunchuk and wiimote effectively. For example, if you run at a constant pace, every few seconds you will get alternating instructions such as "too slow" and "perfect" as the Active is not interpreting the data properly. This also creates a frequent lag between your actions and the result on the screen. This becomes very annoying in the timing games (tennis, baseball, etc.). Instead of "just working," like Wii Sports Tennis, you change the timing your swing to adjust for the lag. Active has you exaggerate your actions during the exercises (e.g. "point the numchuk at the ground at the conclusion of the exercise") to compensate. As a result you need to concentrate on complying with these exaggerated actions to complete the exercise. And no matter how hard to concentrate you will never always get it right, resulting in Active nagging you and wasting your time. So while you should be getting in a positive frame of mind with an exercise product, with Active you end up getting frustrated with the poor product quality. Not fun.

There are many, many other shortcomings, but I will mention a few. The workouts are geared towards women. Like most men, I need cardio and abdominal/core work. You will not get much of either with Active. Workouts emphasize toning arms and legs, typically not an issue for men. What passes for cardio is high impact jumping. You will jump over 100 times a workout. So unless you are under 25 and/or a runner be prepared for sore knees. If you dig deep you can find one low impact (and even lower cardio) workout and the ability to customize workouts. However, it takes several minutes to set up a customized workout and it does not save them. So no cardio either.

There are plenty of other shortcomings - a really lame Me creator, Sega Genesis era graphics, balance board integration an afterthought - but you get the idea. On the positive side, Active has helped my wife get some exercise while the kids are home for the summer. In addition, the 30 day challenge provides some structure for those who are not self motivated. Our three kids, who love anything Wii, tried Active a couple times and dumped it.

We own Fifa 09 for the Wii. EA knows how to make games for the Wii. I am not sure what happened with the is product, but save your money, it is a disaster.

title: Worked great right up until it didn't.
text:
This was a Christmas gift from "Santa" and I have absolutely LOVED it, but after continued use it wears out fast and have become more and more disappointed.

First, the good. The picture and color quality is fantastic! I never new my old NES games could look so amazing. Nearly all my old games and controllers work perfectly with this little machine. Battletoads, Castlevania, Mario, Contra, Classic controllers, NES Max, NES Advantage...all work great.

Now the bad: 1. The biggest problem is in how tightly the pin connector holds cartridges. After only a few days of swapping out games the system became a lot more finicky with the cartridges. Any minor bump of the table it was on and the system froze up. I have little kids so I was having my games reset a lot. After looking at it closer, the reasoning for it freezing up is likely because (as it turns out) the pins were getting pulled out by process of changing cartridges. Yes you read that right...the normal process of changing out games was actually breaking it (see picture). After a while I felt the system was becoming just as finicky as my old NES was. It became very frustrating. Second, I can't seem to get any PowerPad games to work. The games will load up, some times but only if they are on a split cartridge like World Track/Mario/Duck Hunt...and even then the power pad is never registered. I was never really big into those titles anyway so it was no big deal to me, but that might be a deal breaker or some. Finally, for SOME games the audio is off a bit. This variedfrom game to game. Some I could hardly tell anything different while others had a rather clear problem. Collecting coins in Mario (for example) just sounds...off. I don't know how else to describe it. It's not bad...just off. For me, I didn't mind as much about the audio difference. For the price it was a minor distraction at best.

The price and all the other positives seemed to outweigh most of these negatives for me until the pin connector started to have issues (after not even two weeks of use, mind you). If you have just a couple games that you plan to play then I would recommend this. If you're wanting to breath new life into their old NES stuff collecting dust in their attic then this is an inexpensive option that will work with modern HD tvs...just don't swap out games a lot because it apparently isn't built for that kind of abuse and will go down hill quickly with that behavior.

title: Great Fitness game
text:
I'm not fit AT ALL, but I wanted to get started on being healthier. Working out is easier for me than changing my diet, so I'm starting with that. I bought the Wii Fit, but wasn't really motivated to use it often, but I also didn't want to give up on being healthier/TRYING to lose weight, so I got EA Sports Active: More Workouts. I LOVE this game. I really like the six-week challenge option. I'm just on week one, but already have used this more than any of the other fitness games I've purchased. I'm a plan person, and I like that the 6-week challenge sets up a changeable schedule for you, so I know which days I have to plan my after work running around to fit in working out. I'm a robot, what can I say. I've also realized that I'm VERY competitive, and the competition aspect of squash, the obstacle course, and the beach run (the only ones I've encountered so far), interspersed with the classic exercise routines really keeps me motivated to finish and also makes me look forward to my next workout.

I also like that it's compatible with my balance board, which so far, it doesn't use alot, but the exercises it does use it for, I get great feedback. I have it set on beginner, and I still work up a sweat & definitely feel as if I've accomplished something when I'm finished. I'm going to take it up a level in a week or so (pray for me).

I got this game, which doesn't come with the accessories (leg holster for the nunchuk & a resistance band) and a non-EA Sports accessories pack for about $5 less than the official one at Target, which seems pretty sturdily made. I'm going to partly measure my success by how much more give I have on that leg strap, which is now (through NO fault of it's own), hanging on by velcro teeth.

Overall, I'm excited about working out again, and this game has really helped me get going. I definitely recommend it.

title: A controller to make Luigi jump for joy
text:
This is the one to get! The aesthetic is a match to the Luigi Wiimote, though the buttons are colored per the original Gamecube controller, unlike the PDP version which actually matched the Luigi Wiimote paintjob exactly.
What is so great about this controller is that it feels great. It has close to the same shape as the original Gamecube controller, which fits nice in the hand and gives you access to all the face buttons, which look and feel identical to the original Gamecube buttons except for the back shoulder buttons, which are shorter and easier to press -- a huge plus for games like Smash where input timing is everything and finger strain is inevitable. The d-pad may also be a bit larger, also a nice touch. I have not played too much with the turbo mode but it seems to be customizable on a per-button basis (or at the least you assign the turbo function to a specific button).
This will also work with any game that is Classic Controller Pro enabled -- see the list here: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_games_that_use_the_Classic_Controller
All in all, a wonderful controller that is a joy to use!

title: Everything you need to know!
text:
If you've always loved GameCube Controllers and you're deciding between this controller and SuperSmash Edition GameCube Controllers with adapter, BUY THESE!
If you have GameCube Controllers already, just buy the Super Smash Adapter but *NOTE* that Adapter ONLY WORKS on the Wii Smash and Wii U Smash Brothers. The Adapter DOES NOT support your original GameCube Controller on any other Wii U game..

Restrictions:
So far the only Multi-Player Games that are on the LIST below are Lego games that don't allow Hori Battle Pads but every other game will. Only VERY FEW games won't let you play with this controller and they're mostly Single Player so just use a GamePad! This registers as a Classic Controller even though it's mandatory to ONLY connect to the Wii Remote Plus/Wii Remote.

List:
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Wii_U_games_that_use_the_Wii_U_Pro_Controller

NOTE:
This requires you to connect the controller in to WII Remote. If you want to save $$$ and don't care about a faulty Wii Remote in terms of Motion Control, go on Nintendo website and purchase a refurbished $15 Wii Remote because you only really need these to power up this amazing controller! You can connect these to cheap 3rd party Wii Remotes as well, worth.
If you care about Motion Control (very few games require this) I bought 2 Mario Remote Plus for $60 total ($30 each) +Free S/H on Amazon if you're lucky!

The feels on this control are real, a little lighter and may seem a little bit smaller than the original (can't confirm yet) in terms of size but a solid build regardless in terms of grip and decently sturdy.
Buttons feel solid, need to be broken in for picky users but still great.
The L and R buttons are shallow in comparison but still viable for Super Smash and every other game!
Cord is pretty lengthy considering you only have to connect it to any Wii Remote (even 3rd-party ones)

I couldn't stand playing Super Smash on the GamePad or Pro Controller that's the main reason why I bought these, now I can play it with all my other Wii U games (Super Smash, Mario Kart 8, Bayonetta 2, etc. etc. etc. etc. etc.)

Unless you're a PROFESSIONAL gamer which is very rare, I recommend getting the Smash Controller with Adapter so you don't end up doubting your loss in tournaments? Corded is always better but even on the Hori Battle Pads, there is literally no room to even tell if there's any input lag (maybe if Wii Remote's in low battery)?

Hori I believe is licensed from Nintendo as well.

Cons: Nothing really, the price ($30, DON'T PAY $40+) and the fact I can use this controller on nearly every game is so worth it.
Ask questions if you have any, I'll try to provide specifics if requested.

Also plan on buying the only made in Japan.. PIKACHU HORI PAD!

Note: Controllers aren't region-locked unless it's a GamePad!

Now the real thing that I find awesome with this setup is that I can run a full desktop pc 3.5" hard drive. I chose a western digital black 2TB 7,200 rpm drive for the performance and mainly the quality of western digital hard drives. It has been noticeably slightly faster in everything it does, especially initial loads of video games. I have 47 video games and about a dozen apps currently installed on the hard drive and still have 820 gb left! I also really liked how the wall outlet is what powers the hard drive, not the ps4's power supply. Theoretically the PS4's power supply should last longer and generate less heat, because the load needed from the factory hard drive is no longer there. In fact, this was a huge decision in why I bought this in the first place.
The only thing I think they could improve was maybe somehow utilize the ps4's cooling fan, or a seperate fan to cool the hard drive, because as installed there is no air flow going by the hard drive to cool it down. Not sure if this will be an issue at all, but as a consumer I would have like to see something done for a cooling aspect is all.

title: Beautiful, relaxing single player and console-to-console multiplayer game
text:
From the adult single player perspective, this is the most involved version of Animal Crossing to date. Customization is virtually limitless and it introduces the option of terraforming the land itself. The ways you can build up your island stretch beyond the imagination. New Horizons introduces crafting, seasonal items and recipes, download-based events that last longer than one day so they really feel like holidays, and advanced character customization right from the beginning. I'll break down the pros and cons at the end of my review.

I think there is some confusion, especially for people new to the series, regarding how multiplayer works.
Animal Crossing has always been a ONE town/island game, with the option for up to 3 more players to share that land, since the idea is that you'd be building your oasis together. Unfortunately the co-op in this version is lackluster, especially since the Switch is marketed as a more social console than others Nintendo has released in the past. The multiplayer in a single town is, plain and simple, not worth it. Like others have said, you can really only play follow the leader and collect things together. It kinda defeats the purpose of true multiplayer mode, which is much more comprehensive in the console-to-console visiting (as it has been in the past as well). The true fun in multiplayer for ACNH is in visiting other islands entirely, seeing how they have built and organized their land, and exchanging exclusive fruits and rare items with each other (not to mention hitting each other endlessly with nets). If you have multiple consoles in your house or have friends with their own Switch and copy of the game, you'll find LOTS of enjoyment in the multiplayer.

PROS:
- Character customization is great. Skin tone is finally a choice, alongside many hairstyles and colors which become unlockable over time. Many basics are included right from the beginning and can be changed whenever you'd like.
- Able Sisters is a true boutique. Every day they have a large stock of clothing, including many color variants. You can also layer multiple facial accessories.
- Designing is a joy. The designer feature seems to "read" what shapes and colors you use and will round out sharp edges. This means any user-designed paths, stones, and clothing will blend in seamlessly with the soft graphics of the game. You can choose from different styles of clothing while you design, such as sweaters, robes, bowler hats, and beanies. Additionally, there is now an option for transparent patterns. No more having 4 different stepping stone designs for every season so the grass around your rocks will blend in with the natural grass. There is also a "face paint" option, which is very useful for equipping your character with eyebrows, freckles, etc.
- Nook Miles ticket islands are worthwhile to work for, and allow you access to more crafting resources that you may have exhausted out of your own island for the day. They also have a chance to spawn rare creatures, Bell rocks, foreign fruits, and hybrid flowers.
- The graphics have received a huge update. Everything in the game, including returning items, has a new model and looks better than ever. Wind rustles trees, flowers, and even items that have hanging bits, such as the clothing racks.
- Your storage system is automatically built into your home, and home design is streamlined into a drag and drop menu for easy decorating.
- Being able to put any item outdoors and build pathways has transformed the possibilities in this game. You can make so many things: trading booths, actual gardens, shop stands, playgrounds, cafes, spas, raffles, relay races, you name it. I've seen an incredible amount of creativity in the first week of release.
- You can choose where your new villagers will move, and move any building at any time, save for the plaza and Resident Services within it. There is a cost involved but it's well worth it if you hate where something is placed.
- So far I have not yet reached the cap on constructing inclines and bridges. You can make a bunch.

CONS:
- Terraforming takes a bit to unlock and can be finicky to navigate. You may think you're standing on the correct tile to place a path or build a cliff, but you'll be pushed to another tile, have to erase, and try again. Understanding where you are in space is just a little more difficult because the layout of your island looks a lot less geometric than it did in the past, but overall that is still a positive. Just makes terraforming a bit harder.
- In the 3DS New Leaf: Welcome Amiibo version, scanning an Amiibo card would allow you to replace any resident villager with the one on your card, and they would move in the next day. In this version, scanning a card will put the villager in your campsite, but you must invite them to move in THREE times before they will agree. It just seems like a bit of work, since any random villager you find on a Nook Miles Island will move in the very next day after you ask them.
- This is my big one: Blathers' museum, while changed drastically to be incredibly beautiful, no longer displays facts for donated creatures. Reading a sign will just give you the name of the creature and donor. To learn about a creature, you need to have it in your inventory and give it to Blathers under the request to learn more. This feels like a huge hit to the museum which is already lacking features. It seemed like they removed the one main reason to visit.
- No sign of my favorite NPCs, Katrina (fortune teller) and Brewster (cafe owner). Hopefully, though, there are plans to implement them at a later date, as the game receives regular updates.

Overall, this is a staple in any casual gamer's collection, a great intro for anyone new to the series, and something pleasant to pick up whenever and wherever, regardless of whether you have countless hours or just a few minutes. Give it a try!

title: Great effort but...
text:
...there are some definite issues with this. Obviously this is meant to do the same thing as the Wii Fit did, which was give you a solid workout. This EA Sports Active does do. As most others said on here, DO NOT try this thing out on hard at first because you will feel about dead afterwards. Try to get the grasp of it before you do that.

One thing I complained about the Wii Fit was the lack of strenuous activity outside of maybe a handful of exercises. Most of them to be honest were more balance-oriented and yoga-based. Active on the other hand, focuses on strength and cardio. The only thing it doesn't have, surprisingly, is any ab exercises which I find very strange. The Wii fit I thought did a great job of the jacknife so I was really surprised there was not any crunches, sit ups, etc.

My other complaints are these. While the game comes with resistance bands for the strength exercises, I found them useless and didn't get much of a workout at all. If you want a real work out upper body from active, I highly suggest getting real resistance bands from Golden Gym or other brands. Once I did that, in no time, I felt some real results in my upper body.

The only other complaint I have for Active is that there are a couple activities at times, where you're doing the exercise 100 percent correctly and a message appears, saying you aren't doing anything. The ones that I've had this problem tend to be the curls and on one occasion the regular lunge. Considering the release date of this, I really find it interesting that they didn't have this game compatible with the wii motion because I think if it was, it would get rid of this problem. Another problem with this, is that if you don't do it right, the game will sit at a stand still until you do it right, so eventually I got annoyed and finished without the game knowing and skipping the exercise. Personally, I think if after a certain amount of time, it should move onto the next rep.

Besides those gripes though, this is a great experience. I feel a lot more toned than I did from the Wii Fit and I also work a much bigger sweat as well. So if you want something a bit more challenging than the Wii Fit I highly suggest this product. I just hope the next time EA produces something like this, they include ab exercises and tighten the sensitivity, which I'm sure they will since the Motion Plus is now available.

title: Great Animal Crossing game, but not as “family-friendly” as Nintendo asserts!
text:
There is a lot to love about this game, but Nintendo has made a lot of bad choices. In this review I will start by addressing what is wonderful and then address the BIG mistakes.

To start, if you love Animal Crossing, then you will love playing this game. The story, though original harkens back to the story from older versions of this game. That is to say, human you finds yourself welcomed to a new home in a new land where Tom Nook promptly informs you that you are in debt to him. Classic characters join the cast and there is a lot of familiar gameplay. You will be catching bugs and fishing and shooting presents out of the sky.

There are many improvements over previous titles. The graphics are quite impressive: leaves rustle in the wind, fish you catch and display swim around their tanks, you can turn your in-game Switch on and off! They are certainly not attempting to make realistic graphics but the world feels far more like a real place than ever before! Crafting is also deeper and more rich and while breaking tools can certainly be an annoyance, it’s not as bad as other games (I’m looking at you, Breath of the Wild). There are some fun multiplayer and online components. Couch co-op with family members is fun and light. Visiting mystery islands is a great way to expand access to resources.

All of these things are great, but there are some ENORMOUS missteps by Nintendo in this game. First of all (and you’ve likely heard about this one), you can only have one island per Switch. That means everyone on your Switch shares an island. I would be fine if it was one island per copy of the game as $60 is a relatively small price to pay to play the game privately, but if you want your own island, you need to buy a $300 Switch AND another copy of the game. Also, the first player to create a character becomes the “resident representative” and makes the majority of choices about building placement and is responsible for progressing island growth. This is extremely frustrating! At one point you need to gather various resources to move your island forward and a secondary resident can’t even hand in the resources. There is no way to change the resident representative short of restarting the game. There is absolutely no warning that this will happen and so by letting my child create a character first, I have made island progression less convenient.

The other poor choice by Nintendo is the lack of online back ups of save data. The primary reason I pay for Switch Online is to have online back ups. This is not a competitive multiplayer game so cheaters who take advantage of changing internally clocks and fudging save data really only hurt themselves. Additionally, there are other ways to prevent this kind of cheating. These decisions by Nintendo really make me question if they are making decisions with their core player community in mind.

To sum up, if you are a Switch owner who is the only user of your Switch and you like Animal Crossing, this game is perfect...it would actually be four and a half or five stars. If you share your Switch, think carefully about whether this title is right for you or whether it will strain rather than build relationships in your house.

title: a mixed bag
text: There are a lot of good things about the Thing, but there are also quite a few blunders. First off the game feels rushed, there is so much about it that lacks polish or feels looked over. The boss battles for instance just feel thrown together. The design of the boss "things" look nice, but there is very little action in fighting them. Plus they are hard! They aren't hard in the challenging sense, they are hard in the cheap/unfair sense. It could be that I am playing the game horribly, but I don't think so. Being hit by a boss the second I enter a room with zero reaction time is just plain cheap. My main problem about this game is, Cheap Deaths!!!! There are just so many! Possibly more cheap hits then deaths though. Coming in contact with a small fire seems to take a large chunk of your life away, which is just as frusterating as can be. Also the control is a little sluggish and the control layout can be confusing during stressful situations. There were also times where the game would freeze up on me, usually at the worst possible times to. That made me very unhappy. It's mostly just filled with bugs like that, they don't really ruin the game, they just make you want to smash the controller against the wall. But enough bad stuff. I really did like this game, despite the three star rating. The graphics (while not up to current PS2 standards) for the most part are good, there aren't any eyesores in the game, but nothing to really get excited about either. The blood effects and all the gore look really good though, plus a great looking head shot effect. The voice acting is good with excessive profanity and all. Having a squad to control is great, though you are alone sometimes. They can prove to be very helpful, though it's kind of a bummer to watch them mutate. It's great to have NPC help, but sometimes they can be way to dumb! Sometimes they just get stuck on a box or will just stand there when they are supposed to follow you. They are good when it comes to fighting though. There are some great action scenes in the game. A lot of the time it can make your heart race while fighting off hordes of 'thing' things. To sum it up, the game is just really cool. Though, with a little more time in development it could have been far better, which is a little disapointing. Fans of the movie should check it out, it is pretty faithful to the movies atmosphere. Otherwise rent it.

title: Needs more variety
text:

title: The greatest controller of all time is back
text:
If you have any skepticism concerning this controller's status as a third party product, allow me to ease your worries. The Hori Battle Pad is one of the greatest controllers I have ever used, and whatever downsides there are to be had with it pale in comparison to the positives.
Hori is a Japanese manufacturer that has close ties with Nintendo, and they've been making officially licensed accessories for Nintendo's consoles for decades now. In fact, one of their N64 controllers served as the basis for which Nintendo made their Gamecube controller. Their products, ranging from controllrs to fight sticks to cases and sleeve covers, are of high build quality, and the Battle Pad is no exception.
First, let's get the obvious comparisons out of the way. This is the closest you're gonna get to a genuine Gamecube style classic controller without one of those Mayflash adapters. The look and button layout are identical to the original, but with a few additions (and subtractions). What most people will immediately notice is that the controller has a second Z button, and that's as glorious as you'd expect. Adding a whole extra button input really does take the Gamecube controller to a whole new level, allowing it to tackle more modern games that utilize as much as they can. They also added a home and select button, which is a nice addition. There's a turbo function as well, but I never use it and have no plans to.
The biggest improvement besides the addition of a second Z is the larger D-pad. Smash players won't care too much about this but since I bought this with the intention of using it for more than just Smash, it's a really, REALLY good change. It's a bit stiff, but it's as fluid and responsive as the real deal, something I've never thought would be possible with a third party controller, which are notorious for having faulty d-pads. I tested it in a game of Super Mario Bros. on the virtual console and while playing Injustice, and it felt just as easy to use and responsive (while a bit stiff as mentioned) if I was using one made by Ninty. I never dropped a directional input once.
Most of you are probably reading this since you want it for Smash, and while I highly recommend it, there are some things to note first. The biggest flaw is the removal of the analog triggers from the Gamecube controller (and original Classic Controller). I got used to it, but doing shields and evades felt weird at first, since you can't really rest your finger on it as much or you risk shielding at the wrong place, considering it's a digital button. It's not super sensitive where merely touching it sets it off, but rather it's knowing there's no leeway for when you press it. It's hinged, so it still feels like a trigger instead of a plain button like on the Classic Controller Pro or Dualshock 2. The rumble feature is also removed, considering it's literally a classic controller, which doesn't support rumble. It makes the controller lighter, which I prefer, but if you want a heavier controller, consider opening it up and putting a weight in it. The most glaring issue other than the triggers for me is the analog sticks. They feel too light, and I find it hard to slow to walk in games like Monster Hunter or Smash. Again, not a huge problem, but it's annoying to have to hold the thumbstick at a VERY specific distance to walk.
Besides these three flaws, I have nothing but praise for it. The buttons feel like the real thing, the extra Z button is appreciated, and since it's a Classic Controller, you can use it for other Wii U games! Playing Mario Kart 8 with it feels divine (with steering being identical to the Gamecube, oddly. Maybe the thumbstick only has problems with certain games?), Injustice feels much better than using any other controller (which is high praise considering I've also played it on PS4), and even playing Bayonetta 2 with it feels like a lot of fun (although I wish it had fully rebindable controls). It feels great in Smash too, and I'd say in a non-tournament setting it makes an excellent replacement for the Gamecube Adapter. While I miss the analog triggers, it's a small price to pay for a controller that not only delivers, but improves in several key ways. Highly recommended!

Pros:
+The Gamecube experiance on the Wii U
+More button inputs, including an extra Z
+Larger D-Pad
+Compatible with any game that can use a Classic Controller
+High build quality, comfortable

Cons:
-Digital triggers instead of analog
-No rumble
-Slightly weird analog stick
-Functional but useless turbo

Either or:
•Lighter weight
•Wireless (plugs into Wiimote)
•Slightly wider to accomodate Home and Plus / Minus buttons

Overall: 4.5 / 5

title: COULD HAVE BEEN A CONTENDER, instead it's just a chump.
text:
PROS:
-Video upscaling to 4K is ok. I'm using an LG OLED65B6P late 2016 panel. A lot has to do with the TV processing and cleaning up the signal. To say the least it's passable but far from the quality of a Nes Classic, a Retropie, or a RetroUSB AVS.
-The Device accepts ANY old NES controllers with ease. It's nice that they have also included some OK at best controllers in the box. They actually play well, just feel light and kinda hollow and light.
-Everything you need is in the box, and there's even an included HDMI cable to get started. That's pretty nice.
The system is pretty well built feeling, its compact, and the cartridge slot doesn't grab too tightly for it being a top loader.
Instructions explain everything out of the box, and are easy to understand.
-The company backing the device stands by it's warranty and I hear the customer support is legendary.

CONS:
-This thing has a serious problem with audio playback with some carts. Notable Castlevanias, MegaMan2, SpyVsSpy, Journey to Silius, etc. In some cases the game audio is so torn up and mis-handled by the unit, it makes the games seriously unplayable. I'm noticing this with newer titled cartridges that are usually uncommon titles. Its PRETTY bad, and is one of the reasons why I dropped the score 2 stars.
-Reproduction carts, and some of the new PCB styles crash horribly. I have a good collection of Repro carts from Sweet Home, River City Ransom 2, Splatterhouse, New Ghostbusters 2, Summer Carnival 92, and Crisis Force. The system will boot some of these titles, others it just will fail miserably. While this is not a HUGE deal, my toaster NES and AVS play these games flawlessly. I can only guess why this happening.
-There's no updating the system for firmware, or being able to do anything else other than a Nintendo clone. Again, not a huge deal, but it would be nice if there was a way to increase compatibility with specific carts, fix audio playback, and maybe add on other features.

REVIEW UPDATE 02092017 : If you use a Game Genie with repro carts, it seems to improve stability of some repro carts and audio issues. It MUST be a proper OG Game Genie, top or front slot loader unit.

Overall, it's a good go-to Nes game player on the cheap that will get your games in semi-crisp digital glory up on your HDMI monitor. It's not perfect with rendering audio with a good 20-40% of the NES library, but it generally gets the job done. I could see this being a useful device with travelling to shows, or coming over to a friend's house for game night. Just don't bring any incompatible games with it, and you'll be fine. Is it worth the price? Well you get what you pay for. It's ALL IN THE BOX, and again generally does it's job, just not that great. The bigger problem is the wanting for it to be MORE than what it is. Only if this thing had it's problems fixed, it would literally fly off the shelf, and be in every NES collector's media centers. For the meantime, the RetroUSB makes this thing look stupid. Hate to say it, the 8-Bit HD Entertainment System could have been a contender! Pictured below are times when I hucked my controller at the ground for it constantly locking up on some Repro titles, and pixel accuracy on a 4K Oled panel.
